### Watch: Hurt in an Accident? When You Need Legal Representation

### Common questions
If no one was injured beyond very minor soreness that resolved quickly, no one saw a doctor, property damage is modest, and the other driver's insurance accepted fault, you probably don't need a lawyer. A competent adult can handle a straightforward property-damage claim directly with the insurance company.
Under Texas's 51% bar rule, your recovery is barred if you are found 51% or more at fault for the accident. If the other driver's insurance adjuster is disputing fault, you could be fighting this rule without legal experience, which is one of the key reasons the post recommends talking to an attorney before speaking with any insurer.
The post strongly advises against accepting any settlement offer without first understanding it. Once you sign the release, the case is settled forever — if a soft-tissue injury develops into chronic pain months later, you cannot reopen the claim. At minimum, get a free consultation before signing anything.
According to the post, a contingency-fee attorney — typically charging 33% of the recovery — identifies every available insurance policy, carefully maps fault to defend against the 51% bar, negotiates reductions on medical bills at resolution, and handles all insurance communications so you don't accidentally say something that hurts your case. On serious injury cases, that work often produces a net recovery higher than what an unrepresented victim would receive.

## The Trucker's Logbook That Could Win Your Case. and Why You Have Six Months to Get It
Source: https://nalawtx.com/blog/fmcsa-hours-of-service-violations-your-texas-truck-accident

If a fatigued 18-wheeler driver hit you in Texas, federal records prove how long that driver had been behind the wheel. But those records disappear after six months. Here's what hours-of-service violations mean for your claim, and exactly what needs to happen right now.
By Vu Nguyen, Founder & Managing Partner · Updated November 2, 2026
A trucker's electronic logbook (ELD) records every minute of driving time and can prove a driver violated federal hours-of-service rules before hitting you. But federal regulations only require carriers to keep that data for six months. If a commercial truck hit you in Texas, that six-month window is your most urgent deadline.
- Federal law (49 C.F.R. Part 395) limits property-carrying truck drivers to 11 hours of driving after 10 consecutive hours off duty.
- ELD data is automatically recorded and tamper-resistant, but carriers only must keep it for six months — after that it may be gone.
- Violating hours-of-service rules can trigger 'negligence per se,' making the violation automatic evidence of negligence under Texas law.
- Texas's two-year filing deadline (Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 16.003) is separate from the six-month evidence deadline — don't confuse them.
Picture a loaded semi rolling south on I-45 toward Houston at 2 a.m. The driver has been on the road for 13 hours. Federal law says he should have stopped at 11. Nobody flagged it. His company needed the delivery on time. And then he drifted into your lane near the Beltway 8 interchange.
The crash report will say "driver error." What it won't say, unless someone digs for it, is that the driver was operating illegally, in violation of federal hours-of-service rules that exist for one reason: to keep exhausted truckers off the road. That distinction matters enormously for your claim. It's the difference between a standard negligence case and one where the trucker's employer may have handed you proof of fault on a silver platter.

### What Hours-of-Service Rules Actually Say
The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (the FMCSA, the federal agency that regulates commercial trucking) sets mandatory limits on how long a truck driver can work before stopping to rest. These aren't suggestions. They're federal law, codified in 49 C.F.R. Part 395.
For property-carrying drivers (the 18-wheelers you see on I-10 and the Gulf Freeway every day), the core limits are:
- 11-hour driving limit: A driver may not drive more than 11 hours after 10 consecutive hours off duty.
- 14-hour on-duty window: A driver may not drive beyond the 14th hour after coming on duty, even if they took breaks during that time.
- 30-minute break requirement: After 8 cumulative hours of driving, a driver must take a 30-minute break.
- 60/70-hour weekly limit: A driver can't drive after accumulating 60 hours on duty in 7 consecutive days, or 70 hours in 8 days.
Every one of those rules has a paper trail. And increasingly, a digital one.

### ELDs: The Black Box in the Cab
Since December 2017, most commercial carriers operating in interstate commerce have been required to equip their trucks with an Electronic Logging Device, or ELD. An ELD automatically records driving time by connecting directly to the truck's engine. It's tamper-resistant by design. The driver can't conveniently "forget" to log a stretch of highway the way they could with an old paper logbook.
ELD data captures when the engine was running, the vehicle's speed and location at regular intervals, when the driver switched duty status, and whether any manual edits were made to the record. In a crash case, this data is extraordinarily powerful. It shows a court exactly how long that driver was moving before impact.
ELD data doesn't lie. A paper logbook can be falsified. An ELD connected to the engine's ECM records what the truck actually did, minute by minute.
There's one critical catch: under FMCSA regulations, carriers are only required to retain ELD records for six months. After that window closes, the data may be gone. Trucking companies know this. Some don't go out of their way to preserve records once the retention period expires.
Six months sounds like a long time. It isn't. Between recovering from your injuries, dealing with insurance calls, and figuring out what happened, that window closes fast.

### What "Negligence Per Se" Means for Your Claim
In a standard negligence case, you have to show four things: the defendant owed you a duty, they breached it, the breach caused your injuries, and you suffered real damages. Proving breach, that the driver actually did something wrong, takes work.
Hours-of-service violations can change that through a legal theory called negligence per se. Here's the plain-English version: when a defendant violates a safety statute or regulation designed to prevent the kind of harm you suffered, Texas courts can treat that violation as automatic evidence of negligence. You don't have to separately argue that driving fatigued was unreasonable. The law already decided it was.
Texas courts have applied this doctrine in trucking cases where FMCSA hours-of-service regulations were violated. The regulation exists to protect other drivers on the road. You're a driver on the road who got hurt. The logic is direct.
That doesn't mean you win automatically. You still have to prove the violation happened and connect it to your crash. But it shifts the conversation significantly, especially in front of a Houston jury that understands what it's like to share the road with an 80,000-pound truck.

### Paper Logs, Falsified Records, and What to Look For
Not every truck is equipped with a compliant ELD. Older vehicles, short-haul exemptions, and some agricultural haulers still use paper logs. And even with ELDs in place, fraud happens. Drivers operating for high-pressure carriers sometimes manipulate their duty status, logging themselves as "off duty" or "in the sleeper berth" while still driving, or split driving time across multiple logbooks.
Signs of a falsified or suspicious logbook include:
- Logs showing perfectly round-numbered hours that never vary
- Driving times that don't match fuel receipts, toll records, or GPS data
- Missing logs for dates before the crash
- Edits to electronic records made after the fact, with no legitimate explanation
- Discrepancies between the ELD data and what the driver reported to police
An attorney working a truck accident claim will typically issue a preservation demand, a formal legal letter telling the trucking company to preserve all ELD data, paper logs, dispatch records, and communications related to the driver, within days of being retained. Without that letter, records that should exist may not be there when you need them.

### The Carrier Can Be on the Hook Too
Trucking companies have their own federal obligations. They're required to audit driver logs, monitor hours compliance, and refuse to dispatch a driver who is over their hours limit. When a carrier ignores known violations, or builds a culture where drivers feel pressured to push past legal limits to meet delivery deadlines, the company itself can bear liability alongside the driver.
This matters because individual truck drivers often don't carry enough personal assets to fully compensate someone with serious injuries. The carrier, on the other hand, is required under federal law to carry substantial liability insurance: a minimum of $750,000 for most freight, and $1,000,000 or more for hazardous materials. Establishing the company's role in the violation is often central to making sure there's enough coverage to address what happened to you.
When a carrier's dispatch records show the driver was given an impossible schedule, that's not just driver error anymore. That's a company decision.

#### What a Dispatcher's Records Can Show
Dispatch logs and trip assignment records can reveal that the carrier knew, or should have known, the driver couldn't complete the route legally within their available hours. If a Houston-based carrier sent a driver from Dallas to Laredo and back with a 4-hour delivery window that only worked if the driver skipped their mandatory rest period, that's in the records. So are the communications: texts, load assignment apps, email threads.
These documents are also subject to the six-month (and sometimes shorter) retention cycles. The preservation demand has to cover all of it.

### How This Plays Out in a Harris County Courtroom
Most truck accident claims in Houston fall under the jurisdiction of Harris County District Courts. If your case proceeds to litigation, the ELD data and logbook records become exhibits. An expert witness, often a former FMCSA compliance officer or a certified accident reconstructionist, will walk the jury through what the data shows.
Jurors in Harris County understand trucking. Houston is one of the largest freight hubs in the country. I-10, I-69, and the Port of Houston move an enormous volume of commercial traffic every day. That context cuts both ways: jurors understand the industry's pressures, but they also understand that a driver who's been behind the wheel for 13 hours is not safe at any speed.
Under Texas law, specifically the modified comparative fault rule, your recovery gets reduced by your own percentage of fault, if any. But a trucking company arguing that a driver who violated federal regulations is only partly to blame faces a difficult case. Documented hours-of-service violations are hard to explain away in front of a jury.

### Texas's Two-Year Deadline, and Why You Shouldn't Wait That Long
Under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003, you generally have two years from the date of your injury to file a personal injury lawsuit. Two years feels like plenty of time until it isn't.
In truck accident cases specifically, the evidence clock runs faster than the legal clock. ELD data: six months. Some carriers purge dispatch records on similar cycles. Dashcam footage from the truck cab or trailing cameras is often overwritten within weeks. Surveillance footage from businesses near the crash site, a gas station on the Katy Freeway, a commercial lot near the Ship Channel, disappears even faster.
The two-year statute of limitations tells you the last possible day to file. It says nothing about when evidence stops being available. Those are two very different deadlines, and confusing them is one of the most damaging mistakes a crash victim can make.
If you were hit by a commercial truck anywhere in the Houston metro, Harris County, Fort Bend, Montgomery, Galveston, Brazoria, the safest move is to talk to an attorney before the six-month ELD window closes. A preservation demand costs you nothing to send. Failing to send one can cost you your strongest evidence.

### What to Do Right Now If a Truck Hit You
You don't need to understand the FMCSA's regulatory framework to protect yourself. But there are a few practical steps that matter immediately:
- Get the truck's DOT number and carrier name. It's usually on the door or the cab. Photograph it. This identifies the carrier and lets an attorney pull their safety inspection history from the FMCSA database.
- Request the police report. Texas Department of Transportation crash reports document the commercial vehicle information and any violations cited at the scene.
- Write down everything you remember about the driver's behavior. Was the driver confused? Did they mention being tired? Did they react slowly? This goes in your notes, not on social media.
- Don't give a recorded statement to the trucking company's insurer. Their adjuster's job is not to help you. See our post on how adjusters operate after a crash for more on this.
- Talk to a truck accident attorney fast. Not because the legal deadline is close, but because the evidence deadline is.
Our 18-wheeler accident practice page covers the full scope of what these cases involve. If you want to talk through the specific facts of what happened to you, a free case review is the right first step.
This article provides general information about Texas law, not legal advice for your specific situation. Every case is different. If you've been injured in Houston or anywhere in Texas, talk with a licensed attorney about the facts of yours. Free case review here, or call (713) 842-9442.

### Common questions
Under FMCSA regulations, carriers are only required to retain ELD records for six months. After that window closes, the data may be gone. A formal preservation demand letter sent by an attorney can require the company to hold that data before it is purged.
Negligence per se means that when a defendant violates a safety regulation designed to prevent the kind of harm you suffered, Texas courts can treat that violation as automatic evidence of negligence. If a trucker broke federal hours-of-service rules before hitting you, you may not have to separately argue that driving fatigued was unreasonable — the law already decided it was.
Yes. Carriers are federally required to audit driver logs, monitor hours compliance, and refuse to dispatch an over-hours driver. When a company pressures drivers to push past legal limits, it can bear liability alongside the driver. Federal law also requires carriers to carry minimum liability insurance of $750,000 for most freight and $1,000,000 or more for hazardous materials.
Under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003, you generally have two years from the date of your injury to file a personal injury lawsuit. However, critical evidence like ELD data disappears after six months, and dashcam footage can be overwritten within weeks. Waiting until the legal deadline can mean losing your strongest evidence long before you file.

## Houston Bicycle Accident Claims: What Texas Law Actually Does for Cyclists
Source: https://nalawtx.com/blog/houston-bicycle-accident-claims-what-texas-law-actually

Bicyclist fatalities in Texas rose 58% in just four years, and Harris County is one of the deadliest places in the state to ride. If a driver hit you, here's what your claim looks like under Texas law, why bias against cyclists is a real obstacle, and what to do before you talk to any insurance company.
By Vu Nguyen, Founder & Managing Partner · Updated November 16, 2026
Texas law treats your bicycle as a vehicle, giving you the right to seek compensation when a driver's negligence causes a crash. However, Texas's modified comparative fault rule means your recovery is reduced by your share of blame, and disappears entirely if you're found 51% or more at fault. Acting quickly to preserve evidence and avoiding recorded statements protect your claim.
- Texas law classifies a bicycle as a vehicle, so drivers owe you the same duty of care they owe other road users.
- If you're found 51% or more at fault under Texas's comparative fault rule, you recover nothing.
- Houston's VRU ordinance requires drivers to give cyclists at least three feet of clearance — a violation is evidence of negligence.
- Your own auto insurance's UM/UIM coverage may protect you after a hit-and-run, even when you were on a bicycle.
You were riding your bike. A driver ran a red light, drifted into the shoulder, or opened a car door into your path. Now you're in the emergency room at Memorial Hermann or Ben Taub with broken bones, road rash, or worse. Your phone is already lighting up with a call from an insurance adjuster.
What happens next matters a lot. Texas law gives injured cyclists real legal rights. But there's a gap between what the law says and what actually happens in a claim. That gap often comes down to one uncomfortable truth: a lot of insurance adjusters, defense lawyers, and even jurors start from the assumption that cyclists are partly to blame just for being on the road.
This post explains how Texas law treats bicycle accident claims, what tools you have when a driver hits you, and why cyclist bias is a documented problem you need to understand before you say anything to an adjuster.

### Harris County Is One of the Most Dangerous Places in Texas to Ride
That's not an opinion. It comes from TxDOT's own crash data. Texas recorded a 58% increase in bicyclist fatalities between 2019 and 2023. Harris County, which includes Houston and its inner suburbs, consistently sits at or near the top of the statewide death count.
Cycling is growing in Houston. More people use bikes for commuting, recreation, and deliveries than ever before. The road infrastructure hasn't kept up. Protected bike lanes are sparse. Drivers along corridors like Westheimer, Navigation Boulevard, and Memorial Drive share lanes with cyclists but often don't treat them like they belong there.
When crashes happen, they're not minor fender-benders. A cyclist hit by a 4,000-pound vehicle at 35 mph absorbs massive force with no metal cage around them. Traumatic brain injuries, spinal fractures, and internal injuries are common even when the rider was wearing a helmet and doing everything right.

### Your Basic Rights Under Texas Law
Under Texas law, a bicycle is a vehicle. The Texas Transportation Code treats cyclists with the same legal status as drivers on most public roads. You have the right to ride on the roadway. Drivers must give you space. They must yield when required. They cannot simply brush you off as an obstacle.
When a driver's negligence causes a crash, that driver can be held legally responsible for your injuries. Running a stop sign, speeding, texting, failing to check mirrors before opening a door. The legal theory is straightforward: negligence. The driver owed you a duty of care, they breached it, and you got hurt because of it.
What makes bicycle cases complicated isn't the basic law. It's the fault fight that follows.

### Texas Comparative Fault. and Why It Matters So Much for Cyclists
Texas uses a system called modified comparative fault. Your recovery gets reduced by whatever percentage of fault is assigned to you. If a jury decides you were 20% at fault for the crash, you recover 80% of your total damages. If they decide you were 51% or more at fault, you recover nothing at all.
That 51% threshold is the knife's edge in bicycle cases. Insurance adjusters know it. They look for any reason to push your fault percentage above 50%, because at that point, they owe you zero.
Common arguments adjusters and defense lawyers use to shift blame onto cyclists:
- You weren't wearing a helmet (even though Texas law doesn't require adults to wear helmets)
- You were riding at night without lights
- You were riding on a road where cyclists "shouldn't" be, even if it was legal
- You failed to signal a turn
- You were in the driver's blind spot
Some of those might be legitimate facts. Some are just noise designed to make you seem reckless. The key is understanding that in Texas, partial fault doesn't automatically end your case. It reduces it. The fight is over how much fault you bear, and that fight starts the moment the adjuster picks up the phone.
An adjuster's first call isn't a courtesy check. It's a data-gathering mission. What you say in that first conversation can be used to push your fault percentage up, which directly reduces what the insurer has to pay you.

### The Houston VRU Ordinance. Extra Protection You May Not Know About
Houston has its own local ordinance that provides additional protections for Vulnerable Road Users (VRUs), a category that includes cyclists, pedestrians, and others without the protection of a vehicle frame around them.
Under Houston's VRU ordinance, drivers must give cyclists at least three feet of clearance when passing. Violation of that rule is evidence of negligence. If a driver passed you closer than three feet and clipped you, that specific violation can be powerful evidence in your claim. It goes beyond general "careless driving" to a concrete, measurable breach of a local safety rule.
Keep this in mind when you're documenting the crash. If witnesses saw the driver pass close, or if there's dashcam or traffic camera footage from somewhere like the intersection at Montrose and Allen Parkway, that footage could show the spacing violation directly.

### Hit-and-Run? You Still Have Options.
Hit-and-run bicycle crashes happen more often than most people realize. A driver clips a cyclist and keeps going. Sometimes it's panic. Sometimes it's intentional. Either way, you're left with real injuries and no one to sue directly.
Here's what a lot of cyclists don't know: your own auto insurance, specifically uninsured/underinsured motorist (UM/UIM) coverage, may cover you even though you were on a bicycle, not in a car.
UM/UIM coverage is designed to protect you when the at-fault driver has no insurance or can't be identified. Under Texas law, if you have auto insurance with UM/UIM coverage, that policy generally follows you as a person, not just when you're driving. A hit-and-run while you were on your bike may trigger that coverage.
There are conditions and limits, and every policy is different. But if you've been in a hit-and-run, the first call you make should be to an attorney, not the insurance company. Understand what coverage you have before you say anything that could affect your claim.
Also worth checking: your homeowner's or renter's insurance policy. Some include personal liability or medical payments coverage that can apply to bicycle accident injuries.

### The Bias Problem Is Real. Here's What It Looks Like
Texas law treats cyclists as legitimate road users. Juries and adjusters don't always follow the law's lead.
Studies on mock jury behavior in bicycle accident cases consistently find that jurors assign more blame to cyclists than the evidence warrants, particularly when the cyclist was riding in a lane with vehicle traffic rather than on a dedicated path. The underlying assumption: cyclists take a risk by riding on roads with cars, so they accept some responsibility for whatever happens.
That assumption is legally wrong. Texas law doesn't work that way. But it's a real dynamic that experienced plaintiff attorneys deal with constantly.
What this means practically: how your case is built and presented matters enormously. Evidence that the driver was speeding, distracted, or violated a specific traffic rule helps shift the narrative. Witness statements collected quickly, before memories fade, help. Dashcam footage, if any exists, is gold. Medical records documenting the full extent of your injuries, gathered right away and not six weeks later, help too.
Cyclist bias is also why the recorded statement problem is so acute in these cases. When an adjuster gets you on the phone within hours of the crash, they're looking for anything you say that sounds like you weren't sure of your own position, speed, or actions. They write it down. They use it later. The best thing to say to an adjuster before you've spoken with an attorney is nothing at all.

### What Damages Can You Recover?
Texas personal injury law allows injured cyclists to seek compensation for both economic and non-economic losses. Economic damages are the financial costs: medical bills, future medical care, lost wages if you couldn't work while you recovered, and lost earning capacity if the injury affects your ability to work long-term.
Non-economic damages cover the human losses: physical pain, emotional suffering, and loss of enjoyment of life. For serious bicycle injuries, a fractured pelvis, a traumatic brain injury, a spinal cord injury, non-economic damages can be substantial. These injuries don't just cost money. They change lives.
Texas does not cap non-economic damages in personal injury cases against private defendants (unlike medical malpractice, which has its own rules). That matters.
One thing to understand about property damage: your bicycle is covered separately from your personal injury claim. Document the damage thoroughly. Keep the bike. Don't throw it away or let the insurance company take it without documentation, because it's physical evidence of the force of the crash.

### The Two-Year Clock
Under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003, you generally have two years from the date of your bicycle accident to file a personal injury lawsuit. Miss that deadline and your claim is gone, regardless of how strong it was.
Two years sounds like a long time. It isn't. Evidence disappears. Witnesses move away. Traffic camera footage gets overwritten within days or weeks. The earlier you start building your case, the better your position.
There are limited exceptions to the two-year rule. If the injured person is a minor, for instance, the clock may be paused. But exceptions are narrow. Don't plan around them.
The statute of limitations isn't just a legal deadline. It's a practical one. The best evidence in your case exists right now, today, and it's disappearing fast.

### Steps to Take Right Now If You Were Hit
If you haven't done these things yet, do them as soon as you're physically able:
- Get medical attention, and keep going. Go to the ER, urgent care, or your doctor. If you were taken to Ben Taub, Memorial Hermann, or Houston Methodist, get copies of your records. If symptoms get worse in the following days (headaches, dizziness, back pain), go back. Don't dismiss symptoms that show up after the adrenaline wears off.
- Document everything at the scene if you can. Photos of your bike, the vehicle, the road surface, skid marks, traffic signals, and your injuries. Get the driver's license plate, insurance information, and name. If witnesses are present, get their contact information.
- File a police report. In Houston, you can contact HPD or TxDOT depending on where the crash occurred. A police report creates an official record of the crash. It matters.
- Don't give the adjuster a recorded statement. You are not legally required to give a recorded statement to the other driver's insurance company. Politely decline until you've spoken with an attorney.
- Keep your bike and all gear. Don't repair or dispose of anything until your attorney has seen it. The physical evidence tells a story.
- Write down everything you remember. As soon as you can, write a detailed account of what happened: where you were, what direction you were going, what the driver did, weather conditions, time of day. Memory fades fast.

### When You Need a Houston Bicycle Accident Lawyer
Not every crash requires an attorney. If you have minor injuries, the other driver clearly was at fault, and the insurance company is cooperating, you might handle it yourself.
But in most serious bicycle accident cases, an attorney makes a real difference. Here's why.
Bicycle cases are fault fights. The comparative fault system means the insurance company has a financial incentive to push your share of blame as high as possible. An attorney who handles Houston injury cases knows those tactics and knows how to counter them with evidence.
UM/UIM claims after hit-and-runs have their own procedural requirements under Texas law. Getting those wrong can waive coverage you're entitled to.
Serious injuries, brain injuries, spinal injuries, fractures that require surgery, involve future damages that are genuinely complex to calculate. Medical experts, life care planners, and economists sometimes have to get involved. An adjuster's early offer almost never accounts for those future costs accurately.
At Nguyen & Associates, we represent injured cyclists in Houston and throughout Harris County. We work on contingency. You pay nothing unless your case resolves. Free case review here, or call us directly at (713) 842-9442.
This article provides general information about Texas law, not legal advice for your specific situation. Every case is different. If you've been injured in Houston or anywhere in Texas, talk with a licensed attorney about the facts of yours. Free case review here, or call (713) 842-9442.

### Common questions

Missing that deadline means your claim is gone regardless of how strong it was. Traffic camera footage can be overwritten within days or weeks, so starting early gives you the best chance of preserving evidence.
Texas law does not require adult cyclists to wear helmets, so not wearing one does not automatically bar your claim. However, insurance adjusters may use it as an argument to increase your share of fault under Texas's comparative fault system. The fight is over how much fault you bear, and that affects how much you can recover.

Your own auto insurance policy's uninsured/underinsured motorist (UM/UIM) coverage may apply even though you were on a bicycle rather than in a car, because under Texas law that coverage generally follows you as a person. ## Houston Hit-and-Run Victims Can Still Get Compensated. Even When the Driver Is Never Found.
Source: https://nalawtx.com/blog/houston-hit-and-run-victims-how-to-get-compensated

The driver who hit you is gone. That's terrifying, and it's also a crime. But it doesn't mean you're stuck paying your own bills. Here's exactly how Houston hit-and-run victims recover compensation, and what you need to do fast to protect that path.
By Vu Nguyen, Founder & Managing Partner · Updated July 13, 2026
Even if the driver who hit you is never found, you may still recover compensation through your own uninsured motorist (UM) coverage, which Texas law requires insurers to offer. You can also use MedPay, health insurance, or the Texas Crime Victims' Compensation program. Acting quickly to file a police report and document evidence is essential.
- A hit-and-run driver is treated legally the same as an uninsured driver, so your UM coverage may pay your medical bills, lost wages, and pain and suffering.
- A police report is non-negotiable — your UM insurer will almost certainly require one to pay a hit-and-run claim.
- Security footage at nearby businesses is often overwritten within 30 to 72 hours, so documenting the scene fast is critical.
- Texas's general deadline to file a personal injury lawsuit is two years from the accident date under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003.
You're sitting on the side of I-610 or the Katy Freeway, shaking, watching the car that just hit you disappear into traffic. Maybe you caught a partial plate. Maybe you got nothing at all. Either way, you're wondering: if they never find this person, am I just stuck?
The short answer is no. Texas law and your own auto insurance policy may cover you, even when the at-fault driver is completely anonymous. But there are things you have to do quickly, and there are traps that can cut off your options if you're not careful. This post walks through both.

### Why Hit-and-Runs Are Such a Problem in Houston
Houston freeways consistently rank among the most dangerous in the country, and hit-and-run crashes are a significant part of that picture. High-speed corridors like I-45 (the Gulf Freeway), US-59, and the I-10 interchange near downtown see a disproportionate share of these incidents. Roads where a driver can be gone in seconds and swallowed by interchange ramps before anyone can react.
Texas law makes leaving the scene of an accident a criminal offense under the Texas Transportation Code. If someone is injured, it can be a felony. But criminal penalties don't put money in your pocket or pay your medical bills at Memorial Hermann or HCA Houston Healthcare. You need a civil recovery path, and that usually runs through your own insurance policy.

### The Main Recovery Path: Uninsured Motorist Coverage
If there's one thing to understand about hit-and-run compensation, it's this: a driver who flees is treated legally the same as an uninsured driver. Your own uninsured motorist (UM) coverage steps in to pay what the at-fault driver's insurance would have paid, if they had any and if you could find them.
Under Texas law, insurance companies are required to offer UM/UIM coverage (uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage) when they sell you a policy. You can reject it in writing, but most people don't. Pull out your declarations page right now and look for "UM" or "UMBI" (uninsured motorist bodily injury) coverage. If you have it, that's your primary compensation path in a hit-and-run.
UM coverage pays for your medical bills, lost wages, and pain and suffering. The same categories of damages you'd pursue against the driver who hit you. The fact that they ran doesn't eliminate those damages. It just changes who you file the claim against.
There's an important catch with hit-and-runs specifically: many UM policies require some form of physical contact between the fleeing vehicle and yours. If a car cut you off and you swerved into a barrier with no direct contact, some insurers will fight that claim. A few policies are more flexible about "phantom vehicle" scenarios, but expect pushback if there's no contact. This is one of the first things an attorney will look at in your specific policy language.

### Other Compensation Sources Worth Knowing About
UM coverage is usually the biggest source of recovery, but it's not the only one. Depending on the facts of your crash, other options may be available.

#### Your Own Medical Payments Coverage (MedPay)
MedPay pays your medical bills regardless of who was at fault. No liability questions, no waiting for a claim to resolve. If you have it, use it immediately. It won't compensate you for pain and suffering or lost wages, but it keeps your medical bills from going to collections while the bigger claim is sorted out.

#### Health Insurance
Your health insurance covers accident injuries just like any other injury. Use it. Don't avoid the ER at Ben Taub or urgent care because you're worried about cost. Going to the doctor creates the medical record that supports your UM claim. Delaying treatment is one of the biggest mistakes hit-and-run victims make, and insurance companies use those gaps against you later.

#### Texas Crime Victims' Compensation
Because hit-and-run is a crime in Texas, victims may qualify for assistance through the Texas Crime Victims' Compensation program, administered by the Office of the Attorney General. It's not a lawsuit. It's a state fund for crime victims. It has eligibility requirements and caps, but it's a real option, especially when other coverage is limited. You generally need to report the crime to law enforcement to qualify.

#### If the Driver Is Later Identified
Sometimes police do find the driver, days, weeks, or even months later through surveillance footage, traffic cameras, or witness tips. In Harris County, law enforcement has access to a growing network of red-light cameras and TxDOT traffic monitoring systems. If the driver is identified and they have insurance, the case changes entirely. If they're uninsured, your UM coverage still applies, but now you may also have a direct claim against them personally. Don't assume the investigation is closed just because you haven't heard anything.

### What You Need to Do in the Hours After a Hit-and-Run
The actions you take in the first few hours directly affect whether your UM claim succeeds. Here's what matters most.

#### Call 911 and Make a Police Report
This is non-negotiable. Your UM insurer will almost certainly require a police report to pay a hit-and-run claim. Houston Police Department (HPD) or the Harris County Sheriff's Office will respond depending on where the crash occurred. Get the incident number before you leave the scene or the hospital.
If the officer tells you the crash doesn't meet the threshold for an on-scene report, which sometimes happens with property-damage-only crashes, go to an HPD reporting station or file online through the Texas Department of Transportation crash reporting system. You need something in writing.

#### Document Everything You Can Remember
Write down every detail about the fleeing vehicle while it's fresh: color, make, model, body damage, any part of the plate, direction of travel, time of day, road conditions. If you were near a business, a gas station on Westheimer or a shopping center near Beltway 8, note that too. Private businesses often have exterior cameras that aren't obvious. That footage can be subpoenaed, but only if someone asks for it before it's overwritten, which often happens within 30 to 72 hours.

#### Photograph Your Vehicle and Your Injuries
Before your car is moved or repaired, take photos from every angle. Photograph the point of impact, any paint transfer, and the surrounding road. Photograph any visible injuries on your body. Time-stamped photos are evidence. They establish what happened and when.

#### Gather Witness Information
Other drivers, pedestrians, workers at a nearby construction site, anyone who saw the crash should be identified before they leave. Names and phone numbers. People have busy lives and good intentions; they may forget to follow up unless you have their contact information in hand.

#### Notify Your Insurance Company, But Watch What You Say
You're required to notify your insurer of a hit-and-run within a reasonable time. Most policies spell this out. Call to report the incident. But be careful: your own UM insurer is not automatically on your side. They still have a financial incentive to minimize what they pay. Don't give a recorded statement without understanding what it's for and how it might be used. If an adjuster calls and asks to record you, it's okay to say you'd like to speak with an attorney first.
Your own insurance company is not your enemy, but they're not your advocate either. The adjuster's job is to settle your claim for as little as possible. Knowing that going in changes how you handle every conversation.

### What UM Claims Actually Cover
When people hear "insurance claim," they often picture just getting their car fixed. A UM bodily injury claim covers much more than that.
Medical expenses are the most obvious: ER visits, surgeries, physical therapy, follow-up care. But UM claims also cover lost income if your injuries kept you from working, future medical treatment if your recovery is ongoing, and pain and suffering. Texas also recognizes loss of consortium for spouses and, in fatal crashes, wrongful death claims by surviving family members.
What you can recover is capped by your policy's UM coverage amount. If you have $30,000 in UM bodily injury coverage and your damages exceed that, the gap is real. This is why the amount of UM coverage you carry matters, and why many attorneys recommend carrying more than the state minimum if you can afford it.

### The Statute of Limitations. Don't Miss This Deadline.
In Texas, the general deadline to file a personal injury lawsuit is two years from the date of the accident, under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003. That clock applies to hit-and-run claims too, both against an identified driver and, in some situations, as part of a UM dispute that goes to litigation.
Two years sounds like a long time. It isn't. Evidence disappears. Witnesses forget. Security footage is long gone. Medical records need to be gathered. An attorney needs time to investigate. Starting early isn't about being aggressive. It's about protecting your options.
There are also separate deadlines in your insurance policy itself. Most UM policies have their own notice and cooperation requirements. Missing those internal deadlines can give the insurer grounds to deny the claim even before the legal statute of limitations runs out. Read your policy or have an attorney read it for you.

### When Does It Make Sense to Hire a Houston Hit-and-Run Lawyer?
Not every hit-and-run claim requires an attorney. If you had a minor fender-bender, no injuries, and your car damage is covered cleanly by your collision coverage, you may be fine handling it yourself.
But if you were hurt, even injuries that seem minor at first, like neck stiffness or headaches, the calculus shifts. UM claims involving bodily injury are more complex. Insurers dispute the severity of injuries. They question whether your treatment was necessary. They make lowball offers early, hoping you'll take them before you know how serious your injuries are.
A Houston car accident attorney who handles UM claims knows those tactics. They can help gather evidence while it still exists, interpret your policy language, deal with the insurer on your behalf, and make sure you're not settling before you understand the full scope of your injuries and treatment costs.
Most personal injury attorneys in Texas work on contingency, meaning you pay nothing upfront and no attorney fees unless there's a recovery. So cost isn't usually the barrier. For serious injuries, having someone in your corner almost always makes a difference.

### A Note on Hit-and-Run Crashes That Killed Someone
If you lost a family member in a Houston hit-and-run crash, the legal path is the same in structure: police report, UM claim, potential litigation. But the stakes are higher and the process is harder to handle alone. Texas recognizes wrongful death claims by surviving spouses, children, and parents under the Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code. If the driver is later identified, a direct claim against them becomes possible. If they're not, the UM wrongful death claim is often the primary path. Please talk to an attorney before making any decisions.
This article provides general information about Texas law, not legal advice for your specific situation. Every case is different. If you've been injured in Houston or anywhere in Texas, talk with a licensed attorney about the facts of yours. Free case review here, or call (713) 842-9442.

### Watch: Uninsured Driver Hit You? Here's What to Do

### Common questions
Yes. Under Texas law, a driver who flees is treated the same as an uninsured driver, so your own uninsured motorist (UM) coverage can step in. UM coverage pays for medical bills, lost wages, and pain and suffering — the same damages you would pursue against the at-fault driver. You may also have access to MedPay, health insurance, or the Texas Crime Victims' Compensation program.

## Houston Motorcycle Accident Claims: Why Bias Against Riders Makes Legal Representation Critical
Source: https://nalawtx.com/blog/houston-motorcycle-accident-lawyer-why-rider-bias-changes

Texas lost 581 motorcycle riders in 2024. Harris County led the state. If you were hurt on a Houston road, the at-fault driver's insurance company already has a theory about what happened. It starts with blaming you.
By Vu Nguyen, Founder & Managing Partner · Updated July 6, 2026
Motorcycle riders in Houston face insurance adjusters who often assume rider fault from the start, using Texas's modified comparative fault system to reduce or eliminate your claim. Bias against riders, combined with higher injury severity, makes legal representation especially important. If you were hurt, you have two years from the crash date to file a lawsuit under Texas law.
- Texas uses modified comparative fault — if you're found 51% or more at fault, you recover nothing.
- You are not required to give a recorded statement to the other driver's insurance company.
- Lane-splitting is illegal in Texas, but it doesn't automatically make you at fault for a crash.
- Under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003, you generally have two years from the crash to file suit.
You're riding westbound on I-10 near the Katy Freeway interchange. A driver merges left without checking their blind spot. You hit the pavement. You survive, but you're looking at a broken collarbone, road rash across your left side, and a totaled bike.
Within two days, the other driver's insurance adjuster calls. They're polite. They're sympathetic. And they're already building a file designed to reduce what you're owed, or wipe it out entirely. For motorcycle riders, that process starts earlier and cuts deeper than it does for people hurt in car crashes. Here's why, and what you can do about it.

### The Numbers in Harris County Are Stark
Texas recorded 581 motorcycle fatalities in 2024. Harris County consistently ranks among the highest counties in the state for both crashes and rider deaths. The Houston metro's combination of high-speed freeways (I-45, Beltway 8, US-59), dense surface-street traffic, and aggressive driving creates serious exposure for riders year-round.
Those numbers matter for your claim, too. When crashes happen this often, adjusters develop assumptions. They process hundreds of motorcycle claims. Over time, many start treating every rider as a risk-taker who probably contributed to their own crash. That's not a legal standard. It's a bias. But it shapes how your claim gets handled from day one.

### What "Comparative Fault" Means for You, and How Adjusters Exploit It
Texas uses a system called modified comparative fault. Plain English: if you were partly responsible for your own crash, your compensation gets reduced by your percentage of blame. If you were 20% at fault, you recover 80% of your damages. If you were 51% or more at fault, you recover nothing.
That 51% threshold is exactly what adjusters aim for in motorcycle cases. Their goal isn't always to win outright. It's to push your assigned fault percentage high enough to gut your claim or force a lowball settlement.
The tactics are predictable. Adjusters will ask whether you were wearing all your gear. They'll ask about your speed, even just an estimate. They'll ask if you'd been lane-splitting (more on that in a moment). They'll look for anything in your recorded statement that lets them say you were reckless. Every detail they collect can be used to inflate your fault percentage.
You don't have to give a recorded statement to the other driver's insurance company. You really don't. An adjuster asking for one is standard procedure. Saying no is too.
If you've already gotten that call, don't panic. But do talk to an attorney before you say anything else. The practice areas page has more detail on how we handle motorcycle cases specifically.

### The Lane-Splitting Misconception
Lane-splitting (riding between lanes of slow or stopped traffic) is illegal in Texas. Full stop. The Texas Transportation Code does not permit it.
But here's what adjusters get wrong, and what actually matters legally: the fact that a practice is illegal doesn't automatically mean a rider was at fault for a crash. Fault depends on causation. If you were lane-splitting at 5 mph in stopped traffic on Loop 610 and a driver flung open their door into your path, the door, not your lane position, may be the proximate cause of the crash.
Adjusters treat "they were lane-splitting" as a case-ender. It isn't. Under Texas law, comparative fault requires a real analysis of whether your conduct actually caused or contributed to your injuries. A reflexive assumption isn't that analysis.
That said, lane-splitting does create legal exposure. If you were doing it, be honest with your attorney. They need the full picture to protect you, not a cleaned-up version.

### Texas Helmet Law and What It Can and Can't Do to Your Claim
Texas requires helmets for riders under 21. Riders 21 and older can ride without one if they've completed an approved safety course or carry certain medical insurance coverage under Texas Transportation Code § 661.003.
If you were 21 or older, legally exempt, and riding without a helmet when you crashed, the other driver's insurer will bring it up. They'll argue your head or brain injuries were worse because you weren't helmeted, and that you should bear some responsibility for that.
Texas courts have allowed this argument under a doctrine called avoidable consequences. Basically, a jury can reduce compensation for injuries the plaintiff could have avoided through reasonable care. Not wearing a helmet, even when legal, can factor into that calculation.
What it cannot do is eliminate your claim. If the other driver ran a red light on Westheimer and broke your arm, your helmet status has nothing to do with your arm. The defense can only use helmet evidence to reduce damages specifically tied to head or brain injuries.
An experienced Houston motorcycle accident attorney knows how to fight these arguments by isolating which injuries were actually affected by helmet use and which weren't. That line matters enormously when damages are calculated.

### Why "Reckless Rider" Is a Story, Not a Fact
Insurance defense strategies work by constructing a narrative. For motorcycle crashes, that narrative is almost always some version of: "The rider was aggressive, taking risks, and the crash was inevitable."
Adjusters build this story using a few reliable tools:
- Your recorded statement. Anything you say about speed, lane changes, or your state of mind goes in the file. Adjusters are trained to ask open-ended questions that prompt you to fill silence with details you didn't need to share.
- Social media. Photos of you at track days, videos of spirited riding, posts about your bike's horsepower. All of it gets used to paint you as a thrill-seeker.
- Crash report ambiguity. Houston Police Department and TxDOT crash reports sometimes list "unsafe speed" or "failed to control speed" as contributing factors when there's uncertainty. Adjusters take that checkbox and run with it.
Countering this story requires evidence. Not just your word against theirs. That means surveillance footage from businesses on the corridor where the crash happened (many along I-69 and the Hardy Toll Road have cameras), witness statements gathered before memories fade, and in serious cases, an accident reconstruction expert who can establish what the physics actually show.
That evidence window closes fast. Footage gets overwritten. Witnesses move on. The 48 hours after a crash are critical for preservation.

### Left-Turn Crashes: The Most Common Scenario in Houston
Statistically, the most common deadly motorcycle crash involves a vehicle making a left turn in front of an oncoming rider. The driver claims they "didn't see" the motorcycle. The rider had no time to react.
This happens across Houston constantly: at intersections on Westheimer, at cross-traffic cuts along Richmond Avenue, at the uncontrolled turns off feeder roads on I-10. Motorcycles are physically smaller and can be hidden by A-pillars, sun glare, and visual clutter. Drivers simply fail to see them.
"I didn't see them" is not a defense. A driver who fails to see a motorcycle that was visible and in their path of travel wasn't paying adequate attention. That's negligence.
But adjusters often respond to these crashes by suggesting the rider was speeding, arguing that if the rider had been going the speed limit, the driver would have had time to complete the turn safely. It's circular logic that shifts blame without evidence. Pushing back requires a clear record of the road conditions, the sight lines, and the timing.
In Texas, a driver making a left turn has a duty to yield to oncoming traffic. That duty doesn't disappear because a motorcycle is harder to see than a pickup truck.

### Damages in Motorcycle Cases Are Typically Higher, Which Raises the Stakes
Motorcycles offer no crumple zone, no airbags, no door between you and the road. When crashes happen, the injuries tend to be severe: traumatic brain injury, spinal fractures, amputations, extensive soft-tissue damage, long-term chronic pain.
Higher damages mean the insurance company has more financial incentive to fight hard or delay. A claim worth $30,000 gets routine processing. A claim worth $300,000 or more gets a defense attorney, an adjuster, a medical review team, and a strategy session.
Texas law allows injured riders to pursue two main categories of damages. Economic damages cover the concrete financial losses: medical bills (emergency care at Memorial Hermann or Ben Taub, surgeries, rehab, future care), lost income during recovery, and property damage to the bike. Non-economic damages cover pain and suffering, loss of enjoyment of life, and the physical and emotional impact of your injuries. In cases of extreme misconduct (drunk driving, for instance) exemplary (punitive) damages may also be available under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 41.003.
Texas does not cap non-economic damages in personal injury cases (the cap applies to medical malpractice). That's meaningful for riders with serious, life-altering injuries.

### The Two-Year Clock Is Running
Under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003, you generally have two years from the date of your crash to file a personal injury lawsuit. Miss that deadline and you lose your right to sue. Doesn't matter how strong your case is.
Two years sounds like plenty of time. It isn't, for a few reasons. Insurance negotiations often drag on for months. Medical treatment needs to reach a stable endpoint before damages can be accurately calculated. Evidence gathering, expert retention, and demand letter preparation all take time. Attorneys need enough runway to build the case properly.
Waiting also sends a signal. Adjusters know that a claimant who waits 18 months to get representation is less likely to have preserved key evidence. It weakens your position at the negotiating table.
If you were hurt in a crash in Harris County, on Beltway 8, on Highway 290, at an intersection anywhere in the Houston metro, the clock started the day of the crash.

### What to Do Right Now If You Were in a Motorcycle Crash
If you're reading this from a hospital bed or a couch while you recover, here's the practical order of operations:
- Get your medical care documented. Every visit, every diagnosis, every prescription. Don't skip follow-ups because you feel like you should tough it out. Gaps in treatment get used against you.
- Don't give a recorded statement to the other driver's insurer. You're not required to. Politely decline and say your attorney will be in touch.
- Write down everything you remember. The road, the weather, the sequence of events, what the other driver said at the scene. Your memory will fade. Write it now.
- Preserve your gear. Don't throw away your helmet, jacket, or boots. They can be evidence, both of the impact force and of the protective measures you were taking.
- Talk to an attorney. A free case review costs you nothing and tells you where you stand.
Motorcycle crash claims in Texas require someone in your corner who understands both the law and the bias you're up against. The other driver's insurer has handled these cases before. You're probably handling yours for the first time.
This article provides general information about Texas law, not legal advice for your specific situation. Every case is different. If you've been injured in Houston or anywhere in Texas, talk with a licensed attorney about the facts of yours. Free case review here, or call (713) 842-9442.

### Common questions
Yes, as long as you were less than 51% at fault under Texas's modified comparative fault system. Your compensation is reduced by your percentage of fault. If you were 20% at fault, you recover 80% of your damages. At 51% or more, you recover nothing.
If you were 21 or older and legally exempt under Texas Transportation Code § 661.003, riding without a helmet can still be used to reduce damages specifically tied to head or brain injuries under the avoidable consequences doctrine. However, it cannot eliminate your entire claim. Injuries unrelated to helmet use, like a broken arm, are not affected by your helmet status.

Under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003, you generally have two years from the date of your crash to file a personal injury lawsuit. Missing that deadline means losing your right to sue, regardless of how strong your case is. Evidence also disappears quickly, so acting sooner rather than later strengthens your position.

## Houston Nursing Home Abuse: What Texas Law Lets Families Recover
Source: https://nalawtx.com/blog/houston-nursing-home-abuse-what-texas-law-lets-families

Texas classifies many nursing home claims as medical malpractice, triggering expert report deadlines most families never see coming. This post breaks down the rules, the warning signs, and what your family can actually pursue.
By Vu Nguyen, Founder & Managing Partner · Updated October 19, 2026
Texas law gives families of nursing home abuse victims several ways to seek compensation, including medical expenses, pain and suffering, and wrongful death damages. However, many claims are classified as medical malpractice under Chapter 74, triggering a strict 120-day expert report deadline after filing suit. Missing that deadline can end your case permanently.
- Many nursing home claims fall under Texas Chapter 74, requiring a qualified expert report within 120 days of filing suit.
- Families can pursue medical expenses, pain and suffering, mental anguish, and wrongful death damages depending on the situation.
- Regulatory investigations by HHSC or APS do not replace a civil lawsuit and cannot compensate your family.
- Documenting injuries, preserving facility records, and consulting an attorney early protects your legal options.
Your mother moved into a Houston-area nursing facility because she needed care you couldn't safely provide at home. Six months later, she has unexplained bruises, has lost 20 pounds, and flinches when a staff member walks into her room. You know something is wrong. What you may not know is that the legal path forward is more complicated, and more time-sensitive, than most families realize.
Texas has specific laws governing nursing home and assisted living claims. Some of those laws protect residents. Others, if you miss them, can end your family's case before it starts. Understanding both sides matters before you take a single step.

### The Scale of the Problem in Texas
Texas has more than 4.8 million residents aged 65 and older. That number keeps climbing, and the elder care industry has grown to match it. Harris County alone has hundreds of licensed nursing facilities, assisted living communities, and memory care centers.
In 2025, Texas Adult Protective Services confirmed nearly 360,000 elder abuse cases statewide. That figure, from APS's own data, covers physical abuse, emotional abuse, sexual abuse, financial exploitation, and neglect. Neglect is the most commonly confirmed type.
These are not rare or isolated events. Understaffed facilities, high employee turnover, and inadequate training create conditions where residents get hurt, sometimes severely. Bedsores that go untreated. Falls that happen because no one answered a call light. Medication errors that nobody documents. Residents who can no longer advocate for themselves, left in rooms where nothing gets reported.

### What Counts as Abuse or Neglect
Texas law defines these terms broadly. Under the Texas Human Resources Code, abuse includes physical harm inflicted by a caregiver, sexual contact without consent, and emotional or verbal abuse. Neglect covers a caregiver's failure to provide food, water, shelter, medication, or medical care when that failure causes harm or puts a resident at substantial risk of harm.
In practical terms, families typically encounter several patterns:
- Physical abuse. unexplained bruising, broken bones, injuries inconsistent with the explanation offered by staff
- Neglect. pressure ulcers (bedsores) that develop because a resident isn't being repositioned, dehydration, malnutrition, poor hygiene
- Medication errors. wrong drug, wrong dose, missed doses, or medications given to the wrong resident
- Fall injuries. inadequate supervision, missing bed rails, wet floors, failure to follow a fall-prevention care plan
- Emotional abuse. staff who berate, threaten, or isolate residents
- Financial exploitation. a separate civil and criminal track; we'll note it here but it requires its own analysis
Not every bad outcome is abuse or neglect. Residents in nursing facilities are often medically fragile. Some decline despite good care. But when harm results from what a facility did, or failed to do, Texas law gives families options.

### The Chapter 74 Problem: When Texas Treats This as Medical Malpractice
This is where most families get blindsided. It's also what makes nursing home cases genuinely different from other personal injury claims.
Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code Chapter 74 governs medical malpractice claims. When a nursing home provides services that constitute "health care". things like wound care, medication management, fall prevention protocols. a claim based on those services may be classified as a health care liability claim under Chapter 74, not a standard negligence claim.
That classification triggers two requirements most people don't know exist.

#### The Expert Report Deadline
Under Chapter 74, within 120 days of filing suit, you must serve an expert report on every defendant. The report has to come from a qualified medical professional. It must set out the standard of care the facility was supposed to meet, how the facility breached that standard, and how that breach caused the resident's injuries.
Miss that 120-day window, even by one day, and the defendant can ask the court to dismiss your case and award them attorney's fees. Courts have very limited discretion to extend the deadline. In practice, a missed expert report deadline usually ends the case.
That's not a technicality. It's a real cliff that has ended legitimate claims by families who didn't know it existed.

#### The Statute of Limitations
Standard personal injury claims in Texas generally carry a two-year statute of limitations under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003. Health care liability claims under Chapter 74 also carry a two-year limit, but the clock can start differently, and there are specific discovery-rule nuances for cases involving fraudulent concealment of injuries. For deceased residents, survival and wrongful death claims have their own timing considerations.
The point: there is no safe assumption about when time runs out. The facts of your specific situation determine the deadline, and getting that wrong is irreversible.
The 120-day expert report requirement under Chapter 74 has ended more legitimate nursing home cases than most people realize. Families lose their rights not because they waited too long to call, but because no one told them this rule existed.

### Not All Nursing Home Claims Fall Under Chapter 74
Here's the other side of that: not every claim against a nursing home is automatically a medical malpractice claim. Texas courts have spent years sorting out where Chapter 74 applies and where it doesn't.
If the claim is based on the facility's failure as a business operator, security failures, physical plant hazards, negligent hiring of staff with known histories of abuse, courts have sometimes found those claims fall outside Chapter 74. That means no expert report requirement and a potentially simpler path to trial.
The distinction matters enormously. A resident sexually abused by a staff member who had prior misconduct on his record, and whom the facility hired anyway, may look very different legally from a claim about improper wound care protocol.
Figuring out which track applies requires analyzing the specific facts of what happened. This is not something to guess at. The wrong classification can either cost your case its procedural footing or cause you to over-build a case around requirements that don't actually apply.

### What Families Can Recover
If a nursing home claim succeeds, Texas law allows families to pursue several categories of damages.

#### For Injured Residents Who Are Still Living
- Medical expenses. past and future costs to treat the injuries caused by abuse or neglect
- Pain and suffering. physical pain and emotional distress the resident experienced
- Mental anguish. Texas law recognizes this as a separate category of harm
- Disfigurement. relevant in cases involving severe pressure wounds or scarring
- Physical impairment. if the abuse or neglect caused lasting functional loss

#### When a Resident Dies
Texas law allows two types of claims after a resident dies from nursing home abuse or neglect.
A survival claim is brought on behalf of the resident's estate. It covers the harm the resident personally experienced, their pain, their suffering, their medical costs, before death.
A wrongful death claim is brought by eligible family members: spouses, children, and parents. It covers the loss those family members suffered, grief, loss of companionship, loss of financial support.
Both claims can often be pursued at the same time. They serve different purposes and compensate for different harms.

#### Exemplary Damages
Texas law permits exemplary damages, sometimes called punitive damages, in cases involving malice, fraud, or gross negligence. Gross negligence means the defendant's conduct involved an extreme degree of risk, and they proceeded with conscious indifference to the rights and welfare of others.
A nursing home that knew a staff member was abusing residents and concealed it. A facility that repeatedly ignored documented bedsores. Cases with that kind of deliberate or reckless disregard can support an exemplary damages claim, which goes beyond compensating the family and is meant to punish the wrongdoer.
Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 41.008 caps exemplary damages in most civil cases. The cap calculation depends on the facts of the case. The cap does not apply to intentional conduct or certain other categories, which is another reason the specific classification of the claim matters.

### What Texas Regulators Can and Cannot Do
Families often report nursing home abuse to the Texas Health and Human Services Commission (HHSC), which licenses and inspects facilities. They may also contact Adult Protective Services or local law enforcement. Those are the right steps, and they can trigger investigations, citations, and even license revocations.
But regulatory action and a civil lawsuit are separate tracks.
HHSC can fine a facility or require a corrective action plan. It cannot compensate your family. An APS substantiation of abuse confirms something happened, but APS doesn't file a lawsuit on your behalf. Criminal charges, if pursued by the Harris County District Attorney's office, address punishment of the abuser, not compensation for your family.
If your family wants compensation for what happened to your loved one, that requires a separate civil case. The regulatory findings can be powerful evidence in that case, but they don't replace it.

### Warning Signs Families Often Miss
Nursing facilities are skilled at limiting information flow. Staff are often coached on what to say, and what not to say, when something goes wrong. Some warning signs families don't always connect to abuse or neglect:
- Staff who are evasive when you ask how an injury happened
- Records that seem to appear or change after an incident
- A facility that discourages unannounced visits
- Residents who become withdrawn or fearful of specific staff members
- Repeated infections, UTIs, pneumonia, that suggest inadequate hygiene protocols
- Sudden or unexplained changes in a resident's mental or emotional state
- Weight loss that staff attribute only to the resident's underlying condition
Trust your instincts. If something feels wrong, start documenting everything: dates, staff names, what was said, photographs of any visible injuries. That record becomes evidence.

### What to Do Right Now If You Suspect Abuse
If your loved one is in immediate danger, call 911. Physical safety comes first.
If the situation is serious but not an emergency, contact the Texas HHSC complaint line at 1-800-458-9858. You can report nursing home neglect or abuse 24 hours a day.
Preserve records. Request copies of the facility's incident reports, care plans, and medication administration records. Texas law gives you rights to those records. The facility cannot lawfully deny access to a resident's authorized representative.
Photograph injuries as soon as you see them. Document the date, time, and location. If a resident can speak and is willing to describe what happened, note that too.
Then talk to an attorney before you say anything further to the facility or its insurer. Nursing home companies carry liability insurance, and their adjusters handle these calls all day. Your family is not in an equal position in that conversation without legal guidance.
The 120-day expert report clock starts running once suit is filed. The two-year limitations period runs before suit must be filed. Time is a real factor. An attorney handling nursing home and elder abuse cases can assess quickly whether Chapter 74 applies and what deadlines govern your situation.
Families who wait to see how things develop sometimes run out of legal options before they realize the clock was running. If you suspect abuse, a consultation costs nothing and tells you where you stand.

### Choosing an Attorney for a Houston Nursing Home Case
Nursing home litigation in Texas is genuinely specialized. It sits at the intersection of elder law, medical malpractice procedure, and personal injury. Not every personal injury attorney has handled it.
Ask the attorney you consult with whether they have experience specifically with Chapter 74 health care liability claims. Ask whether they work with qualified medical experts who can produce the required expert report. Ask how they assess whether a claim falls inside or outside Chapter 74, because the answer matters to your case strategy.
At Nguyen & Associates, we represent families dealing with serious injury claims throughout Houston and Harris County, including nursing home and elder abuse cases. We offer free consultations in English, Español, and Tiếng Việt. You can start a free case review online or call us directly at any hour.
You placed your loved one in that facility because you trusted they would be safe. If that trust was broken, Texas law gives your family a path. The rules around that path are strict and unforgiving about deadlines, which is exactly why knowing them early matters.
