### Common questions
Texas generally imposes a two-year statute of limitations on personal injury and health care liability claims. When a nursing home claim qualifies as a health care liability claim under Chapter 74, the clock can start differently depending on the facts, including discovery-rule nuances for fraudulent concealment. There is no safe assumption about when time runs out, so getting the deadline wrong is irreversible.
Under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code Chapter 74, once a health care liability lawsuit is filed, you must serve a qualified expert report on every defendant within 120 days. The report must identify the applicable standard of care, explain how the facility breached it, and connect that breach to the resident's injuries. Missing the deadline by even one day can result in dismissal of the case and an award of attorney's fees to the defendant.
For a living resident, recoverable damages can include past and future medical expenses, pain and suffering, mental anguish, disfigurement, and physical impairment. If a resident dies, families may bring both a survival claim on behalf of the estate and a wrongful death claim covering grief, loss of companionship, and loss of financial support. In cases involving gross negligence, malice, or fraud, Texas law also permits exemplary damages, though Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 41.008 caps those amounts in most civil cases.
Reporting to the Texas Health and Human Services Commission or Adult Protective Services can trigger inspections, citations, and investigations, but those regulatory actions are separate from a civil lawsuit. HHSC can fine a facility or require corrective action, but it cannot compensate your family. If you want financial compensation for what happened to your loved one, you must file a separate civil case, though regulatory findings can serve as powerful evidence in that case.

## Houston Rideshare Accidents: How Uber & Lyft Insurance Actually Works
Source: https://nalawtx.com/blog/houston-rideshare-accidents-how-uber-amp-lyft-insurance

The app status at the moment of your crash determines which insurance applies, and how much. Here's the breakdown, in plain English, plus when Texas law may let you sue Uber or Lyft directly.
By Vu Nguyen, Founder & Managing Partner · Updated May 17, 2026
Which insurance covers your Houston rideshare crash depends on the driver's app status at the exact moment of impact. Uber and Lyft each maintain three coverage phases, ranging from no involvement when the app is off to at least $1 million in liability when a trip is active. Getting the app records is essential to knowing which coverage applies to your claim.
- The driver's app status at the moment of impact controls which insurance phase—and how much coverage—applies to your claim.
- Phase 3 (ride accepted through drop-off) triggers Uber and Lyft's full $1 million commercial liability coverage.
- Texas HB 1733 requires TNCs to background-check drivers, creating a potential direct-liability hook if they approved a disqualified driver.
- Texas modified comparative fault (§ 33.001) reduces your recovery by your share of blame; over 50% at fault means no recovery.
You're sitting in the back of a Lyft somewhere on I-610 when the driver runs a red light and T-bones another car. Or you're the one in the other car, minding your business on Westheimer, and an Uber driver plows into you. Either way, your first call is 911. Your second thought, once the adrenaline settles, is probably: whose insurance pays for this?
That question trips up a lot of people, including some lawyers who don't handle rideshare cases regularly. The answer isn't "Uber's insurance" or "the driver's insurance." The answer is: it depends on exactly what the driver was doing in the app at the moment of impact. There are three distinct phases, each with different coverage. Miss which phase applies, and you could be talking to the wrong insurance company entirely.
This post walks through how rideshare insurance actually stacks up in Texas, what changed when Texas HB 1733 was signed into law, and the specific circumstances where you may have a claim directly against Uber or Lyft, not just their driver.

### First: Uber and Lyft Drivers Are Not Employees
This is the core legal move both companies made from day one. Uber and Lyft classify their drivers as independent contractors. Under that classification, the companies argue they can't be held vicariously liable, meaning responsible for the driver's negligence, the same way an employer would be for an employee's on-the-clock mistake.
Texas courts have generally accepted that framework, which is why these cases don't work the same way as, say, a FedEx truck driver hitting someone while on a delivery route. With a FedEx driver, you go after FedEx. With a rideshare driver, the path to the company is more complicated.
That doesn't mean Uber and Lyft are untouchable. It means you need a different legal theory. Texas law does provide one, which we'll get to below.

### The Three Insurance Phases
Texas law, specifically the framework governing Transportation Network Companies (TNCs), divides a rideshare driver's time into three phases. The coverage available to you as an injured party is entirely different depending on which phase was active when the crash happened.

#### Phase 1: App Is Off
The driver is in their personal car, not logged into the Uber or Lyft app at all. This is just a regular car accident. You're dealing with the driver's personal auto insurance, whatever policy they carry. Uber and Lyft have zero involvement. Their commercial coverage doesn't apply.
If the driver is uninsured or underinsured, your own UM/UIM coverage (uninsured/underinsured motorist, the part of your policy that protects you when the at-fault driver doesn't have enough insurance) becomes critical.

#### Phase 2: App Is On, No Ride Accepted Yet
The driver has the app open and is waiting for a match, cruising around Midtown or parked near George Bush Intercontinental Airport waiting for a fare, but hasn't accepted a specific ride request yet.
This phase carries contingent liability coverage from Uber or Lyft. Under Texas law, that's at least $50,000 per person / $100,000 per accident in bodily injury liability, and $25,000 in property damage. But this matters: that coverage is contingent, meaning it only kicks in if the driver's personal insurance doesn't cover the loss first or denies the claim.
Phase 2 is where most disputes happen. The driver's personal insurer may try to deny the claim because the driver was using the vehicle commercially. Uber or Lyft's insurer may resist paying because they claim the driver's personal policy should respond first. You can end up caught in the middle of that fight while your medical bills pile up.

#### Phase 3: Ride Accepted Through Trip Completion
The driver accepted a ride request and the trip is active, meaning from the moment they tapped "Accept" through dropping off the passenger. This is when Uber and Lyft's full commercial coverage applies.
Both companies maintain at least $1 million in third-party liability coverage during Phase 3, plus uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage. If you were a passenger in the car, or a driver or pedestrian hit by an active Uber or Lyft vehicle, this is the coverage that applies to your claim.
The app status at the exact moment of impact controls everything. A driver who accepted a ride five minutes ago but hasn't picked up the passenger yet is still in Phase 3. A driver who just dropped someone off and ended the trip in the app is back in Phase 1 or 2. Get the trip records.

### How Do You Find Out Which Phase Applied?
You ask for the records. Uber and Lyft maintain detailed logs: when the app was opened, when a ride was accepted, when the passenger was picked up, when the trip ended. That data exists and it's obtainable through a personal injury lawsuit via discovery, the formal process where your attorney demands documents from the other side.
You can also request your own trip history if you were a passenger. Screenshot it immediately. The app records are timestamped and will show whether the trip was active at the time of your crash.
If you were the other driver and the rideshare driver claimed "I wasn't working," don't take their word for it. Get the police report, get witnesses, and talk to an attorney before you accept any version of events from the other driver or their insurer.

### When Can You Sue Uber or Lyft Directly?
This is the question most people actually want answered. The short version: it's difficult but not impossible, and Texas law created a specific opening in 2023.

#### The Independent Contractor Shield, and Its Limits
Uber and Lyft's main defense is that their drivers aren't employees. Texas courts have recognized this. But Texas law has long recognized that even when someone hires an independent contractor, they can still be liable for injuries caused by that contractor if they were negligent in selecting, hiring, or retaining that contractor.
This is called negligent hiring, and it's a live legal theory against rideshare companies in Texas right now.

#### Texas HB 1733 and What It Changed
In 2023, Texas enacted HB 1733, which updated the state's TNC regulatory framework. Among its requirements: TNCs must conduct background checks on drivers and disqualify applicants with certain criminal histories, serious traffic violations, and other disqualifying factors.
That mandate cuts both ways. It strengthens the companies' general safety argument, since they're required to screen drivers. But it also creates a legal hook: if Uber or Lyft approved a driver who should have been disqualified under HB 1733's standards, and that driver then hurt someone, the company may be directly liable for failing to properly screen the driver they put on the road.
Litigation applying HB 1733 is still developing in Texas courts as of 2026. This is an active and increasingly important theory. It's one reason rideshare injury cases benefit from an attorney who follows Texas TNC law specifically, not just general personal injury practice.

#### Other Direct Liability Theories
Beyond negligent hiring, there are two other situations where Uber or Lyft's direct liability comes into play.
Negligent retention. If a driver had incidents, complaints, prior crashes, or safety flags on their record while driving for Uber or Lyft, and the company kept them active anyway, that's a potential negligent retention claim. The companies maintain internal incident records. Getting those records requires litigation.
App or platform design. If the interface Uber or Lyft requires drivers to use, accepting rides, confirming pickups, navigating, contributed to distracted driving, there's an emerging argument about the company's own role in creating unsafe conditions. These cases are harder to win but they're being pursued in courts across the country.

### What Insurance Adjusters Will Do, and Why You Should Be Careful
After a rideshare crash, you may get calls from multiple insurance companies: the driver's personal insurer, Uber or Lyft's third-party claims administrator (James River Insurance handles Uber claims; Lyft uses different carriers depending on the situation), and possibly your own insurer.
Each adjuster has one job: resolve your claim for as little as possible. A few things to know.
They will ask for a recorded statement early. In a rideshare case, recorded statements are particularly risky because the companies' adjusters are specifically trained to get you to say something that blurs which phase was active or implies you contributed to the accident. Don't give a recorded statement to any rideshare insurer without talking to an attorney first.
They may offer a quick settlement. Early settlements in rideshare cases are almost always low, often before the full scope of your injuries is clear. Once you sign a release, you can't come back for more, even if your injuries turn out to be more serious than they initially appeared.
They may dispute which phase applied. If the phase is genuinely contested, don't let the insurer's determination be the final word. Your attorney can demand the trip data directly.
The adjuster calling you works for the insurance company, not for you. That's not a criticism of any individual. It's just how the system is built. Get someone in your corner before you talk to them.

### What to Do Right After a Houston Rideshare Crash
The steps you take in the first 24-48 hours affect everything that follows.
Call 911. Get a police report. Make sure the responding officer notes that the vehicle involved was operating as a rideshare. Harris County law enforcement is familiar with rideshare accidents. Make sure the report reflects the driver's app status if known.
Get medical attention the same day. Even if you feel okay. Memorial Hermann, Houston Methodist, and most major Houston-area ERs can document your injuries. Delays in treatment are one of the first things insurance adjusters point to when questioning the seriousness of a claim.
Screenshot everything. Your Uber or Lyft app showing the trip. The driver's name and vehicle info. Your pickup and dropoff locations. The trip receipt. Take photos of the scene, damage, and your injuries. Get witness names and contact information.
Don't post about the accident on social media. Rideshare companies' legal teams monitor social media. Anything you post can be used against your claim.
Talk to an attorney before you talk to their insurance. A car accident attorney with rideshare experience can identify which phase applied, which insurer is responsible, and whether a direct claim against Uber or Lyft is viable, before you say anything that might limit your options.

### How Texas's Fault Rules Affect Your Rideshare Claim
Texas follows modified comparative fault. Texas reduces what you can recover by your percentage of blame for the accident. If you're found 20% at fault, you recover 80% of your damages. If you're found more than 50% at fault, you recover nothing.
Under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 33.001, your comparative fault percentage must be established, and contested, before damages are reduced. This is one reason documentation matters so much from the start.

### Rideshare Volume in Houston Is Only Growing
Houston's population and its reliance on rideshare have both grown significantly. The Medical Center, Greenway Plaza, downtown, and the Energy Corridor generate constant rideshare demand around the clock. The Loop, 59, and the feeder roads around Hobby Airport and Bush IAH see high volumes of rideshare traffic at all hours.
More rideshare volume means more exposure: more crashes, more insurance complexity, more injured people who don't know where to turn. The legal framework is still catching up to the reality of how many Ubers and Lyfts are on Houston roads every day.
If you've been hurt in a rideshare crash, as a passenger, as a driver in another vehicle, or as a pedestrian, don't assume which coverage applies or accept the first answer you get from an insurance company. The phases matter. The app records matter. And the question of direct liability against the company is worth asking.
Our firm handles rideshare and car accident cases across Harris County and the greater Houston area. If you have questions about what happened to you, a free case review is the right first step.
This article provides general information about Texas law, not legal advice for your specific situation. Every case is different. If you've been injured in Houston or anywhere in Texas, talk with a licensed attorney about the facts of yours. Free case review here, or call (713) 842-9442.

### Common questions
It depends on what the driver was doing in the app at the moment of the crash. If no ride was accepted yet, contingent coverage from Uber or Lyft applies—at least $50,000 per person in bodily injury. If the driver had accepted a ride and the trip was active, Uber and Lyft's full commercial coverage of at least $1 million applies.
It is difficult but not impossible. Because drivers are classified as independent contractors, Uber and Lyft generally avoid vicarious liability. However, Texas law recognizes negligent hiring and negligent retention claims, and Texas HB 1733 created an additional hook if the company approved a driver who should have been disqualified under the law's background-check standards.
Phase 2 means the driver's app is on and they are waiting for a ride request but have not yet accepted one. During this phase, Uber or Lyft's contingent liability coverage—at least $50,000 per person, $100,000 per accident, and $25,000 in property damage—only kicks in if the driver's personal insurance denies the claim or doesn't cover the loss. This phase generates the most insurance disputes.
Uber and Lyft maintain detailed, timestamped logs showing when the app was opened, when a ride was accepted, and when a trip ended. ## Houston set a traffic death record in 2024. What that means now.
Source: https://nalawtx.com/blog/houston-traffic-deaths-2024-record

The numbers landed in early 2025 and they were grim. Houston recorded 301 traffic fatalities in 2024 — the highest annual total in the city's history, surpassing the previous record of 295 set in 2021. Statewide, traffic deaths actually declined slightly. So what's happening in Houston?
By Vu Nguyen, Founder & Managing Partner · Updated April 12, 2026
Houston recorded 301 traffic fatalities in 2024, the highest in city history, with most deaths occurring at surface-street intersections on roads posted at 45 mph or higher. Pedestrian deaths have surged, and Texas's 51% comparative-fault rule means insurance companies will work hard to shift blame onto you if you're hurt.
- Houston's 301 traffic deaths in 2024 broke the previous record of 295 set in 2021.
- 119 pedestrians were killed — nearly one every three days — mostly in daylight on high-speed surface streets.
- A pedestrian hit at 40 mph has roughly a 20% survival chance, compared to 90% at 20 mph.
- Texas's 51% comparative-fault rule lets insurers aggressively argue you share blame — don't give recorded statements.

### Where the deaths happened
Roughly 40% of Houston traffic crashes happen at intersections. The 2024 fatality data follows that pattern. Surface-street intersections — not freeways — were where most of the increase showed up. Speed limits in the 45–50 mph range, combined with frequent driveways, U-turn lanes, and pedestrian crossings, create what urban planners call a "stroad" — a hybrid road designed for highway speeds but used like a city street.
We've documented twelve of the worst examples on our dangerous intersections page. The pattern is consistent: feeder roads carrying traffic at 50 mph meeting cross-streets that need to handle pedestrians, turning movements, and commercial driveways.

### Pedestrian deaths surged
119 pedestrians were killed on Houston streets in 2024 — nearly one pedestrian death every three days. Most of those happened in daylight, on major surface streets, on roads with posted speed limits of 45 mph or higher.
The math here is brutal. A pedestrian struck at 20 mph has roughly a 90% chance of surviving. At 40 mph, that drops to about 20%. Houston's wide arterials and feeder roads put pedestrians in the worst possible speed range when they're crossing to bus stops, businesses, or parking lots.

### Why Vision Zero hasn't worked yet
Houston adopted the Vision Zero plan several years ago with a goal of zero traffic deaths by 2030. The 2024 numbers make it clear we're not on track. Road redesigns take years. Enforcement has been inconsistent. Drivers don't change behavior until something forces them to.
By comparison, Austin — which adopted Vision Zero a decade ago — has seen its traffic fatality rate decrease on city-owned streets. The difference is sustained, multi-year work on the streets themselves, not just public messaging.

### What this means for you, practically
If you drive in Houston, you cannot assume other drivers will obey signals, yield to pedestrians, or maintain safe speeds. The data says they often don't. Defensive habits matter: longer following distances, hesitation through green lights at known-bad intersections, and extra caution at the dozens of feeder-road crossings throughout the city.
If you're a pedestrian, the data says daylight doesn't protect you. The majority of pedestrian deaths in 2024 happened during daylight hours. Wider corridors with limited crosswalk infrastructure are dangerous regardless of time of day.
If you've been hit, you should know that Texas law generally favors injured pedestrians and cyclists in crosswalks — but also follows a 51% comparative-fault rule that insurance companies will use aggressively to push fault onto you. Read how that works.

### If you're hurt: what to do in the next 24 hours
Get medical attention even if you feel okay — adrenaline masks injuries, and gaps in treatment are the #1 argument insurance companies use to reduce claims. Document everything at the scene. Do not give a recorded statement to the at-fault driver's insurance company. Do not sign anything in the first days or weeks — early offers are almost always far below case value.
Our full first 24 hours guide walks through every step.

## Hurt in a Houston Construction Zone? Here's Who Can Be Held Liable Under Texas Law
Source: https://nalawtx.com/blog/hurt-in-a-houston-construction-zone-who-can-be-liable

Harris County recorded 1,900 work-zone crashes in 2024. If you were one of them, more than one party may owe you for your injuries. Figuring out who is the first step.
By Vu Nguyen, Founder & Managing Partner · Updated July 20, 2026
In a Houston construction zone crash, more than one party may owe you for your injuries — including the other driver, the construction contractor, TxDOT, or a property owner. Texas law lets you pursue each responsible party. The key is acting quickly, because critical evidence disappears fast and government claims require a notice filing within six months.
- Harris County recorded 1,900 work-zone crashes in 2024, making it one of Texas's most dangerous counties for these collisions.
- Multiple parties — drivers, contractors, TxDOT, and property owners — can each share legal responsibility for your injuries.
- If a government entity like TxDOT is involved, you typically have only six months to file a formal written notice of claim.
- Construction zone evidence such as dashcam footage and inspection logs can disappear within 30 to 60 days — act fast.
You're driving on I-10 near Katy Freeway, the lanes narrow, the orange barrels crowd in, and then: impact. Maybe another driver rear-ended you. Maybe you hit a pothole that opened up overnight with no warning signs. Maybe a piece of construction equipment crossed into your lane. Whatever happened, you're hurt, your car is wrecked, and now someone is telling you the construction zone makes your situation "complicated."
It is complicated. But complicated doesn't mean hopeless. Work-zone crashes in Texas often involve multiple responsible parties, and Texas law allows you to pursue each one. This post breaks down who those parties are, what you have to prove against each of them, and the deadlines that can cut off your rights if you miss them.

### The Numbers Are Hard to Ignore
TxDOT data shows Harris County recorded 1,900 work-zone crashes in 2024, with 12 fatalities. That makes Harris County one of the most dangerous counties in Texas for construction-zone collisions, which makes sense given that Houston consistently ranks among the most actively constructed metro areas in the country. The 288 corridor, the Grand Parkway expansion, the ongoing I-45 North Houston Highway Improvement Project: if you live here, you spend time in work zones every single week.
One statistic worth knowing: 81 percent of work-zone fatalities in Texas are drivers and passengers, not construction workers. The people most at risk in these zones are you and everyone else in a vehicle moving through them. That's a different picture than what most people imagine when they hear "construction zone accident."

### Who Can Actually Be Responsible?
This is where construction zone cases get legally interesting, and where they differ sharply from a standard two-car crash on the 610 Loop. Instead of one at-fault driver, you may be looking at a chain of responsibility stretching from the person behind you all the way to a state agency.

#### The Other Driver
Most work-zone crashes still start with driver error. Speeding through a reduced-speed zone, following too closely, distracted driving, ignoring merge signs. These are all routine negligence claims against the at-fault driver. Texas uses modified comparative fault: each party's percentage of blame determines their share of the damages. If you're found less than 51 percent at fault, you can still recover, though your recovery is reduced by your own percentage. Under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 33.001, that 51 percent threshold is the line between recovering something and recovering nothing.
In a work zone, speeding carries extra legal weight. Texas doubles fines for traffic violations in active work zones when workers are present. But the bigger point for your case is this: if the other driver was exceeding the posted work-zone speed limit, that fact alone tends to strengthen a negligence claim considerably.

#### The General Contractor or Construction Company
This is where many injury victims leave money on the table. The construction company operating in the zone has its own legal duties, separate from the driver who hit you. Those duties include:
- Properly placing and maintaining traffic control devices (cones, barrels, signs, arrow boards)
- Ensuring adequate lighting in nighttime work zones
- Keeping the roadway surface reasonably safe, including patching excavations, covering gaps, and marking hazards
- Training flaggers and traffic control personnel
- Complying with the Texas Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (TMUTCD)
When a contractor fails at any of those duties and that failure contributes to your crash, they can be liable. The TMUTCD is essentially the rulebook for how work zones in Texas must be set up. If investigators find the zone wasn't configured to its standards. wrong sign placement, missing channelizing devices, inadequate advance warning. that's a documented breach of duty.
Contractors also frequently use subcontractors. If a subcontractor's crew set up a lane closure incorrectly, the general contractor may still share responsibility. Construction liability can run through the whole project chain.

#### TxDOT or the Relevant Government Entity
This one surprises people. Can you sue the Texas Department of Transportation? Sometimes, yes. Texas waived certain governmental immunity protections under the Texas Tort Claims Act ( Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 101.001 et seq.), which allows injury claims against state and local government entities in limited circumstances, including certain roadway and premises conditions.
If TxDOT designed a work-zone traffic control plan that was inherently unsafe, or if a TxDOT employee's actions contributed to the crash, there may be a viable claim. The same applies to Harris County or the City of Houston if the project was on a county or municipal road.
But there's a critical catch: claims against government entities in Texas come with a strict notice requirement and shorter deadlines. Under the Texas Tort Claims Act, you typically have six months to file a formal written notice of claim with the government entity before you can sue. Miss that window and you may be permanently barred from the claim, even if your two-year statute of limitations hasn't run yet. More on that below.

#### The Property Owner or Project Owner
On private construction projects, a new commercial development along the Westheimer corridor, a warehouse going up in Katy, a mixed-use project near The Heights, the property owner who hired the contractor may also bear responsibility if they had control over how the work was done or how traffic was managed around it.
Texas premises liability law requires property owners to keep conditions reasonably safe for people who have a right to be on or near the property. A driver navigating a construction entrance or a pedestrian walking past an active job site may have a premises liability claim against the project owner if inadequate precautions caused the injury.

### What You Have to Prove
Regardless of which party (or parties) you're pursuing, the core of any Texas negligence claim is the same four elements: duty, breach, causation, and damages.
Duty means the defendant owed you a legal obligation. Drivers owe a duty of reasonable care to others on the road. Contractors owe a duty to maintain a safe work zone. TxDOT owes certain duties to the traveling public.
Breach means they failed to meet that duty. The other driver was speeding. The contractor left a gap in the lane markings with no warning. The traffic control plan had inadequate advance notice distance for highway speeds.
Causation means their breach actually caused your crash and your injuries, not some independent cause. This is where construction zone cases get technically demanding, because defense attorneys will argue the dangerous road condition was obvious and you should have slowed down or chosen a different route.
Damages means you suffered actual harm: medical bills, lost wages, pain, property damage. Texas lets injured parties recover both economic damages (things with a dollar figure) and non-economic damages (pain and suffering, mental anguish, loss of enjoyment of life).
When more than one party is at fault, Texas law lets the jury assign a percentage of responsibility to each. Your attorney's job is to make sure all the responsible parties are identified and named, because you can only recover from defendants who are actually in the case.

### Evidence That Wins These Cases, and Disappears Fast
Construction zone crashes generate a specific category of evidence you can't get anywhere else, and it tends to vanish quickly once a project moves forward.
Traffic control plans. Every TxDOT project requires a detailed TCP showing exactly how lanes, signs, and devices were supposed to be arranged. If the actual setup didn't match the plan, that's a documented breach. These plans are public record through TxDOT, but they're tied to specific project phases that get updated as work progresses.
Project inspection logs. Contractors are typically required to keep daily inspection logs of their traffic control setup. Those logs, or gaps in them, can be critical.
Dashcam and construction site cameras. Many active work zones have cameras for project monitoring. Private dashcam footage from other drivers in the same zone can be priceless. Both types of footage routinely get overwritten within 30 to 60 days.
The physical scene. Skid marks, gouge marks, paint transfers, and the position of traffic control devices all tell a story. Once the next phase of construction begins, that evidence is gone permanently.
Witness statements. Other drivers, flaggers, and construction workers may have seen what happened. Their memory fades. Their contact information gets harder to track down the longer you wait.
The practical takeaway: the sooner an attorney can get investigators out to the scene and send document preservation notices to the contractor and TxDOT, the better. This is not the type of case where waiting a few months to "see how things shake out" serves you.

### Deadlines You Cannot Afford to Miss
Texas has a two-year statute of limitations for personal injury claims. Under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003, you generally have two years from the date of the accident to file suit. Miss that deadline and your case is over, no matter how strong it was.
But in construction zone cases where a government entity may be liable (TxDOT, Harris County, the City of Houston) the timeline is tighter. The Texas Tort Claims Act requires written notice of your claim to be filed with the appropriate governmental unit, typically within six months of the incident. That notice must include specific information: the date, time, and place of the incident, a description of your injuries, and the damage you're claiming.
Six months sounds like a long time when you're still in physical therapy and dealing with insurance calls. It isn't. Many injured people don't realize a government entity is a potential defendant until an attorney reviews their case. By then, the notice deadline may have already passed.
If a government entity is even a possible defendant in your construction zone crash, treat the six-month notice deadline as the real deadline. Not the two-year statute of limitations.

### What Insurance Companies Do in These Cases
Multi-party construction zone claims are exactly the type of case where insurance companies get creative about pointing fingers at each other. The driver's insurer says the contractor set up a dangerous zone. The contractor's insurer says the driver was speeding. TxDOT's legal team argues governmental immunity. Each one is hoping you'll take a quick settlement from one of them and go away before you understand the full picture of who was responsible.
Recorded statements are particularly dangerous here. An adjuster from the contractor's insurer may call you within days of the crash, framing it as a routine follow-up. Anything you say about the layout of the zone, your speed, your visibility, or your awareness of the construction area can be used to reduce or eliminate what you can recover. You have no obligation to give that statement, and doing so without an attorney reviewing your case first is rarely in your interest.
Our car accident practice page covers what to do in the immediate aftermath of any Houston crash. Those same steps apply in a construction zone, with even more urgency given the evidence timeline.

### Workers Hurt on the Job Site: Different Rules Apply
If you're a construction worker who was injured in the work zone, not a driver passing through, your situation involves a different legal framework. Texas is the only state that doesn't require most private employers to carry workers' compensation insurance. If your employer opted out of the Texas workers' comp system, your rights and remedies are different than those of an employee covered by a traditional policy.
Workers injured on a TxDOT project site may also have claims against the general contractor, subcontractors, or equipment manufacturers depending on what caused the injury. These cases cross employment law, personal injury law, and sometimes product liability. An attorney familiar with Texas construction injury law can help sort out which claims apply to your situation.

### Questions to Ask When You Talk to an Attorney
Not every attorney handles construction zone cases regularly. These cases require familiarity with TxDOT procurement contracts, traffic control standards, and the Texas Tort Claims Act notice procedures. When you consult with a lawyer, ask:
- Have you handled work-zone accident cases in Harris County before?
- Do you have access to accident reconstruction experts?
- Will you send document preservation notices to the contractor and TxDOT immediately?
- Do you handle the case on contingency, meaning you only get paid if I recover?
That last point matters. Most personal injury attorneys in Texas, including our firm, work on a contingency fee basis. You pay nothing upfront. The attorney's fee comes out of the recovery, if there is one. That arrangement means your attorney has every incentive to pursue every responsible party, not just the easiest one.
If you were hurt in a Houston construction zone crash, talk to someone who handles these cases before you talk to any insurance adjuster. The consultation at nalawtx.com is free, and it gives you a clear picture of what you're actually dealing with.
This article provides general information about Texas law, not legal advice for your specific situation. Every case is different. If you've been injured in Houston or anywhere in Texas, talk with a licensed attorney about the facts of yours. Free case review here, or call (713) 842-9442.

### Common questions
Sometimes, yes. Texas waived certain governmental immunity protections under the Texas Tort Claims Act (Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 101.001 et seq.), which allows injury claims against state and local government entities in limited circumstances. If TxDOT designed an unsafe traffic control plan or a TxDOT employee's actions contributed to the crash, there may be a viable claim. However, you typically must file a formal written notice of claim with the government entity within six months of the incident.
Liability can extend to the at-fault driver, the general contractor or construction company, TxDOT or another government entity, and even the property or project owner. Each party has separate legal duties — for example, contractors must properly place traffic control devices and comply with the Texas Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (TMUTCD). Texas law allows you to pursue each responsible party, and a jury can assign a percentage of fault to each one.
Texas generally gives you two years from the date of the accident to file a personal injury lawsuit under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003. However, if a government entity like TxDOT, Harris County, or the City of Houston is a potential defendant, the Texas Tort Claims Act requires written notice of your claim within six months of the incident. Missing that six-month window can permanently bar your claim against the government entity, even if the two-year deadline hasn't passed.
Key evidence includes the contractor's traffic control plan (TCP), daily project inspection logs, dashcam footage from nearby vehicles, construction site camera recordings, and the physical scene itself. Dashcam and site camera footage is often overwritten within 30 to 60 days, and once the next phase of construction begins, physical evidence like skid marks and device positions is gone permanently. Sending document preservation notices to the contractor and TxDOT as early as possible is critical.

## Injured as a Passenger in a Houston Car Wreck? Why You're Almost Never at Fault and How to Claim Against Multiple Drivers
Source: https://nalawtx.com/blog/injured-as-a-passenger-in-a-houston-car-wreck-heres-how-to

As a passenger, you didn't cause the crash. But getting compensated can still get complicated fast, especially when two drivers are pointing fingers at each other. Here's what Texas law says about your rights and exactly how to protect them.
By Vu Nguyen, Founder & Managing Partner · Updated November 9, 2026
As a passenger in a Houston car wreck, you are almost never at fault because you weren't driving. Texas law allows you to file claims against both drivers simultaneously, and you may have access to multiple insurance policies. You have two years from the crash date to file a lawsuit under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003.
- As a passenger, you can file claims against both drivers' insurance policies at the same time without choosing one.
- Texas requires drivers to carry minimum liability coverage, but those limits can be quickly exhausted by serious injuries.
- You are not required to give a recorded statement to any insurance adjuster before speaking with an attorney.
- The two-year filing deadline under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003 goes faster than it seems — start early.
You were just along for the ride. Maybe a friend was driving you home from a Texans game. Maybe you were in a rideshare crossing the I-10/Loop 610 interchange. Maybe you were a passenger on 290 when another car ran a red light and T-boned you. It doesn't matter how you got there. You were sitting in that seat, you got hurt, and now you're trying to figure out whose insurance pays for it.
Here's the short answer: almost certainly not yours. As a passenger, you typically had no control over what happened. Texas law reflects that. But "not your fault" and "easy to collect" are two different things. When two drivers each blame the other, which happens constantly in Houston two-car collisions, you can find yourself stuck in the middle while your medical bills pile up. This post walks you through how passenger claims actually work in Texas, what to do right now, and what insurance adjusters won't tell you.

### Passengers and Fault: The Short Version
Texas uses a fault-based system for car accidents. Whoever caused the crash is financially responsible for injuries. As a passenger, you weren't driving, so in nearly every accident scenario, you bear zero responsibility for what happened.
There are narrow exceptions. If you grabbed the steering wheel, if you were distracting the driver in a way that caused the crash, if you somehow contributed to the collision, a court could find you partially at fault. In practice, those scenarios are rare. The vast majority of passenger injury cases involve fault that belongs entirely to one or both drivers.
Texas follows modified comparative fault. Basically, your ability to recover is reduced by whatever percentage of blame is assigned to you. If a jury found you 10% at fault, you'd recover 10% less. If you're found more than 50% at fault, you recover nothing. For passengers, that threshold almost never comes into play. But it's worth knowing the rule exists under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 33.001.

### Who Actually Pays When You're Injured as a Passenger?
This is where passengers get surprised. You have more options than you might think, and potentially more insurance policies available to you than either driver does.

#### The at-fault driver's liability insurance
Texas requires drivers to carry a minimum of $30,000 per person / $60,000 per accident in bodily injury liability coverage. If one driver caused the crash, their liability policy is your first target. You file a third-party claim directly against the at-fault driver's insurance.
The problem: Texas minimums are low. A single night at Memorial Hermann or Texas Medical Center can exceed $30,000. If the at-fault driver only carries the state minimum, or if they're uninsured, that limit won't cover serious injuries.

#### The driver of your vehicle
If the driver you were riding with contributed to the crash, their liability insurance is also potentially on the hook for your injuries. This feels awkward when it's your friend or family member. But their insurance is exactly what it's there for, and making a claim against it doesn't necessarily mean suing them personally.
Some passengers hesitate to make a claim against someone they know. That hesitation is understandable, but it usually works against you financially. The driver's insurer, not the driver personally, is the one paying.

#### Uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage (UM/UIM)
If the at-fault driver has no insurance, or not enough to cover your injuries, uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage fills the gap. Under Texas law, insurers are required to offer UM/UIM coverage, though drivers can decline it in writing. If you have your own auto policy, your UM/UIM coverage may apply even though you weren't driving. The driver's policy UM/UIM coverage may also be available to you as a passenger in their vehicle.

#### Your own health insurance
Your health insurance can cover medical treatment regardless of fault. Using it right away, before any insurance claim settles, keeps you out of medical debt while everything gets sorted out. Your health insurer may later assert a lien against any settlement you receive (this is called subrogation), but that's a problem your attorney helps manage.

### The Hardest Scenario: Both Drivers Are Partly at Fault
Two-car accidents in Houston often come down to a dispute. Driver A says Driver B ran the light. Driver B says Driver A was speeding. Both insurers open investigations. Both may deny or minimize liability. Meanwhile, you're the injured passenger with legitimate claims against both of them, and neither insurer is in a hurry to pay.
As a passenger, you can file claims against both drivers simultaneously. You don't have to wait for them to sort out whose fault it was. You don't have to pick one.
Texas law allows you to pursue both drivers, and both insurance policies, at the same time. Each insurer may argue the other driver bears more blame. That's their problem to work out, not yours. Your job is to document your injuries and let your attorney manage the competing claims.
What this looks like practically: you may receive partial offers from each insurer, each pointing at the other driver. Neither offer alone may fully compensate you. An attorney's job in this situation is to negotiate across both policies simultaneously and, if necessary, file suit against both defendants so a Harris County jury can apportion fault between them.

### What to Do in the Hours and Days After the Crash
The steps you take right after a crash matter. A lot. Evidence disappears fast in Houston traffic. Here's what to prioritize.

#### Get medical attention immediately
If you were transported by ambulance, to Ben Taub, Memorial Hermann, Houston Methodist, or anywhere else, follow up with every appointment. If you weren't taken by ambulance, still get evaluated the same day or the next morning. Soft tissue injuries, concussions, and internal injuries don't always show symptoms at the scene. A gap in medical treatment gives insurers ammunition to argue your injuries weren't serious or weren't caused by the crash.

#### Document everything at the scene
If you're physically able: photograph both vehicles, the road conditions, any skid marks, traffic signals, and the surrounding intersection. Get the names, license plate numbers, and insurance information for both drivers. Get contact information from witnesses. All of this is harder to reconstruct later.

#### Get the police report
If Houston Police Department or Harris County Sheriff's Office responded, a crash report was filed. You can request it through the Texas Department of Transportation's TxDOT Crash Report portal. The report documents the responding officer's assessment of fault, which matters when insurers dispute liability.

#### Be careful what you say to adjusters
Both insurers will call you quickly. They're friendly. They sound helpful. They want a recorded statement. You are not required to give one, especially not before you've spoken to an attorney. What you say in those early calls can be used to minimize your claim. If an adjuster calls, you can confirm the basics (you were a passenger, you were injured) and tell them you'll be in touch once you've consulted with counsel.

### The Two-Year Clock in Texas
Texas gives most personal injury victims two years from the date of the accident to file a lawsuit. That's the statute of limitations under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003. Miss that deadline and you generally lose your right to sue, no matter how strong your case is.
Two years sounds like a lot of time. It goes fast when you're recovering, dealing with medical appointments, and waiting on insurance negotiations. The practical reality: evidence degrades, witnesses forget details, and building a strong case takes time. Most attorneys want to be involved well before the deadline, not racing toward it.
There are limited exceptions, for minors, for cases involving government vehicles, and a few others, but don't assume an exception applies to you. Talk to an attorney early.

### Rideshare Crashes: Uber and Lyft Passengers Have Additional Considerations
Houston has a large rideshare presence, and passenger injury claims involving Uber or Lyft add another layer of complexity. Both companies carry commercial liability policies, up to $1 million per occurrence when a driver has an active fare, but the coverage depends on exactly what phase of the trip the driver was in at the time of the crash.
If your Lyft driver caused the crash, Lyft's commercial policy is the primary target. If a third-party driver hit your Lyft, you have claims against that driver and potentially against Lyft's underinsured motorist coverage. The rideshare company's insurance adjusters handle these situations routinely. You probably don't.
Rideshare injury claims also involve preserving your trip records. Screenshot your app confirmation and trip details immediately. That documentation ties the driver to the platform at the time of the crash, which matters for coverage purposes.

### What Damages Can You Recover as an Injured Passenger?
Texas law allows injured passengers to pursue the same categories of damages as any other injury victim.
Economic damages are the concrete financial losses: medical bills (past and future), lost wages if your injuries kept you from working, and costs of future care or rehabilitation.
Non-economic damages cover things that don't have an invoice: physical pain and suffering, mental anguish, loss of enjoyment of life, and in serious cases, disfigurement or physical impairment.
Texas does not cap non-economic damages in car accident cases (unlike medical malpractice cases, which have different rules). What you can recover depends on the specific facts of your injury, your treatment, and your life. Not on a formula.
Being a passenger actually puts you in a stronger legal position than either driver in most crashes. You didn't cause it. The fight over fault happens between the drivers, not between you and either of them.

### When Does a Passenger Injury Claim Need an Attorney?
Not every crash requires legal representation. If you walked away with a minor scrape and your medical bills were handled quickly, you may not need one. But passenger injury claims involving more than minor injuries, especially when two drivers are disputing fault, almost always benefit from attorney involvement.
Here's why: you have claims against potentially two insurance companies, each of whom has adjusters and attorneys whose job is to pay as little as possible. You're managing your own recovery at the same time. An attorney handles the insurance communications, preserves evidence, coordinates your medical documentation, and negotiates across both policies. If a fair resolution isn't reached, they file suit in Harris County District Court on your behalf.
Personal injury attorneys in Texas, including our firm, work on contingency. You pay nothing upfront and nothing at all unless your case resolves in your favor. There's no financial risk in at least having a conversation. You can start a free case review here or call us directly at (713) 842-9442.
For a broader look at how car accident claims work in Texas, see our car accident practice page.

### A Quick Summary: Your Rights as an Injured Passenger
- You are almost never at fault as a passenger, and Texas law protects your right to full recovery.
- You can file claims against both drivers simultaneously if both contributed to the crash.
- You may have access to multiple insurance policies: both drivers' liability coverage, UM/UIM coverage, and your own health insurance.
- You are not required to give a recorded statement to any insurance adjuster before consulting an attorney.
- You have two years from the date of the crash to file suit under Texas law, but starting early protects your evidence and options.
- Rideshare passengers have additional coverage layers but also additional complexity.
The crash wasn't your fault. Getting the compensation you're owed shouldn't require you to become an expert in Texas insurance law on your own. That's what we're here for.
This article provides general information about Texas law, not legal advice for your specific situation. Every case is different. If you've been injured as a passenger in Houston or anywhere in Texas, talk with a licensed attorney about the facts of yours. Free case review here, or call (713) 842-9442.

### Common questions
In nearly every scenario, passengers bear zero responsibility for a crash because they weren't driving. Under Texas's modified comparative fault rule in Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 33.001, fault could theoretically be assigned if you grabbed the wheel or directly caused the collision, but those situations are rare. For most passengers, fault belongs entirely to one or both drivers.
You may have access to several policies at once: the at-fault driver's liability insurance, the driver of your vehicle's liability insurance if they contributed to the crash, uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage from either policy, and your own health insurance. You don't have to wait for the drivers to settle their dispute before pursuing your claims. An attorney can negotiate across multiple policies simultaneously.
Rideshare passengers have additional coverage layers to consider. Both Uber and Lyft carry commercial liability policies of up to $1 million per occurrence when a driver has an active fare, but the coverage depends on what phase of the trip the driver was in at the time of the crash. Screenshot your app confirmation and trip details immediately, as that documentation ties the driver to the platform and matters for coverage purposes.
No, you are not required to give a recorded statement to any insurance adjuster before consulting an attorney. Adjusters may call quickly and sound helpful, but what you say in those early calls can be used to minimize your claim. You can confirm basic facts — that you were a passenger and were injured — and let them know you'll be in touch after speaking with counsel.

## Injured at Work in Texas? What Happens When Your Employer Skipped Workers' Comp
Source: https://nalawtx.com/blog/injured-at-work-in-texas-how-non-subscriber-claims-work

Texas is the only state where private employers can opt out of workers' compensation entirely. Hundreds of thousands of workers don't know their employer did exactly that. Here's what it means for you if you're hurt on the job.
By Vu Nguyen, Founder & Managing Partner · Updated November 21, 2026
If your employer in Texas never bought workers' compensation insurance, they are a 'non-subscriber,' and you keep your right to sue them directly for negligence. Texas law also strips non-subscribers of their most powerful defenses, such as blaming you or a coworker. This can put you in a stronger position than a standard workers' comp claim.
- Texas is the only state where private employers can legally skip workers' compensation coverage.
- Non-subscriber employers cannot use contributory negligence, assumption of risk, or the fellow servant rule as defenses.
- You can pursue full damages in a lawsuit, including pain and suffering and lost earning capacity, not just a capped formula.
- Texas law gives you two years to file a lawsuit under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003, but evidence disappears fast.
You got hurt at work. Maybe a forklift clipped you in a warehouse off Beltway 8. Maybe you fell from scaffolding at a construction site in Katy. Maybe a piece of equipment failed and took off part of your hand.
Your first assumption, the same one most people make, is that workers' compensation covers you. You'll file a claim, get your medical bills paid, collect some wage replacement while you heal, and eventually go back to work.
Then you find out your employer is a non-subscriber. They never bought workers' comp insurance. And suddenly the path forward looks completely different from anything you expected.
This is a good moment to stop and actually understand what that means. In Texas, being an injured employee of a non-subscriber is not necessarily worse than being covered by workers' comp. In some ways, it's significantly better.

### Texas Is the Only State Where This Is Legal
Every other state in the country requires private employers to carry workers' compensation insurance. Texas does not. Under Texas law, workers' comp coverage is entirely voluntary for most private employers.
That single fact reshapes everything about workplace injury claims in this state.
Estimates put the share of Texas private employers who have opted out (called "non-subscribers") somewhere between 25% and 40%. That's not a fringe phenomenon. Some of the largest employers in the Houston area are non-subscribers, including major retailers and distribution companies whose workers handle physically demanding jobs every day.
If your employer is one of them and you get hurt, you are not without options. You're just on a different legal track than a standard workers' comp claim. And that track has real teeth.

### How to Find Out If Your Employer Is a Non-Subscriber
Texas employers are required to notify employees in writing whether they carry workers' comp coverage. That notice should be posted at your workplace and given to you when you're hired. Under Texas Labor Code § 406.004, non-subscribing employers must file an annual notice with the Texas Department of Insurance, Division of Workers' Compensation.
In practice, a lot of workers never read that notice or don't remember seeing it. Here's how to check:
- Look at your onboarding paperwork. Non-subscribers are required to give new hires written notice of their non-subscriber status.
- Check the Texas Department of Insurance's online database. You can search by employer name to see whether a company has filed as a non-subscriber.
- Ask your HR department directly. They're required to tell you.
- Call an attorney. If you've been injured and you're not sure, a quick consultation can answer that question fast, and it costs you nothing.

### What Changes When Your Employer Doesn't Have Workers' Comp
Workers' compensation is a trade-off system. Employees give up the right to sue their employer in exchange for automatic, no-fault coverage: medical bills paid, partial wage replacement, no need to prove anyone was negligent. It's predictable. It's also capped.
When your employer is a non-subscriber, that trade-off never happened. You kept your right to sue.
That matters enormously. In a standard workers' comp claim in Texas, you generally cannot recover for pain and suffering, full lost wages, or loss of future earning capacity. The system pays a formula, not what your injury actually cost you as a person.
In a non-subscriber lawsuit, you can pursue the full range of damages a negligence claim allows: past and future medical expenses, lost income, reduced earning capacity, pain and suffering, and in some cases damages for how the injury has changed your daily life.
The non-subscriber system in Texas was designed to give employers flexibility. But it also removes the legal shields they'd have under workers' comp. That's real negotiating power you can use.

### The Big Advantage: Non-Subscribers Can't Use Most Common Defenses
Here's where the law gets notably favorable for injured workers.
Under Texas Labor Code § 406.033, when an employer is a non-subscriber and an employee is injured, the employer cannot use three of the most powerful defenses available in a typical negligence lawsuit:
- Contributory negligence. the argument that the worker was partly at fault
- Assumption of risk. the argument that the worker knew the job was dangerous and accepted that risk
- Fellow servant rule. the argument that a coworker's negligence, not the employer's, caused the injury
Stripping those defenses away is a big deal. In most personal injury cases in Texas, the defense team spends enormous energy trying to shift some of the blame onto you. Modified comparative fault is one of the most common tools insurers use to drive down settlements. Basically, Texas reduces what you can recover by your share of the blame.
Non-subscriber cases largely sidestep that. You still have to show the employer's negligence caused your injury. But the employer can't walk in and say "well, you should have known better" or "a coworker made a mistake, not us."

### What You Have to Prove in a Non-Subscriber Case
This is the part people sometimes misunderstand. A non-subscriber lawsuit is not automatic. You do have to prove that your employer's negligence caused your injury. The burden of proof is on you.
Negligence in a workplace context usually means one of a few things:
- The employer failed to maintain a safe work environment
- The employer didn't provide adequate safety equipment or training
- The employer knew about a dangerous condition and did nothing about it
- A supervisor or manager's actions directly caused the injury
Building that case requires evidence: incident reports, OSHA logs, maintenance records, witness statements, photos of the scene, and your medical records. The earlier you start gathering that evidence, the stronger your position. Evidence disappears fast at job sites. Equipment gets repaired. Witnesses move on.
If you've been injured at a Harris County work site, a Montgomery County warehouse, or anywhere else in the Houston region, the clock on preserving that evidence started the moment you got hurt.

### What a 2025 Texas Supreme Court Ruling Changed
In In re East Texas Medical Center Athens (No. 23-1039), decided April 25, 2025, the Texas Supreme Court held that a non-subscribing employer can designate responsible third parties under Texas's proportionate responsibility law, Chapter 33 of the Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code.
The practical effect: your employer can now ask the jury to assign part of the blame to someone else, such as an equipment maker or an outside contractor, and that can reduce what the employer owes you. What did not change is the Labor Code protection described above. A non-subscribing employer still cannot use your own negligence, assumption of risk, or a coworker's negligence as a defense.
That is not good news for injured workers, but it can be managed with early investigation into everyone who may share fault. We cover the decision in detail in our post on the 2025 ruling.

### What Employers Do Instead of Carrying Workers' Comp
Non-subscriber employers don't just leave themselves exposed. Most of them buy something called an "occupational accident" policy, a private insurance product that looks like workers' comp from the outside but operates very differently.
These policies are not regulated the same way workers' comp is. They're written to protect the employer's interests, not yours. They commonly include:
- Benefit caps well below what a lawsuit might recover
- Short windows to report your injury and file a claim
- Requirements that you sign documents limiting your rights before receiving any benefits
- Clauses that deny coverage if you don't follow specific internal procedures
This is where a lot of injured workers get hurt a second time. They accept a small payout from an occupational accident policy, sign a release, and later realize they gave up the right to sue for a fraction of what their case was worth.
Do not sign anything from your employer or their insurance company after a serious workplace injury without talking to an attorney first. That's not alarmism. That's just the reality of how these policies are structured.
An occupational accident policy is not workers' comp. It was written by the employer's insurer, for the employer's benefit. Read it, and read it with help, before you accept anything.

### The Deadline You Cannot Miss
Texas law gives injured workers two years to file a personal injury lawsuit. That deadline comes from Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003. Two years sounds like a long time. It isn't, once you account for everything a non-subscriber case requires: gathering records, identifying witnesses, retaining experts, building the liability picture.
Waiting also hurts your case in a practical way. Security camera footage gets overwritten. Coworkers who saw what happened move to other jobs or other cities. Equipment gets replaced or repaired. The sooner you move, the more of that evidence is still available.
Some non-subscriber policies have their own internal deadlines, sometimes as short as 30 or 90 days to report your injury. Missing those deadlines can complicate your claim even if you still have time to file a lawsuit. Get legal advice early.

### Steps to Take Right Now If You Were Hurt at Work
The first week after a workplace injury is when you make decisions that will shape everything that follows. Here's what matters most:
- Get medical care immediately. Don't wait. If you're at a job site in the Houston area, Memorial Hermann, HCA Houston Healthcare, and Harris Health System all have trauma-capable facilities. Your health comes first, and your medical records become the backbone of your claim.
- Report the injury to your employer in writing. Verbal reports get forgotten or disputed. Put it in writing, keep a copy, note the date and who you told.
- Document everything you can. Photos of the scene, photos of your injuries, names and contact information of coworkers who witnessed what happened. If you can write down a detailed account of exactly what occurred while it's fresh, do it.
- Find out whether your employer carries workers' comp. The answer to that question changes your entire legal strategy.
- Don't sign anything from your employer or their insurer. Not until you've spoken with an attorney about what it says and what you'd be giving up.
- Talk to an attorney before you give a recorded statement. If an adjuster calls, and they will call fast, you are not required to give a recorded statement on the spot. What you say can be used to limit your recovery later.

### What a Non-Subscriber Case Actually Looks Like
Most non-subscriber cases in Texas don't go to trial. They resolve through negotiation or mediation. But the credible threat of a jury trial, in Harris County District Court or wherever the case is venued, is what drives fair settlements.
Non-subscriber cases that go to trial are decided by juries who hear the full human story: what your injury did to your life, your family, your ability to work and do the things you used to do. That's very different from a workers' comp administrative proceeding, which is a bureaucratic process decided by hearing officers applying statutory formulas.
Juries in Texas can and do hold employers accountable when the evidence shows they put workers in danger and refused to take reasonable precautions. That accountability, the real possibility of it, is exactly why non-subscriber cases carry serious negotiating weight.
If you've been seriously hurt and your employer is a non-subscriber, you are not in a hopeless situation. You may actually be in a stronger position than an employee covered by workers' comp. But only if you act quickly and with proper legal guidance. Our practice areas page covers the types of workplace injury cases we handle across the Houston area.
This article provides general information about Texas law, not legal advice for your specific situation. Every case is different. If you've been injured in Houston or anywhere in Texas, talk with a licensed attorney about the facts of yours. Free case review here, or call (713) 842-9442.

### Common questions
Texas requires employers to notify workers in writing whether they carry workers' comp coverage, and that notice should be posted at your workplace. You can also search the Texas Department of Insurance's online database by employer name. Under Texas Labor Code § 406.004, non-subscribing employers must file an annual notice with the state, so the information is on record.
Unlike a standard workers' comp claim, a non-subscriber lawsuit lets you pursue the full range of damages a negligence claim allows. That includes past and future medical expenses, lost income, reduced earning capacity, pain and suffering, and damages for how the injury has changed your daily life. Workers' comp, by contrast, pays a formula that generally excludes pain and suffering and full lost wages.
Texas law gives you two years to file a personal injury lawsuit under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003. However, some occupational accident policies that non-subscribers carry have internal reporting deadlines as short as 30 or 90 days. Acting quickly also helps preserve evidence like security footage, witness accounts, and equipment records before they disappear.
Yes, in In re East Texas Medical Center Athens (No. 23-1039), decided April 25, 2025, the Texas Supreme Court held that a non-subscribing employer can designate responsible third parties under Chapter 33 of the Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code, potentially shifting part of the blame to others like equipment makers or outside contractors. However, the Labor Code protections were not changed, meaning the employer still cannot use your own negligence, assumption of risk, or a coworker's negligence as a defense.

## Texas laws that shape your injury claim. A 2026 plain-language guide.
Source: https://nalawtx.com/blog/new-texas-laws-affecting-injury-claims

Texas personal injury law has a handful of rules that don't exist in the same form in other states — and that have outsized influence on what happens to your claim. If you're considering filing, these are the ones that matter most.
By Vu Nguyen, Founder & Managing Partner · Updated March 28, 2026
Texas injury claims are shaped by a two-year filing deadline, a modified comparative fault rule that cuts off recovery if you are 51% or more at fault, and several other state-specific rules. Missing any one of these—especially shorter deadlines for government claims—can end your case entirely. Learning how they work before talking to an insurer protects your rights.
- You generally have two years to file, but government entity claims can require notice in as little as 90 days.
- If you are found 51% or more at fault, you recover nothing under Texas's modified comparative fault rule.
- Since 2015, seat belt non-use can be used as evidence to reduce your damages.
- Texas employers can opt out of workers' comp; those non-subscribers lose key defenses, often increasing worker recoveries.

### The two-year statute of limitations
Under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code §16.003, most personal-injury lawsuits must be filed within two years of the date of injury. Miss this deadline and the claim is typically gone forever. Insurance adjusters know this and routinely drag negotiations past the two-year mark when victims don't have counsel.
Important shorter deadlines: claims against Texas government entities require notice within six months under the Texas Tort Claims Act, and the City of Houston requires notice in just 90 days. If your crash involved a METRO bus, a city vehicle, or a public hospital, the 90-day clock matters as much as the two-year one. Full deadlines guide.

### Modified comparative fault — the 51% bar
Texas follows a modified comparative negligence rule. If you are 50% or less at fault for your own injury, you can recover damages — reduced by your percentage of fault. If you are 51% or more at fault, you recover nothing.
Insurance defense lawyers fight hard over fault percentages because of this cliff. Pushing the plaintiff from 49% to 51% can shift the entire case value to zero. How the 51% rule plays out in practice.

### Seat belt evidence is now admissible
Before 2015, Texas law prohibited evidence about whether an injured person was wearing a seat belt. The Texas Supreme Court changed that in Nabors Well Services, Ltd. v. Romero, holding that seat belt non-use evidence can now be presented to reduce damages.
Practical impact: if you were unbelted and the crash made your injuries worse than they would have been with a belt, the defense will argue your damages should be reduced. Were you belted? Document it now — through dashcam, witness, EMS records, anywhere it's verifiable.

### Texas non-subscriber workers' comp
Unlike every other state, Texas allows employers to opt out of the workers' compensation system. Employers who opt out are called "non-subscribers," and the rules change significantly when an employee gets hurt at one of these workplaces.
Non-subscriber employers lose three key defenses : contributory negligence, assumption of the risk, and the fellow-servant rule. That means even if the worker was partially at fault, it does not reduce the recovery in a civil suit. Recoveries against non-subscribers can therefore be significantly larger than what workers' comp would have paid. Full non-subscriber guide.

### Texas Dram Shop Act
Texas Alcoholic Beverage Code Chapter 2 lets victims of drunk-driver crashes sue the bar or restaurant that over-served the driver. The plaintiff must show the establishment served alcohol when the patron was visibly intoxicated and that the intoxication caused the harm.
Why this matters: drunk drivers often have minimum insurance limits — $30,000 per person under Texas's 30/60/25 minimum. Bar commercial general liability policies are often $1 million or more. Adding the bar to the case can transform recovery in a way the driver's policy alone cannot. Full dram shop guide.

### Red light cameras are banned
Texas banned the use of photographic traffic-signal enforcement systems (red-light cameras) in 2019. This means in a typical Houston intersection crash, you cannot rely on automated camera tickets to prove the other driver ran a red light. You need witness testimony, dashcam footage, surveillance video from nearby businesses, or physical evidence to prove signal violations.
This puts a premium on fast evidence preservation — bar surveillance video can be overwritten in 30 days, business cameras in even less.

### The takeaway
These rules create the framework for every Texas injury claim. They explain why insurance adjusters push fault onto you (51% bar), why they delay (waiting out the two-year clock), why they ask about your medical history (looking for arguable pre-existing conditions), and why they ask about seat belt use.
If you've been injured, the time to learn how these rules work is before you talk to any insurance company — not after.
This blog post is general information about Texas law, not legal advice for your specific case. Every case has different facts. For a free case-specific review, call (713) 842-9442 or start an online case review.

If your injury involved a government entity like the City of Houston, you may need to give notice in as little as 90 days. Missing these deadlines typically means losing your claim forever.
Texas follows a modified comparative negligence rule. If you are 50% or less at fault, you can still recover damages, but they are reduced by your percentage of fault. If you are found 51% or more at fault, you recover nothing at all.

Under Texas Alcoholic Beverage Code Chapter 2, known as the Dram Shop Act, victims can sue an establishment that over-served a driver who was visibly intoxicated if that intoxication caused the harm. This matters because bar commercial liability policies are often far larger than a driver's minimum insurance coverage.
