## You Were Hit by a Car in Houston. But You Weren't in a Crosswalk. Can You Still Recover?
Source: https://nalawtx.com/blog/pedestrian-accidents-outside-crosswalks-texas-fault-rules

Texas's comparative fault rules don't automatically bar your claim just because you crossed mid-block. Here's what actually happens to your recovery, and how insurers use the "no crosswalk" argument to pay you less than you deserve.
By Vu Nguyen, Founder & Managing Partner · Updated October 12, 2026
Being hit outside a crosswalk does not automatically bar your recovery in Texas. Under the state's modified comparative fault rules, you can still recover damages as long as you are not found more than 50% at fault. The driver's speed, attention, and other factors all affect how fault is divided.
- Texas law still requires drivers to exercise due care to avoid hitting pedestrians, even mid-block.
- Under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 33.001, you recover nothing only if you are found more than 50% at fault.
- Insurance adjusters' fault percentages are negotiating positions, not legal findings — you don't have to accept them.
- Traffic camera footage can disappear in as little as 24 to 72 hours, so preserving evidence quickly is critical.
A driver hit you. You're dealing with broken bones, hospital bills, and time off work. Then the insurance adjuster calls and says something like: "Our investigation shows you weren't in a marked crosswalk, so we believe you were at fault." They might say it politely. But the message is clear. They think you owe them a favor for answering the phone.
That's not how Texas law works. Being outside a crosswalk when you were struck doesn't automatically make the accident your fault. It doesn't automatically reduce your recovery to zero. But it does create a legal wrinkle you need to understand. If you don't, the insurance company is counting on you to accept far less than you're owed.

### Houston's Pedestrian Crisis Is Real. and Getting Worse
Houston is one of the most dangerous cities in America for people on foot. In 2026 alone, fatal pedestrian crashes have been reported along Westheimer Road, I-45, Highway 6, and Highway 288. These aren't isolated incidents. They're the product of high-speed roadways, inadequate pedestrian infrastructure, and drivers who are distracted, impaired, or simply moving too fast for conditions.
Harris County consistently ranks among the deadliest counties in Texas for pedestrian fatalities. Many of those deaths, and countless serious injuries, happen away from marked crosswalks. That's not surprising in a city built around cars. Marked crosswalks can be blocks apart. Sidewalks disappear mid-street. Crossing at the nearest intersection isn't always physically possible.
When someone gets hit under those conditions, the driver's insurance company often leads with one argument: you shouldn't have been there. Understanding why that argument is legally weaker than they make it sound is the first step to protecting your claim.

### What Texas Law Actually Says About Pedestrians and Crosswalks
Under the Texas Transportation Code, pedestrians do have certain obligations. When you cross at a location that isn't a marked or unmarked intersection crosswalk, you're required to yield the right of way to vehicles. That's real, and it matters to your case.
But here's what the adjuster won't tell you: drivers have obligations too. Texas law requires drivers to exercise due care to avoid colliding with a pedestrian, at all times, in all locations. That duty doesn't disappear just because a pedestrian is mid-block. A driver who's speeding, texting, drunk, or simply not paying attention can still be legally responsible for hitting someone who was crossing outside a crosswalk.
A pedestrian's location, crosswalk or not, affects the fault calculation. It rarely tells the whole story about who caused the crash.
Texas also recognizes that some intersections have unmarked crosswalks. Essentially, the imaginary extension of a sidewalk across a road at an intersection, even if no paint marks it. If you were crossing at an intersection and no marked crosswalk existed, you may have had more legal protection than you realize. These details matter, and they're worth investigating.

### Texas Comparative Fault: What the 51% Rule Means for You
Texas uses a system called modified comparative fault, sometimes called proportionate responsibility. Here's the plain version: if you were partially at fault for the accident, your financial recovery gets reduced by your percentage of fault. But if you're found more than 50% at fault, meaning you bear the majority of the blame, you recover nothing under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 33.001.
That 51% threshold is the critical number in pedestrian cases where a crosswalk wasn't involved.
Say a jury determines you were 30% at fault for crossing mid-block without yielding, and the driver was 70% at fault for speeding and failing to watch for pedestrians. If your total damages are $200,000, you'd recover $140,000, reduced by your 30% share of fault. You still recover something real.
Now flip it. If the jury finds you were 60% at fault, because you crossed against traffic unexpectedly at night without looking, you recover zero. That's the insurance company's goal when they push the "no crosswalk" narrative hard.

### How Insurers Use the Crosswalk Argument Against You
Insurance adjusters are trained negotiators. They know Texas's 51% rule. When they find out you weren't in a marked crosswalk, they often move fast.
First, they'll contact you quickly, sometimes within hours of the crash, hoping to get a recorded statement before you've spoken with anyone. They'll ask you to walk through exactly what happened, where you were, and where you were going. Every answer you give about your position on the road gets used to build a fault argument.
Second, they'll assign you a high fault percentage in their internal evaluation. Some adjusters will tell you directly: "We're finding you 60% at fault, so we can only offer you 40% of your damages." That number didn't come from a jury or a judge. They made it up, strategically.
Third, they'll make a lowball settlement offer and frame it as generous given "your share" of responsibility. Many injured pedestrians accept it because they don't know they have options.
The adjuster's fault percentage isn't a legal finding. It's a negotiating position. You don't have to accept it.
If an insurance company calls you after a pedestrian accident, especially one outside a crosswalk, be careful about giving details before you've talked with a personal injury attorney. What you say early in the process shapes everything that comes after.

### Factors That Actually Drive Fault in These Cases
When a pedestrian case goes to litigation in Harris County, whether that's a negotiation with an insurance company, mediation, or a jury trial in the 11th District Court, the fault analysis is more nuanced than "crosswalk or no crosswalk." Here are the real factors that move the needle.

#### Driver speed and attention
A driver traveling 50 mph in a 35 mph zone has reduced reaction time significantly. Even if a pedestrian darted into the road, a speeding driver may have had no reasonable chance to stop. The speeding is still their fault. Crash reconstruction experts can often calculate whether a driver going the speed limit would have had time to avoid the collision. That analysis is powerful evidence.

#### Visibility conditions
Many of Houston's worst pedestrian crashes happen at dusk, at night, or in rain. Texas law expects drivers to adjust their speed and attention for low-visibility conditions. A driver who hits someone they "couldn't see" because it was dark still has a duty to drive at a speed where they can stop for hazards in their headlight range.

#### Road design and signage
On stretches of Highway 6 or Westheimer where the nearest marked crosswalk is a quarter mile away and no pedestrian signal exists, a person crossing mid-block isn't being reckless. They're doing what the road's design left them to do. Poor infrastructure can shift fault toward the roadway authority, which opens a different legal avenue entirely.

#### Driver impairment or distraction
If the driver was intoxicated or on their phone at the time of impact, that evidence dramatically affects the comparative fault analysis, regardless of where the pedestrian was crossing. A distracted driver on I-45 bears substantial responsibility for the consequences of their inattention.

#### Your actions at the time
Yes, your behavior matters too. Were you looking before you crossed? Were you wearing dark clothing at night on a road with no lighting? Were you crossing somewhere no pedestrian could reasonably expect to cross safely? These facts hurt your case. An experienced attorney won't pretend otherwise. But they'll also put those facts in context against everything the driver did wrong.

### What Evidence Makes or Breaks These Claims
Pedestrian accident cases live and die on evidence. In Houston, much of that evidence disappears fast. Traffic cameras on city corridors overwrite footage on cycles as short as 24 to 72 hours. Skid marks fade. Witnesses move on.
The evidence that most often determines fault includes:
- Traffic and surveillance camera footage. businesses along Westheimer, Houston metro intersections, and TxDOT cameras on state highways may have captured the impact
- The driver's phone records. subpoenaed in litigation to check for calls or texts at the moment of impact
- Event data recorder ("black box") data. most vehicles since 2012 record speed, braking, and steering inputs in the seconds before a crash
- Eyewitness accounts. bystanders, nearby business employees, other drivers
- Police crash report (CR-3). filed by Houston Police Department or Harris County Sheriff's Office; includes the investigating officer's observations and sometimes a preliminary fault notation
- Medical records. documenting the nature and severity of your injuries from day one, ideally from a Houston trauma center like Memorial Hermann or Ben Taub
The sooner this evidence is secured, the better. That's one practical reason to talk with an attorney early. Not to file a lawsuit immediately, but to get the right pieces preserved before they're gone.

### The Statute of Limitations in Texas Pedestrian Cases
Texas gives most personal injury plaintiffs two years from the date of the accident to file a lawsuit, under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003. Two years sounds like a long time. It isn't, especially when you factor in how long it takes to finish medical treatment, understand the full extent of your injuries, and investigate the accident properly.
There are situations where the clock runs differently. If the driver who hit you was a government employee operating a government vehicle, such as a city bus, a TxDOT truck, or a METRO vehicle, different notice deadlines apply, and they're much shorter. Missing those deadlines can end your case before it begins.
If a minor was injured, the limitations period typically doesn't start running until they turn 18. That's a nuance worth confirming with an attorney for your specific facts.

### What a Houston Pedestrian Accident Claim Actually Covers
If you have a valid claim, even one where your fault percentage reduces your recovery, Texas law allows you to seek damages for:
- Past and future medical expenses (emergency care, surgery, physical therapy, ongoing treatment)
- Lost wages and lost earning capacity if your injuries affect your ability to work
- Physical pain and suffering, past and future
- Mental anguish
- Disfigurement, if the crash left permanent scarring or physical changes
- Physical impairment, separate from pain and suffering under Texas law
In cases involving a drunk driver or a driver who acted with gross recklessness, Texas law also permits exemplary damages, a penalty on top of actual damages meant to punish extreme misconduct. These aren't available in every case, but they're worth evaluating when the driver's conduct was especially egregious.
If someone was killed in a pedestrian accident, surviving family members may have a wrongful death claim under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 71.002. The same comparative fault principles apply, but the damages calculation and who has the right to bring the claim follow different rules.

### Practical Steps if You Were Hit Outside a Crosswalk
You can't go back and change where you were standing when the car hit you. But you can control what happens next. Here's what matters most in the hours and days following the crash.
Get medical attention immediately. Even if you think you're okay. Adrenaline masks pain. Traumatic brain injuries, internal injuries, and soft-tissue damage don't always announce themselves right away. Going to a Houston emergency room or urgent care clinic that day creates a medical record tied to the date of the accident. That documentation matters enormously later.
Don't give a recorded statement to the insurance company. The adjuster may tell you it's routine or required. It isn't. You have no legal obligation to give a recorded statement to the other driver's insurer. Politely decline and say you'll be in touch through your attorney.
Document what you can from the scene. If you're physically able, photograph the road, your position, the vehicle, any skid marks, traffic signals, and nearby signage. Take photos of your injuries. Get names and contact information from any witnesses.
Write down what happened while it's fresh. Memory degrades fast. A detailed account of the sequence of events, what you saw, heard, and did before the impact, is far more useful when written on day one than recalled six months later.
Talk to an attorney before accepting anything. A consultation costs you nothing and tells you where your case actually stands. Before you sign a release or accept a check from any insurer, understand what you're giving up. Settlements are final. You can't come back later if your injuries turn out to be more serious than they first appeared.
Our team handles pedestrian accident cases throughout Houston and Harris County. The consultation is free, and we work on contingency, meaning we don't get paid unless your case resolves.

### Common questions
Yes, you can still pursue a claim. Texas uses modified comparative fault, meaning your recovery is reduced by your percentage of fault but is not automatically eliminated because you were outside a crosswalk. You are only barred from recovering if you are found more than 50% at fault under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 33.001.
Texas's proportionate responsibility system reduces your damages by your share of fault. If you are found 51% or more responsible for the crash, you recover nothing. If your fault is 50% or below, you can still recover damages, though the amount is reduced by your fault percentage.
Most pedestrian injury claims must be filed within two years of the accident under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003. ## The Recorded Statement Trap: What the Adjuster Isn't Telling You
Source: https://nalawtx.com/blog/recorded-statement-insurance-adjuster-what-to-say

The insurance adjuster calls within hours of your accident asking for a recorded statement. This post explains what's really happening on that call, and exactly what to say.
By Vu Nguyen, Founder & Managing Partner · Updated May 17, 2026
You are not legally required to give a recorded statement to the other driver's insurance company. You can politely decline until you speak with an attorney. If your own insurer calls, your policy's cooperation clause may require you to give a statement, so keep answers factual and brief.
- The other driver's insurer has no legal right to your recorded statement — you can decline.
- Your own insurer's cooperation clause may require a statement; keep it short and factual.
- Recorded statements taken within 24–48 hours can be used against you before injuries fully appear.
- Evidence like dashcam footage and surveillance video disappears fast — early legal help matters.
Your car is still at the body shop. Your neck hurts. You haven't even seen a doctor yet. And your phone rings. a friendly voice introduces herself as a claims adjuster and says she just needs a "quick recorded statement" to get your claim moving.
That call is not quick, and it's not neutral. What you say in the next ten minutes can follow your case for years. Here's what's actually happening and how to handle it.

### Why adjusters want a recorded statement so fast
Insurance companies are not on your side. That's not a cynical opinion. It's just a structural reality. Their adjusters are trained to settle claims for as little as possible. A recorded statement taken within 24 to 48 hours of a crash serves that goal in several specific ways.
First, your memory is unorganized. You haven't had time to sit down, write out what happened, or talk to a lawyer. You're still in the fog of the accident, and that fog produces imprecise answers. Imprecise answers become ammunition later.
Second, your injuries may not have fully appeared yet. Soft-tissue injuries, herniated discs, and concussions often don't peak until 48 to 72 hours post-crash. If you say "I feel okay" on a Monday morning recorded statement and you're in a cervical collar by Wednesday, that statement will be used to argue you weren't really hurt, or that something else caused your injury.
Third, a recorded statement locks you in. If you later remember a detail differently, or describe the intersection differently than you did on day one, the adjuster has a transcript to use against you.
The adjuster's job is to close your claim. A recorded statement is a tool for doing that at the lowest possible cost.

### Are you required to give a recorded statement?
It depends on which insurance company is calling.
Your own insurance company: Most Texas auto policies contain a "cooperation clause" that requires you to assist in the investigation of your own claim. That typically includes giving a statement. If you refuse entirely, your insurer may have grounds to deny coverage. Check your specific policy language, or ask an attorney to review it.
The other driver's insurance company: You have no legal obligation to give a recorded statement to the at-fault driver's insurer. They will tell you it's required. It is not. Texas law does not compel you to cooperate with an adverse insurer. You can, and often should, decline until you've spoken with an attorney.
That distinction matters enormously. When State Farm or Allstate calls you about the other driver's claim, your polite but firm answer can be: "I'm not in a position to give a recorded statement right now. I'll be in touch through my attorney."

### What adjusters ask, and why each question is loaded
Recorded statement questions sound casual. They're not. Here are the ones that cause the most damage, and the reason behind each.

#### "How are you feeling today?"
This sounds like small talk. It's an opening question designed to get you to say "fine" or "okay" on the record before you've had a chance to be evaluated by a doctor. A one-word answer of "okay" can be clipped from context and used to argue you didn't have serious injuries at the time of the statement.

#### "Can you describe exactly what happened?"
They want a detailed narrative: every lane, every speed, every second. The more specific you are without documentation in front of you, the more likely you are to say something that doesn't match the police report or the physical evidence. Even minor inconsistencies get flagged.

#### "Were you distracted at all before the crash?"
Under Texas's modified comparative fault rule (basically, Texas reduces your recovery by your percentage of fault), even a small concession here can shrink your claim. If you say "I was glancing at my GPS for a second," that becomes a contributory fault argument. Under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 33.001, you can still recover if you're less than 51% at fault. But the adjuster's job is to push your number as high as possible.

#### "Have you had any prior accidents or injuries?"
This is a preexisting condition probe. If you hurt your back in a fender-bender three years ago on I-10, the adjuster wants to know, because they'll argue your current back pain isn't from this accident. You may honestly not remember every prior incident, and getting it wrong on a recorded statement looks bad later.

#### "What doctors have you seen, and what did they say?"
You probably haven't seen a doctor yet, or you've only been to the ER once. Either way, committing to a medical narrative at this stage, before your treatment is complete, is premature. Describing your injuries in a recorded statement before imaging or specialist evaluations can understate what's actually wrong.

### Exactly what to say when the adjuster calls
If it's your own insurer calling about your own collision claim, you likely need to cooperate. Keep it factual, keep it brief, and don't speculate.
If it's the other driver's insurer, here is a word-for-word response that works:
"I appreciate you reaching out. I'm not prepared to give a recorded statement right now. I'm still getting medical attention and I haven't had a chance to speak with an attorney. Please send any requests in writing to [your address or email], and I'll make sure the right person responds."
That's it. You don't owe them an explanation. You don't need to justify why you want an attorney. You are not required to cooperate with the adverse insurer, and saying so politely ends the call without damaging your claim.
If the adjuster pushes back, and they will, your answer is a calm repetition: "I understand. I'm just not in a position to do that right now."

### If you've already given a recorded statement
Don't panic. A recorded statement doesn't end your case. But you should act quickly.
Request a copy of the recording or transcript immediately. You're entitled to it. Review it with an attorney so you know exactly what you said and where the potential vulnerabilities are. An attorney can often provide context for statements that sound worse than intended, explaining, for example, that "I felt okay" was said before you had imaging done and before your herniated disc was diagnosed at Memorial Hermann or a similar facility.
The earlier you get legal guidance after giving a statement, the more options you have.

### The timing problem: why 48 hours matters
Houston traffic is relentless. Crashes happen on the Katy Freeway, on I-45 heading into Galveston, on 290 near Cypress. When they do, evidence disappears fast. Dashcam footage overwrites, surveillance video gets deleted on 48-to-72-hour loops, witnesses forget details and move on.
The window between your accident and the adjuster's first call is often the same window where evidence is still recoverable. An attorney who gets involved early can send preservation letters to businesses near the crash site, pull black box data from the at-fault vehicle, and secure the police report before it's buried. All of that helps your case far more than any recorded statement could hurt it, if you move fast.
Texas's statute of limitations for personal injury cases is generally two years from the date of the accident under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003. That's your hard deadline. But the practical window for gathering strong evidence is much shorter.

### What about giving a statement to the police?
This post is specifically about insurance adjuster recorded statements, not statements to law enforcement. If a Houston Police Department officer or a Harris County Sheriff's deputy asks for your account at the scene, you should cooperate fully and honestly. That's a different situation with different rules and different obligations.
The police report that results from that conversation is actually one of the most useful documents in your case. It's contemporaneous, official, and often includes the officer's assessment of fault. Your attorney will want it.

### When you should talk to an attorney first
Honestly? Before any recorded statement, if you can. Most personal injury attorneys, including ours, offer free consultations, and a 20-minute call before you talk to the adjuster is almost always worth it.
The situations where you most need an attorney before giving any statement:
- You were seriously injured and are still receiving treatment
- Liability is disputed. both drivers have different accounts
- A commercial vehicle or an 18-wheeler was involved
- There were multiple vehicles or multiple injured parties
- The adjuster is asking detailed questions about your prior medical history
If your crash was truly minor, no injuries, no dispute about fault, a small property damage claim, a recorded statement to your own insurer is usually fine. But if any of the above applies to you, the free consultation costs you nothing and could protect you from a mistake that costs you significantly.
You can read more about the full claims process on our Houston car accident page, or get answers to common questions on our FAQ page.

### A quick summary
Here's the short version:
- The other driver's insurer has no right to your recorded statement. Politely decline until you've spoken with an attorney.
- Your own insurer may require cooperation under your policy's cooperation clause. Keep answers factual and brief.
- Don't guess. If you don't know, say you don't know.
- Don't describe your injuries before you've been fully evaluated by a doctor.
- If you've already given a statement, get a copy and talk to an attorney as soon as possible.
- Evidence disappears fast in Houston. The sooner you get legal help, the more you can preserve.
The adjuster's call sounds routine. Treat it like what it is: the first move in a negotiation where only one side is prepared.

Please send any requests in writing.' You don't need to explain further or justify wanting an attorney. If they push back, calmly repeat that you're not in a position to do that right now.

## Slip and Fall at HEB, Kroger, or Walmart in Houston: What Texas Law Requires You to Prove
Source: https://nalawtx.com/blog/slip-and-fall-at-heb-kroger-or-walmart-in-houston

Texas premises liability law puts real burdens on injured shoppers. Big grocery chains know exactly how to use those burdens against you. Here's what you need to prove, where most claims break down, and what a 2024 Texas Supreme Court ruling changed.
By Vu Nguyen, Founder & Managing Partner · Updated May 25, 2026
To win a slip-and-fall claim at a Houston grocery store, you must prove the store created the hazard, knew about it, or should have found it through reasonable inspection. A 2024 Texas Supreme Court ruling made proving the store's knowledge harder. You also have two years from the date of your fall to file a lawsuit under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003.
- You must prove the store created, knew about, or should have discovered the hazard — the hardest part of any claim.
- The 2024 Albertsons v. Mohammadi ruling requires proof the store knew about this specific hazard, not just that spills happen generally.
- Surveillance footage is often overwritten within days — a formal legal hold request must go out quickly.
- Texas's two-year filing deadline under § 16.003 starts the day of your fall, not when you decide to act.
You walked into an HEB on Westheimer or a Walmart off I-45 to grab groceries. You weren't doing anything wrong. Then the floor gave you no warning. a puddle of water, a smear of spilled salsa, a broken floor mat. and you were down before you could react. Maybe you hit your hip. Maybe your wrist took the fall. Maybe you're reading this from a hospital bed at Memorial Hermann or St. Luke's.
The store's manager came over, filled out an incident report, and someone handed you a copy. You might have thought that was the beginning of accountability. It wasn't. It was the beginning of a legal process that large retailers are very well prepared for. Most injured shoppers are not.
This post explains exactly what Texas premises liability law requires you to prove when you slip and fall at a grocery store. It's not simple, and recent court rulings have made it harder. Knowing what the law demands is the first step toward knowing whether you have a claim worth pursuing.

### Texas Premises Liability: The Basic Framework
When you're hurt on someone else's property, your claim falls under premises liability, a category of Texas negligence law that covers injuries caused by dangerous property conditions. It's separate from ordinary negligence, and that distinction matters.
As a paying customer at a grocery store, the law classifies you as an invitee. That's the highest category of protection Texas law provides. A store owes you a duty to inspect the premises, discover dangerous conditions, and either fix them or warn you about them.
But owing you a duty and being legally liable for your injury are two different things. To win a premises liability claim in Texas, you generally have to prove all four of these elements:
- The property owner (or an employee) created the hazardous condition, or the owner had actual knowledge of it, or the condition existed long enough that the owner should have discovered it through reasonable inspection.
- The condition posed an unreasonable risk of harm.
- The owner failed to fix it or warn you about it.
- That failure caused your injury.
Element one is where most slip-and-fall claims in Texas succeed or fail. And it got significantly harder in 2024.

### What the Albertsons v. Mohammadi Ruling Changed
In 2024, the Texas Supreme Court issued its decision in Albertsons LLC v. Mohammadi. The court tightened what it means for a store to have actual knowledge of a hazard and drew a harder line between actual knowledge and constructive knowledge (meaning what the store should have known).
Before this ruling, some courts allowed plaintiffs to argue that because a hazard was "obvious" or had existed for a while, the store must have known about it. The Mohammadi decision made clear that general awareness, knowing, for instance, that produce sections get wet, doesn't satisfy the actual knowledge requirement. The plaintiff has to show the store knew about this specific hazard at this specific location before the fall.
General awareness that spills happen in grocery stores is not the same as knowledge of the particular puddle that caused your fall. Texas courts now treat those as two entirely different things.
This matters practically. If no employee saw the spill, if no customer reported it, and if the store has no inspection log showing the area was recently checked, proving actual knowledge becomes very difficult. That's why the constructive knowledge path, showing the hazard existed long enough that a reasonable inspection would have found it, often becomes the critical alternative theory in these cases.

### The "How Long Was It There?" Question
When actual knowledge is hard to prove, the next question is: how long did the dangerous condition exist before you fell? Texas law calls this the temporal element. You don't have to give an exact minute-by-minute timeline, but you need enough evidence to support a reasonable inference that the hazard existed long enough for a careful store to have found and addressed it.
Courts look at factors like:
- Whether the substance on the floor had dried edges, dirt in it, or footprints through it, suggesting it had been there a while
- Whether the store had any inspection logs or "safety sweep" records for that area
- How frequently store policy required employees to walk the relevant aisle
- Whether other customers had walked through the area before you fell
This is where surveillance footage becomes critical. Large retailers like Walmart and Kroger have extensive camera systems. If the spill appeared on camera 45 minutes before your fall and no employee addressed it, that's strong evidence. But those recordings are typically overwritten within days. The window to preserve them is narrow.

### What Grocery Stores Do After a Slip and Fall
HEB, Kroger, and Walmart each have dedicated loss prevention departments and relationships with insurance carriers whose job is to minimize payouts on claims exactly like yours. The moment an incident report is filed, a process begins. It's not designed with your interests in mind.
Here's what commonly happens:
The incident report gets written by store employees. The language in that report often downplays the hazard or omits key details. One common example: describing the floor as "slightly damp" instead of noting the standing water that caused the fall.
A claims adjuster contacts you quickly. Sometimes within 24 to 48 hours. They sound helpful. They're gathering information they can use to minimize or deny your claim. They may ask you to give a recorded statement before you fully understand the extent of your injuries.
They look for comparative fault arguments. Texas uses modified comparative fault, meaning if you're found partially responsible for your own fall, your recovery is reduced by your percentage of fault. If you're more than 50% at fault, you recover nothing. Stores often argue you weren't watching where you were going, you were on your phone, or you were wearing inappropriate footwear. Any admission you make early can become part of that argument.
Surveillance footage may be preserved selectively, or not at all. Without a formal legal hold request, footage is routinely overwritten. Some stores preserve only the footage they believe helps them.

### What You Should Do After a Grocery Store Fall in Houston
If you're hurt badly enough to consider a claim, the actions you take in the first 48 to 72 hours have an outsized effect on what's recoverable later. The evidence that matters most is also the most perishable.
Get medical attention the same day. Even if you feel like you can walk it off, see a doctor. Injuries from falls, hip fractures, herniated discs, traumatic brain injuries, often don't show their full severity for days. A gap between the fall and your first medical visit becomes an argument that you weren't really hurt, or that something else caused your injuries.
Photograph everything before you leave the store if you can. The spill, the surrounding area, any lack of warning signs, your clothing, your shoes. Get wide shots and close-up shots.
Ask for a copy of the incident report. You're entitled to it. Read it before you sign anything. If anything is inaccurate, note that, but don't sign a version you disagree with.
Get names and contact information from witnesses. Other shoppers who saw the fall or saw the hazard beforehand can be important. Their memories fade quickly.
Do not give a recorded statement to the store's insurer. You're not legally required to, and doing so before you understand the full scope of your injuries can limit what you're able to recover. See our post on what insurance adjusters are actually doing when they call for more on this.
Talk to a Houston slip and fall lawyer before accepting anything. A free consultation costs you nothing and gives you a realistic picture of what your claim is worth and what it would take to pursue it.

### The Damages You Can Pursue Under Texas Law
If you can establish liability, Texas law allows you to pursue compensation for both economic and non-economic losses. These include:
- Medical expenses. past bills and reasonably anticipated future treatment, including surgery, physical therapy, and prescription costs
- Lost income. wages you've missed and earning capacity you may lose if the injury is long-term or permanent
- Physical pain and suffering. the physical experience of the injury and recovery
- Mental anguish. anxiety, depression, and the psychological effects of serious injury
- Impairment. if your ability to do normal life activities is permanently diminished
- Disfigurement. scarring or permanent physical changes
Texas does not cap non-economic damages in premises liability cases the way it does in medical malpractice cases, so the full picture of what you've lost is relevant.

### The Two-Year Deadline. Don't Miss It.
Under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003, you have two years from the date of your injury to file a lawsuit. Two years sounds like a long time. It isn't. Evidence disappears. Witnesses become unavailable. Surveillance footage is long gone. Injuries that seem manageable at first sometimes require surgery six months later, and your attorney needs time before that deadline to investigate, negotiate, and file if necessary.
If you're injured at an HEB in the Heights, a Kroger near Briargrove, or a Walmart in Katy, the two-year clock starts the day of the fall. Not the day you finally decide to do something about it.
The statute of limitations doesn't care that you were trying to avoid a lawsuit. It cares about the date on the calendar.

### When a Slip and Fall Claim Is Hard, and When It Isn't
Not every fall at a grocery store becomes a strong legal claim. Honest assessment matters.
Claims tend to be harder when the hazard was open and obvious (a clearly marked wet floor with multiple yellow cones), the fall left no lasting injury, or there's no evidence the store knew or should have known about the condition.
Claims tend to be stronger when there's video showing the hazard existed for an extended time, an employee was in the immediate area and failed to act, the store's inspection logs show the area hadn't been checked recently, or your injuries required surgery or resulted in lasting limitations.
A real evaluation of your specific facts is the only way to know which situation you're in. That's exactly what a free case review is for.

### Why These Cases Require a Houston Premises Liability Lawyer
Large retailers retain experienced defense lawyers. Their insurers handle hundreds of slip-and-fall claims a year in Harris County and the surrounding counties. They know every argument. They know the Mohammadi ruling and how to use it.
A Houston premises liability attorney who handles these cases regularly knows how to send a litigation hold letter immediately to preserve surveillance footage, how to obtain a store's inspection and maintenance records through discovery, how to work with medical experts who can connect your injury to the fall, and how to counter the comparative fault arguments that retailers use to reduce claims.
If you're trying to handle a serious grocery store injury claim on your own, you're going up against a system that has seen thousands of people try to do exactly that. It usually doesn't end well for them.
Our premises liability practice covers slip-and-fall injuries throughout Houston and across Texas. We work on contingency, meaning you pay nothing unless there's a recovery in your case.

### Common questions
You must prove that the store created the hazardous condition, had actual knowledge of it, or should have discovered it through reasonable inspection. You also have to show the condition posed an unreasonable risk of harm, the store failed to fix or warn you about it, and that failure caused your injury. Element one — proving the store's knowledge — is where most Texas slip-and-fall claims succeed or fail.
The court drew a harder line between actual knowledge and constructive knowledge of a hazard. A store's general awareness that produce sections get wet, for example, no longer satisfies the actual knowledge requirement. You now have to show the store knew about this specific hazard at this specific location before your fall, not just that spills happen in grocery stores.
Under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003, you have two years from the date of your injury to file a lawsuit. The clock starts the day of the fall, not the day you decide to pursue a claim. Evidence disappears and witnesses become unavailable well before that deadline, so acting quickly matters.
Get medical attention the same day, even if your injuries seem minor, since conditions like herniated discs or hip fractures may not show full severity for days. Photograph the hazard, your surroundings, and any missing warning signs before leaving the store, and ask for a copy of the incident report. Do not give a recorded statement to the store's insurer, and talk to a Houston slip-and-fall lawyer before accepting anything.

## Suing the Government After a Houston Pothole Accident: The Notice Deadline That Kills Claims
Source: https://nalawtx.com/blog/suing-the-government-after-a-pothole-accident-in-texas

A bad pothole or crumbling road shoulder can send you to the hospital. But suing a Texas city or county for road defects is nothing like suing another driver. Miss one deadline and your entire claim is gone, no matter how serious your injuries.
By Vu Nguyen, Founder & Managing Partner · Updated June 8, 2026
Yes, you can sometimes sue a Texas city or county for a road defect like a pothole, but you must send formal written notice within six months of the crash under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 101.101. Miss that deadline and your claim is gone, no matter how serious your injuries. The government entity is not going to guide you through the process.
- You have only six months to file written notice of your claim against a Texas governmental unit under the Texas Tort Claims Act.
- Notice must go to the correct government entity — TxDOT, City of Houston, Harris County, or a toll authority — depending on which road it was.
- The government must have known or should have known about the defect before your crash; a brand-new pothole is a much harder claim.
- Even successful claims against a governmental unit are generally capped at $250,000 per person under the TTCA.
You're driving down Westheimer or merging onto I-10 near Katy when a massive pothole blows your front tire. Your car lurches, you overcorrect, and suddenly you're in the median. Or worse, into another lane of traffic. The crash is real. The injuries are real. So is the emergency room bill from Memorial Hermann.
The natural question: can I hold someone accountable for that road condition? The honest answer is yes, sometimes. But when a city, county, or state agency is responsible for that road, you're not dealing with a normal personal injury claim. You're dealing with the Texas Tort Claims Act, a law that gives government entities a powerful shield. The most dangerous part of that shield is a notice requirement that most injured Texans don't even know exists.

### The Government Usually Can't Be Sued. Until the TTCA Says It Can
Texas law starts from a simple premise: you generally cannot sue the government. This principle (called sovereign immunity) dates back centuries. The idea is that the government can't be dragged into court every time something goes wrong.
In 1969, the Texas Legislature passed the Texas Tort Claims Act (TTCA), which punches specific holes in that immunity. Under certain conditions, the law allows injured people to file claims against state agencies, cities, counties, and other governmental units. Road defects (potholes, failed drainage, eroded shoulders, missing guardrails) fall into the category of claims that can sometimes get through.
The key word there is sometimes. The TTCA doesn't open the door wide. It opens a narrow door with specific requirements you have to meet perfectly. One of those requirements is formal notice.

### The 6-Month Notice Deadline and Why It's a Trap
Under the Texas Tort Claims Act, specifically Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 101.101, if you want to sue a Texas governmental unit for personal injury or property damage, you must give written notice of your claim within six months of the incident.
Six months sounds like plenty of time. It isn't, at least not in practice.
Here's why people get burned. After a bad crash, most people spend the first weeks dealing with medical care, car repairs, insurance calls, and just getting back on their feet. The legal clock is running the whole time. The six months move fast. By the time someone decides to explore a claim against the City of Houston or Harris County, weeks or months may already be gone.
The notice deadline under the TTCA is not the same as the regular statute of limitations. It's a separate, earlier requirement. Missing it is usually fatal to your claim, regardless of how strong your case would have been otherwise.
The notice has to go to the right place, contain the right information, and arrive within the deadline. Getting even one of those three things wrong can result in your claim being dismissed before it ever gets a hearing.

### What the Notice Has to Say
The TTCA doesn't just require that you send something. The notice has to give the governmental entity enough information to investigate the claim. That generally means:
- The date and location of the incident, specific enough that the agency can identify the road segment, intersection, or defect involved
- A description of the injury or damage
- Your name and contact information
A social media post about the pothole doesn't count. A complaint submitted to Houston's 311 system may or may not count, depending on what it says and who receives it. A letter to the wrong department at Houston Public Works might not count either.
There's a narrow exception in the statute: if the governmental unit has "actual notice" of your claim, meaning someone with authority to act on it actually knew, the formal written notice requirement may be excused. But courts interpret "actual notice" tightly. The government knowing a pothole exists is not the same as the government knowing you were injured by it. Don't count on the exception to save you.

### Who You're Actually Suing Depends on Which Road It Was
In the Houston area, road maintenance responsibility is split between multiple government entities. This matters because notice has to go to the right one.
Texas Department of Transportation (TxDOT) maintains state highways and most interstates, including I-10, I-45, I-69/US-59, and Beltway 8 (Sam Houston Tollway). If your accident happened on one of those roads, TxDOT is likely the responsible party. It's a state agency, so the same TTCA framework applies, but state agencies have their own procedures.
The City of Houston maintains most streets inside city limits, from major corridors like Westheimer and Memorial Drive down to neighborhood side streets. The City of Houston has its own claims process and its own designated office to receive TTCA notices.
Harris County handles roads in unincorporated areas of the county, roads outside city limits that aren't state highways. If your accident was on a county road near Cypress, Katy, or Humble, Harris County's Precinct is likely involved.
Toll road authorities like HCTRA (Harris County Toll Road Authority) and TxDOT manage the toll infrastructure separately. The Grand Parkway, Hardy Toll Road, and Fort Bend Tollway each involve different entities.
Sending notice to the wrong entity, even if you do it perfectly and on time, may not protect your claim. A Houston injury attorney can help you identify every potentially responsible party before that clock runs out.

### What Kind of Road Defect Claim Even Qualifies?
Not every bad road condition gives rise to a claim. The TTCA requires that the governmental entity had actual or constructive notice of the dangerous condition, meaning they knew about it or should have known through reasonable inspection, and failed to correct it in a reasonable time.
This is a real hurdle. Texas courts have dismissed road defect claims where the plaintiff couldn't prove the government knew about the specific condition before the crash. A pothole that appeared overnight after a heavy rain is a much harder claim than a pothole that had been reported multiple times to 311 over several months.
The conditions that most commonly support claims include:
- Potholes or pavement failures that had been reported or were clearly visible for extended periods
- Missing or damaged guardrails on dangerous curves
- Failed drainage that causes standing water to collect on roadways, a recurring problem on Houston-area roads after heavy rain
- Faded or missing lane markings at dangerous intersections
- Road shoulders that drop off sharply without warning
- Construction zone conditions with inadequate signage or barriers
The TTCA also covers accidents involving government-owned vehicles, like a crash with a City of Houston public works truck or a METRO bus. Those claims involve the same notice requirements.

### Damage Caps: Another TTCA Limitation You Need to Know
Even if you clear the notice hurdle and establish liability, the TTCA limits what you can recover from a governmental entity. Under the Act, a single person's personal injury claim against a governmental unit is generally capped at $250,000. Claims against the State of Texas itself have a separate cap of $250,000 per person and $500,000 per occurrence.
These caps don't apply to every type of government defendant. Certain independent entities may have different rules. But the core point stands: suing a government entity is not the same as suing a private party, and the recovery limits reflect that.
This doesn't mean a road defect claim isn't worth pursuing. Serious injuries (broken bones, spinal injuries, traumatic brain injuries) can generate medical bills that far exceed those caps, and the caps represent real money. It just means you go in with clear eyes about the rules of the game.

### Can You Still Sue the Other Driver Too?
Yes. In many road defect crashes, there are multiple parties involved. If another driver's negligence contributed to the collision, you may have claims against both that driver and the governmental entity responsible for the road condition.
Texas uses a system called modified comparative fault. Your recovery is reduced by your percentage of fault, and you can only recover if you were less than 51% responsible for the crash. When there are multiple defendants (a negligent driver plus a city that failed to fix a dangerous road) your attorney can pursue both tracks while preserving your rights under the TTCA.
This is one reason why consulting an attorney early matters in road defect cases. The TTCA notice clock is running against the government defendant while you also have a separate two-year statute of limitations under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003 for claims against private parties. Different deadlines, same accident.

### What to Do Right Now If You've Been Hurt on a Defective Texas Road
Time is working against you. Here's what matters in the days and weeks after a road defect crash.
Get the location documented precisely. Photos and video of the exact pothole, shoulder drop, or road defect are critical. If the government fixes the condition before you can prove it existed, your claim becomes much harder. Note the street name, direction of travel, nearest cross street or landmark, and the date and time.
Check whether the defect has been previously reported. In Houston, you can search 311 complaint history for a specific address or intersection. If the defect appears in prior complaints, that's evidence the City had notice, which strengthens your claim.
Get the police report. If officers responded to your crash, the accident report will document the location and may note the road condition. You can request your Texas crash report through TxDOT's online portal.
Preserve your medical records. Document every treatment, every diagnosis, every day you missed work. These records connect the crash to your injuries, and you'll need that connection whether you're dealing with a government entity or a private insurer.
Contact an attorney before you contact the government entity. The TTCA notice is a legal document with real consequences. Getting the content and delivery right matters. An experienced personal injury attorney can draft the notice correctly, serve it on the right parties, and preserve your rights while your case is being evaluated.
The six-month TTCA notice deadline doesn't pause while you recover from surgery, deal with your insurance company, or wait to see how serious your injuries are. The clock runs from the day of the crash.

### A Note on Houston's Roads Specifically
Houston's road infrastructure has been a persistent news story for years. The city's extreme heat cycles, heavy rainfall, and high traffic volume create pothole conditions faster than most cities. Houston Public Works receives thousands of 311 road complaints every year.
Harris County and the City of Houston both operate formal claims processes for TTCA notices. The City of Houston Legal Department's Claims Division handles notices directed at the city. But the process is not self-explanatory. The forms, submission methods, and content requirements are not prominently advertised, and a defective notice can be rejected even if it's submitted on time.
If you were hurt on a road in the Houston metro area, whether that's inside Loop 610, out in Fort Bend County, or along a state highway like US-290, the rules above apply to your situation. The government entity is not going to walk you through the process. That's what an attorney is for.
If you have questions about a road defect crash or want to understand your options, schedule a free case review with our team. We serve clients in Houston, Harris County, and throughout Texas, in English, Español, and Tiếng Việt.
This article provides general information about Texas law, not legal advice for your specific situation. Every case is different. If you've been injured in Houston or anywhere in Texas, talk with a licensed attorney about the facts of yours. Free case review here, or call (713) 842-9442.

### Common questions
Under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 101.101, you must give the City of Houston written notice of your injury claim within six months of the incident. This notice deadline is separate from and earlier than the regular statute of limitations. Missing it typically ends your claim entirely, regardless of how strong your case might otherwise be.
Your written notice generally needs to include the date and specific location of the incident, a description of your injury or property damage, and your name and contact information. The goal is to give the government entity enough detail to investigate the claim. A 311 complaint or social media post about the pothole is unlikely to meet this requirement.
It depends on which road was involved. TxDOT maintains state highways and most interstates like I-10 and I-45. The City of Houston handles most streets inside city limits, including major corridors like Westheimer. Harris County is responsible for roads in unincorporated areas outside city limits. Sending your notice to the wrong entity, even on time, may not protect your claim.

Texas uses a modified comparative fault system, so your recovery is reduced by your share of fault, and you can only recover if you were less than 51% responsible. Keep in mind that different deadlines apply — the six-month TTCA notice for the government and the two-year statute of limitations under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003 for private parties.

## Texas Distracted Driving Laws and Your Injury Claim: What Houston Victims Need to Know About Negligence Per Se
Source: https://nalawtx.com/blog/texas-distracted-driving-laws-your-injury-claim

Nearly one in six Texas crashes in 2023 involved a distracted driver. If that driver broke Texas's cell phone law, it may already be doing much of the legal heavy lifting in your injury case.
By Vu Nguyen, Founder & Managing Partner · Updated September 28, 2026
If a driver broke Texas's hands-free cell phone law at the time of your crash, that violation can count as automatic proof of negligence under a legal doctrine called negligence per se. This shifts your case's focus to proving your injuries and damages rather than arguing the driver was careless. You generally have two years from the crash date to file a lawsuit in Texas.
- Texas Transportation Code § 545.4251 bans reading, writing, or sending electronic messages while driving statewide.
- A statutory violation can trigger negligence per se, treating duty and breach as automatically established in your claim.
- Cell phone records are time-sensitive — an attorney can send preservation letters before carriers purge the data.
- Under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003, you generally have two years from the crash to file suit.
Picture the intersection of I-10 and Beltway 8 on a Tuesday afternoon. Traffic slows, then stops. A driver three cars back doesn't notice because they're reading a text. The crash happens in under two seconds. You're the one with whiplash, a totaled car, and a stack of medical bills.
Now the other driver's insurance company is calling. They're friendly. They're asking questions. And they haven't mentioned, even once, that their driver may have violated Texas law at the moment of impact.
That law matters to your claim. Here's why, and what you should do about it.

### Texas's Cell Phone Law: What It Actually Says
Texas passed a statewide hands-free law in 2017. It's codified at Texas Transportation Code § 545.4251. The core rule is straightforward: drivers cannot read, write, or send electronic messages, including texts, emails, and social media posts, while operating a motor vehicle on a public road.
The law applies everywhere in Texas. It doesn't matter whether you're on I-45 in Harris County or a two-lane county road outside of Beaumont. If you're behind the wheel and the car is moving, putting your eyes on your phone screen to compose or read a message is a criminal violation.
First offense: up to a $99 fine. If the crash caused serious injury or death: up to $4,000 and a misdemeanor charge. Those criminal penalties are separate from what happens in your civil injury claim. But they connect directly to it.

### What "Negligence Per Se" Means (In Plain English)
In a typical car accident case, your attorney has to prove four things: the other driver owed you a duty of care, they breached it, that breach caused your injury, and you suffered real damages. The first two elements, duty and breach, usually take work. You have to show the driver was careless.
Negligence per se cuts that work in half.
When a driver breaks a safety statute, a law designed to protect people from a specific type of harm, Texas courts can treat that violation as automatic proof of duty and breach. You don't have to argue that texting while driving was careless. The Texas Legislature already decided it was careless when it passed the law.
Translated: if the other driver was texting and Texas Transportation Code § 545.4251 applies, they were negligent as a matter of law. Your job shifts to proving causation and damages, not whether they were behaving reasonably.
That's a real advantage. It simplifies arguments at trial, makes early settlement negotiations more direct, and gives your attorney a concrete legal hook to point to from day one.

### Does the Law Cover Every Type of Distraction?
No. This is an important limit to understand. Texas Transportation Code § 545.4251 specifically targets electronic messaging. Scrolling through a playlist, adjusting a navigation app, or watching a video could potentially fall under this statute depending on the facts, but the plain language focuses on reading and sending messages.
Other distracted driving behavior, eating, applying makeup, turning around to talk to a passenger, rubbernecking at a wreck on the Southwest Freeway, isn't covered by the same statute. That doesn't make those behaviors legal or defensible. It just means your claim would proceed under traditional negligence rather than negligence per se.
The distinction affects strategy, not necessarily outcome. A driver who causes a crash while eating a burger can still be fully liable. The path to proving it is just a little longer.

### How Phone Records Become Evidence
Proving a driver was on their phone at the moment of impact is one of the most important, and most time-sensitive, tasks in a distracted driving case.
Cell phone carriers keep call and data records. Text timestamps are logged. App usage can be tracked. But carriers don't hold onto detailed records indefinitely, and accessing them requires a proper legal request, typically a subpoena served during litigation or a formal preservation demand sent before a lawsuit is filed.
Here's the practical problem: by the time most injury victims call an attorney, weeks have passed. Records that might have shown the driver was actively texting at 2:47 p.m. on the day of the crash are already at risk of being overwritten or purged.
Getting an attorney involved early, ideally within days of the crash, gives your legal team time to send preservation letters and initiate discovery before critical evidence disappears.
Other evidence worth preserving: the police report (officers sometimes note that a driver admitted to phone use), witness statements, dashcam footage from nearby vehicles or business security cameras, and any social media posts the driver made around the time of the crash. Houston's dense urban grid, especially around areas like the Galleria, Downtown, and the Medical Center, means there are often cameras nearby that captured the moments before impact.

### What the Insurance Company Does With This Information
Insurance adjusters know about negligence per se. They're counting on you not to.
When they call you in the first 24 to 48 hours, and they will call, they're trying to get a recorded statement before you've spoken to an attorney. They'll ask open-ended questions about the accident. They may ask whether you "noticed" the other driver doing anything before impact. They're listening for anything they can use to reduce your claim.
If you've already said on record that you "didn't see" the other driver's phone, that makes it harder later when phone records surface showing they were mid-text. Your own statement gets used against the weight of the evidence.
The safest approach: be polite, get the adjuster's name and contact information, and tell them you'll be in touch after speaking with an attorney. You are not legally required to give a recorded statement to the other driver's insurance company. You're not required to guess, speculate, or fill silence with details you're unsure about.
For a closer look at how these calls work and exactly what to say, read our post on how to handle insurance adjuster calls after a Houston crash.

### Texas's Modified Comparative Fault Rule and Why It Matters Here
Texas uses a system called modified comparative fault. Basically, the state reduces what you can recover by your percentage of blame for the accident. Under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 33.001, if you're found to be more than 50% at fault, you recover nothing.
Insurance companies know this. In distracted driving cases, they often try to assign some fault to the victim. You were going slightly over the speed limit, you failed to brake in time, you had a light that "could have been" yellow. Each percentage point of fault they pin on you is a percentage point less they have to pay.
Negligence per se works as a counterweight here. When the other driver's violation of § 545.4251 is established, it's harder for the defense to pivot the conversation toward your behavior. The legal record already shows what they did wrong. That makes comparative fault arguments more difficult to land.
It's not a guarantee, nothing in litigation is, but it shifts the center of gravity in your favor.

### Steps to Take Right Now If a Distracted Driver Hit You
The decisions you make in the first few days after a crash shape your entire claim. Here's what actually helps:
- Get medical attention immediately. Even if you feel fine, adrenaline masks injury. Soft tissue damage, concussions, and internal injuries can take days to surface. Houston has major trauma centers, Memorial Hermann, Ben Taub, Houston Methodist, with emergency care equipped to document crash-related injuries. Your medical records are evidence.
- File a police report if you haven't already. In Harris County, you can file an online crash report with the Texas Department of Transportation for crashes where law enforcement didn't respond. The report creates an official record of the incident.
- Document everything you saw. Write down what you remember: the exact time, the road, the conditions, the other driver's behavior before impact. Did you see them looking down? Did they brake at all? Write it down now, while it's fresh. Don't post it publicly.
- Photograph the scene, the vehicles, and your injuries. Skid marks, vehicle positions, and visible damage tell a story. So do bruises, lacerations, and swelling. Photograph them over the first several days as they develop.
- Don't give a recorded statement to the other driver's insurer. See above. Worth repeating.
- Contact a Texas personal injury attorney early. The preservation window for phone records and surveillance footage is short. Early involvement by an attorney can make the difference between having that evidence and not having it.

### How Distracted Driving Claims Actually Resolve
Most Texas personal injury claims, including distracted driving cases, settle before trial. When the evidence of a statutory violation is strong, the insurance company has less room to argue liability. Negotiations tend to focus more on the value of your damages: medical bills, lost wages, pain and suffering, future care costs.
Cases go to trial when liability is genuinely disputed, when the insurer low-balls and won't move, or when the damages are severe enough that the settlement offers don't reflect reality. Harris County District Courts, in the courthouse complex Downtown on Congress Avenue, handle civil personal injury trials. Juries here see distracted driving cases regularly.
What drives value in these claims isn't just the statutory violation. It's the documentation of your injury, the consistency of your medical treatment, and the paper trail showing the full impact on your life. That's why the steps above matter so much. A negligence per se hook is valuable. It's even more valuable when it's paired with solid evidence of what your injury actually cost you.

### A Word on Truck Drivers and Commercial Vehicles
If a commercial driver, a trucker, a rideshare driver, a delivery vehicle operator, was the distracted party, the analysis gets more complex. Federal motor carrier regulations layer on top of Texas state law. Commercial drivers are held to stricter standards, and the companies employing them may share liability for the crash.
Harris County sees significant commercial truck traffic along the Port of Houston corridors, on I-610, and along US-59/I-69. If your crash involved a commercial vehicle, the evidence preservation issue is even more urgent. Electronic logging devices and in-cab cameras have data retention windows that close fast. Our 18-wheeler and commercial truck accident page has more on how those cases work.

### The Statute of Limitations: Don't Wait Too Long
Under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003, you generally have two years from the date of a crash to file a personal injury lawsuit in Texas. Miss that deadline and the court will almost certainly dismiss your case, regardless of how strong your negligence per se argument is.
Two years sounds like a long time. It isn't, once you factor in medical treatment, insurance negotiations, attorney investigation, and the time it takes to build a complete damages picture. Cases filed under time pressure, rushed to the deadline, tend to be weaker than cases built with room to breathe.
Contacting an attorney sooner gives your team time to do the work properly.
This article provides general information about Texas law, not legal advice for your specific situation. Every case is different. If you've been injured in Houston or anywhere in Texas, talk with a licensed attorney about the facts of yours. Free case review here, or call (713) 842-9442.

### Common questions
Negligence per se means that when a driver breaks a safety statute like Texas Transportation Code § 545.4251, Texas courts can treat that violation as automatic proof that the driver was negligent. You no longer have to argue they were behaving carelessly — the legislature already decided texting while driving was careless when it passed the law. Your case then focuses on proving causation and the damages you suffered.
No. Texas Transportation Code § 545.4251 specifically targets reading, writing, and sending electronic messages while driving. Distractions like eating, applying makeup, or talking to a passenger are not covered by the same statute. Those behaviors can still lead to full liability, but your claim would proceed under traditional negligence rather than negligence per se.
