Yes. Insurance adjusters often call within the first 24 to 48 hours and ask open-ended questions hoping to get a recorded statement before you speak with an attorney. Anything you say can be used to reduce your claim, for example stating you didn't see the other driver's phone before records show they were texting. You are not legally required to give a recorded statement to the other driver's insurance company.

## Texas Dog Bite Law: Why the 'One Free Bite' Rule Doesn't Always Protect the Owner
Source: https://nalawtx.com/blog/texas-dog-bite-law-houston-what-victims-can-recover

Texas is a one-bite state, but that label is misleading. Dog owners can be held liable even when their pet has never attacked before. Here's what Houston victims actually need to know.
By Vu Nguyen, Founder & Managing Partner · Updated November 21, 2026
Texas is a one-bite state, but dog owners can still be held liable even if their pet has never attacked before. Victims can pursue claims through negligence, local leash law violations, or landlord liability — paths that don't require proving the dog's dangerous history. You have two years from the date of the attack to file a claim.
- The 'one free bite' rule isn't a complete shield — growling, lunging, or snapping can also prove an owner knew their dog was dangerous.
- Violating a Houston or Harris County leash ordinance can automatically establish the owner's breach of duty through negligence per se.
- Landlords can share liability if they knew a tenant kept a dangerous dog and failed to act.
- Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003 gives you two years from the attack date to file — evidence disappears fast, so act early.
Texas ranks second in the country for dog attacks. Houston consistently lands among the most dangerous cities for postal workers, joggers, and kids in their own neighborhoods. If a dog bit you, or someone you love, the first thing you'll probably hear from the owner is some version of "he's never done that before."
That defense has a name. It's called the one-bite rule. And while it's real Texas law, it's nowhere near the complete shield that dog owners think it is. Victims have multiple paths to compensation, and a few of them don't require proving anything about the dog's history at all.

### What the One-Bite Rule Actually Says
Texas doesn't have a statewide dog bite statute the way California or Florida does. Instead, Texas relies on common law, court-made rules developed over decades of cases. Under that framework, an owner is liable if they knew (or should have known) their dog had dangerous propensities.
The "one free bite" shorthand comes from this idea: if a dog has bitten someone before, the owner now has knowledge of the danger. That prior bite is evidence of what the owner knew. But calling it a "free bite" misrepresents how courts actually apply the rule.
Prior biting isn't the only way to prove an owner knew their dog was dangerous. Growling at strangers, lunging on a leash, snapping without contact, a breed history of aggression. courts have accepted all of these as evidence of known dangerous propensities.
In short, if your neighbor's dog has been lunging at kids on the sidewalk for two years but never made contact, and then it bites your child, the owner doesn't get a free pass just because teeth never broke skin before.

### Negligence: The Second Route to Liability
You don't have to win the "dangerous propensity" argument to hold an owner responsible. Texas recognizes a separate negligence claim that works differently.
Negligence here means the owner failed to use reasonable care to control the dog, regardless of what the dog had done in the past. Did the owner let a large, excitable dog run loose in a crowded area? Did they fail to latch a gate? Did they walk the dog off-leash near a school on Westheimer Road? Those choices can be negligent even if the dog had the friendliest history imaginable.
To win on negligence, the victim generally needs to show four things:
- The owner had a duty to control the dog
- They breached that duty through careless behavior
- That breach caused the attack
- The victim suffered real injuries as a result
This path matters especially in cases involving large breeds, unleashed dogs, or situations where the owner was clearly not paying attention. The dog's history becomes less central to the case.

### Negligence Per Se: When a Local Law Creates Automatic Liability
Houston and Harris County have leash laws and animal control ordinances. When a dog owner violates one of those ordinances, say, their dog is running loose in violation of a City of Houston ordinance, and someone gets hurt as a result, the victim may have a negligence per se claim.
Negligence per se means the violation of the law itself establishes the breach of duty. You don't have to argue what "reasonable care" looks like when there's a specific rule the owner ignored. The broken law does that work for you.
This is one of the most underused angles in Houston dog bite cases. A lot of victims don't realize that the same ordinance a Houston Animal Control officer might cite the owner for can also support a civil injury claim.

### Lillian's Law and Criminal Liability
Texas added a criminal dimension to severe dog attacks through what's commonly called Lillian's Law, named after a 76-year-old woman killed by a neighbor's dogs in 2007. The law is codified in the Texas Health & Safety Code and applies when a dog that has been previously declared dangerous, or whose owner was previously found criminally negligent, attacks and causes serious bodily injury or death.
Under this law, a dog owner can face criminal charges ranging from a Class C misdemeanor to a second-degree felony depending on how severe the outcome is and what the owner knew or did. A second-degree felony in Texas carries 2 to 20 years in prison.
For victims, Lillian's Law matters for two reasons. First, a criminal conviction creates a record that can be powerful evidence in a civil case. Second, it signals to insurers that the exposure is serious, which can affect how aggressively they negotiate.
If your attack involved a dog that Animal Control had flagged, a prior dangerous dog declaration, or an owner who knew about past incidents, make sure your attorney knows about the criminal law angle early.

### Landlord Liability: A Path That Surprises People
A lot of Houston dog attacks happen in apartment complexes, rented houses, and other properties where the dog owner is a tenant. The tenant may have little money or no renters insurance. That doesn't mean you're out of options.
Landlords can be liable for dog attacks in certain situations. If a landlord knew a tenant kept a dangerous dog on the property and did nothing, didn't prohibit the dog, didn't enforce a lease provision, didn't take steps to remove the animal, the landlord may share responsibility for what happened.
Texas courts have recognized landlord liability in dog bite cases where the landlord had actual knowledge of the dog's dangerous nature and had the ability to require the tenant to remove the animal. This doesn't apply to every apartment attack, but it's worth investigating when the tenant-owner has no meaningful assets or coverage.
If you were attacked at a complex near the Medical Center, or in a rental property in Pasadena or Katy, ask your attorney whether the property owner knew about the dog's behavior before the attack.

### What Damages Can a Houston Dog Bite Victim Pursue?
Dog attacks cause serious injuries: deep lacerations, nerve damage, broken bones from falls, and in attacks on children, permanent scarring on their faces and hands. The emotional aftermath can be just as lasting. Many victims develop genuine anxiety around dogs and in some cases post-traumatic stress disorder.
In a Texas civil claim, victims typically pursue:
- Medical expenses. emergency care at Ben Taub, Memorial Hermann, or wherever you were treated; follow-up visits; physical therapy; reconstructive surgery
- Lost income. wages missed while recovering, or reduced earning capacity if injuries affect your ability to work
- Pain and suffering. physical pain from the attack and recovery period
- Mental anguish. anxiety, fear, PTSD, and psychological trauma that follows the attack
- Disfigurement. permanent scarring, especially significant in cases involving children or visible areas like the face, neck, or hands
Texas also allows punitive damages, called exemplary damages under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 41.003, in cases involving gross negligence or malice. These are awarded on top of actual damages when the owner's conduct was especially reckless. A dog owner who sicced a dog on someone intentionally, or who ignored repeated warnings about a dangerous animal, could face exemplary damages.

### The Two-Year Deadline You Cannot Miss
Texas personal injury claims, including dog bites, are governed by a two-year statute of limitations under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003. That means you have two years from the date of the attack to file a lawsuit.
Two years sounds like plenty of time. It goes fast. Evidence disappears. Animal Control records get purged. Witnesses move. Wounds heal in ways that make injuries harder to document. The sooner you start building your case, the stronger it will be.
Cases involving minors have a different timeline. The two-year clock typically doesn't start until the child turns 18. But don't rely on that without talking to an attorney first, because there are exceptions and complications that vary by situation.
The worst thing a dog bite victim in Houston can do is wait to see if the owner's homeowners insurance "takes care of it." Insurance companies aren't on your side. They're managing their exposure. Get independent legal advice before you sign anything or give a recorded statement.

### What to Do Right After a Dog Attack in Houston
If you were just attacked, or if this happened recently, here's what helps your case:
- Get medical attention immediately. Dog bites carry infection risk including rabies. Go to an emergency room or urgent care. Your medical records are the foundation of your injury claim.
- Report the attack to Houston Animal Control. Call 311 or go online. A formal report creates an official record and may trigger a dangerous dog investigation. That record can matter a great deal in your civil case.
- Document the scene and your injuries. Photograph wounds before they're cleaned, if possible. Get photos of the location, any broken fencing or open gates, and the dog if you can do so safely. Take pictures of your injuries every few days as they heal.
- Get the owner's information. Name, address, phone number, and their homeowners or renters insurance if they'll provide it.
- Find out if the dog has a history. Ask neighbors. Check with Animal Control. Prior complaints about the same dog become part of your case.
- Talk to an attorney before talking to the owner's insurance. The adjuster who calls you is not trying to help you. They're looking for statements they can use to reduce what you recover.

### How Homeowners Insurance Usually Fits In
Most dog bite claims in Texas run through the dog owner's homeowners or renters insurance policy. Standard homeowners policies cover dog bite liability, though some insurers exclude certain breeds or dogs with a documented bite history.
The insurer will assign an adjuster to your claim. That adjuster may contact you quickly, sound friendly and helpful, and offer a fast settlement. Early settlement offers are almost always lower than what a fully documented claim is worth. Once you sign a release, you give up your right to pursue additional compensation, even if you find out later that your injuries are more serious than they first appeared.
If the owner has no insurance, or if the policy limits are too low for the severity of your injuries, an attorney can help identify other sources of recovery, including landlord liability if applicable, or uninsured/underinsured options depending on your own policy coverage.
Our practice areas page covers the full range of personal injury claims we handle, including dog bites and premises liability. If you want to understand your specific options, a free case review is the fastest way to get a real answer.
This article provides general information about Texas law, not legal advice for your specific situation. Every case is different. If you've been injured in Houston or anywhere in Texas, talk with a licensed attorney about the facts of yours. Free case review here, or call (713) 842-9442.

Not necessarily. Texas courts have accepted evidence like growling at strangers, lunging on a leash, or snapping without contact as proof that an owner knew their dog was dangerous. A prior bite is one way to show that knowledge, but it's not the only way.
If a dog owner violates a local ordinance — such as a Houston or Harris County leash law — and someone is hurt as a result, the victim may have a negligence per se claim. The violation of the law itself establishes the owner's breach of duty, so you don't have to separately argue what 'reasonable care' required.
Texas courts have recognized landlord liability in dog bite cases where the landlord had actual knowledge of the dog's dangerous nature and had the ability to require the tenant to remove the animal. If the tenant has no meaningful assets or insurance, it's worth investigating whether the property owner knew about the dog's behavior before the attack.
Texas personal injury claims, including dog bites, are governed by a two-year statute of limitations under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003, starting from the date of the attack. Cases involving minors typically have a different timeline, with the clock starting when the child turns 18, though exceptions exist. An attorney can clarify how the deadline applies to your situation.

## What the Texas Supreme Court's 2025 Dram Shop Ruling Means If You Were Hit by a Drunk Driver in Houston
Source: https://nalawtx.com/blog/texas-dram-shop-law-in-houston-after-2025-supreme-court

In April 2025, the Texas Supreme Court made it harder to hold bars and restaurants liable when their customers cause DWI crashes. Here's exactly what changed, and what evidence now makes or breaks a dram shop claim in Houston.
By Vu Nguyen, Founder & Managing Partner · Updated November 21, 2026
The Texas Supreme Court's April 2025 ruling in Raoger v. Myers means a post-crash BAC reading alone is no longer enough to support a dram shop claim against a bar or restaurant. You now need direct, contemporaneous evidence — such as surveillance footage, server testimony, or witness accounts — showing the driver was visibly intoxicated when last served.
- Post-crash BAC readings alone no longer prove 'obvious intoxication' at the time of service after Raoger v. Myers.
- Surveillance footage is often critical, but bars can overwrite it within 30 to 72 hours — act fast.
- Your injury claim against the drunk driver is completely separate and unaffected by the Raoger ruling.
- Texas's two-year statute of limitations applies, but the most valuable evidence disappears within days.
You're sitting at a red light on Westheimer. A driver runs a stop sign and T-bones your car. Police arrive. The driver fails a field sobriety test. blood alcohol content of 0.17, more than twice the legal limit. Later you find out he'd been drinking for three hours at a bar three blocks away before he got behind the wheel.
You have a clear injury claim against the drunk driver. But you may also have a claim against the bar that kept serving him. That second claim, against the alcohol provider, is what Texas law calls a dram shop claim. And as of April 2025, winning one just got harder.

### What Is Texas Dram Shop Law?
Texas's dram shop statute is found in the Texas Alcoholic Beverage Code § 2.02. It allows an injured person to sue a bar, restaurant, or other alcohol provider if two conditions are met: the provider served alcohol to someone who was obviously intoxicated at the time of service, and that intoxication was a direct cause of the person's injuries.
The phrase "obviously intoxicated" is the hinge the entire law turns on. Texas doesn't make every alcohol seller responsible for every drunk driver. The law only kicks in when a server or bartender had enough visible, observable evidence in front of them that a reasonable person would have known this customer was drunk, and they kept pouring anyway.
For years, plaintiffs could use a post-crash blood alcohol reading as one piece of that puzzle. A BAC of 0.17 at the time of the crash, combined with a three-hour bar tab and witness accounts of slurred speech, could support a jury's finding that the person was obviously intoxicated when the bar last served them. The April 2025 ruling in Raoger v. Myers changed how that evidence works.

### What Raoger v. Myers Actually Decided
The Texas Supreme Court's decision in Raoger v. Myers drew a sharp line between two kinds of evidence: what a server could have observed at the moment of service, and what investigators measured after a crash.
The court held that a post-crash BAC reading alone, even a high one, is not sufficient direct evidence of obvious intoxication at the time of service. The reasoning: alcohol metabolizes, time passes between last service and a crash, and a BAC number doesn't tell you what a bartender saw or should have seen when they handed over that last drink.
A breathalyzer number from a hospital or roadside test tells you what was in a person's blood after the crash. It doesn't prove what was visible to a server at the bar an hour earlier. The court is requiring plaintiffs to bridge that gap with direct, contemporaneous evidence.
In plain terms: you need eyewitness evidence from someone who was actually at the bar. Bar staff testimony, surveillance footage, receipts showing how many drinks were served over what period, other customers who saw the driver's condition before he left. That's the kind of evidence the court is looking for now.
This is a significant shift. Before this ruling, plaintiffs could sometimes lean heavily on a high BAC number and work backward, arguing that someone with a 0.17 BAC must have been showing signs of intoxication when last served. Post- Raoger, that inferential bridge requires more support from direct observation evidence.

### What This Means for DWI Crash Victims in Houston
Harris County sees thousands of DWI-related crashes every year. Houston's bar and restaurant corridors, Washington Avenue, Midtown, the East End, the Galleria area, generate a lot of late-night traffic that ends in crashes on I-10, Loop 610, and city streets. Many of those crashes involve drivers who were over-served.
The Raoger ruling doesn't eliminate dram shop claims. It raises the evidentiary bar. Here's what that means practically:

#### Evidence preservation becomes urgent
Bars and restaurants routinely overwrite surveillance footage on 30- to 72-hour cycles. If you or your attorney don't send a preservation letter to the establishment within days of the crash, that footage may be gone permanently. In the post- Raoger world, that footage is often the most important evidence you have.
The same urgency applies to receipts, point-of-sale records, and employee shift logs. These records can show exactly which server handled the table, how many drinks were ordered, and over what time period. Bars don't keep these indefinitely.

#### Witness identification matters more now
Other patrons at the bar who observed the drunk driver's behavior before he left, slurred speech, unsteady walking, knocking things over, are now critical witnesses. Their accounts can supply the "observable at time of service" evidence the court is demanding. Those witnesses scatter quickly. Getting their contact information fast is essential.

#### The drunk driver's claim remains separate and unaffected
The Raoger ruling affects only the dram shop portion of your case, the claim against the alcohol provider. Your personal injury claim against the drunk driver himself is completely separate. That driver's liability for hitting you is governed by standard negligence law, and a high BAC reading is highly relevant there. The two claims run parallel to each other.

### The "Obviously Intoxicated" Standard. What Courts Have Looked For
Even before Raoger, Texas courts had been examining what "obviously intoxicated" actually looks like in the real world. The following types of evidence have historically supported a finding of obvious intoxication:
- Server or bartender testimony that the customer was slurring words, stumbling, or behaving erratically
- Bar surveillance video showing the customer's physical condition
- Receipts or drink logs showing a pattern of heavy service over a short period
- Other customers or employees who witnessed the person's condition
- Evidence that the customer had been cut off or that staff discussed their level of intoxication
Post- Raoger, this list didn't change. The ruling just confirmed that a post-crash BAC number can't substitute for contemporaneous observation evidence. Think of it as the court saying: show us what the bar staff saw. Don't just show us what the breathalyzer read two hours later.

### What About the Drunk Driver's Own Responsibility?
Texas uses a system called modified comparative fault. Texas reduces what you can recover by your share of blame for the accident. In a DWI crash where you did nothing wrong, your percentage of fault is zero, and this rule doesn't hurt you at all.
In a dram shop case, comparative fault can get complicated because the court has to split responsibility among multiple parties: the drunk driver, the alcohol provider, and potentially others. That's one more reason these cases need experienced handling. The apportionment fight between the driver and the bar, each trying to shift more blame to the other, is real, and how it lands affects what you recover from each party.

### Texas's Dram Shop Safe Harbor. One More Wrinkle
The Texas Alcoholic Beverage Code § 106.14 includes a provision sometimes called the "safe harbor" defense. An alcohol provider can use it to limit or avoid liability if they can show they required their employees to complete an approved seller-server training program, the employee actually completed it, and the employer didn't directly encourage over-service.
In practice, many Houston bars and restaurants will raise this defense immediately. That's why your attorney needs to look at not just what happened on the night of the crash, but how that establishment trained its staff, whether the program actually qualifies under Texas law, and whether there's evidence the employer's own culture pushed servers to keep drinks flowing regardless of a customer's condition.
A laminated "TABC certified" certificate on the wall doesn't automatically protect a bar. The safe harbor defense has conditions. If an employer looked the other way while staff over-served, that defense has real weaknesses.

### The Two-Year Clock. Don't Let It Run Out
Under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003, the statute of limitations for personal injury claims in Texas is generally two years from the date of the injury. This applies to both the claim against the drunk driver and the dram shop claim against the alcohol provider.
Two years sounds like a long time. It isn't. The evidence you need most, surveillance footage, server recollections, contemporaneous bar records, degrades or disappears in the first few days and weeks. By the time you're approaching the two-year mark, an attorney is left trying to build an "obviously intoxicated" case with almost nothing to work with.
If you were hit by a drunk driver anywhere in Harris County, at the intersection of Shepherd and San Felipe, on I-45 near downtown, or anywhere else in the Houston metro, and you believe alcohol was involved, the time to start preserving evidence is now.

### What You Should Do Right Now If This Happened to You
You don't need to figure out whether a dram shop claim applies to your situation today. That's an attorney's job. But there are steps that protect your options:
- Get the police report. It will identify the establishment where the driver was drinking if that information came out at the scene.
- Note the name of the bar or restaurant if you learn it, from the police, the driver, witnesses, or social media.
- Don't contact the bar yourself. You don't want to tip them off that a claim is coming before a preservation letter goes out.
- See a doctor. Not just for your health. Your medical records document your injuries and create a timeline that matters in court.
- Talk to an attorney fast. The evidence window in dram shop cases is genuinely short. A preservation letter sent on day three is far more valuable than one sent on day thirty.
If the drunk driver had liability insurance, that insurer's adjuster will contact you quickly. They are not on your side. If there's also a dram shop angle to your case, you want someone in your corner before you say anything that could be used to undercut that claim.
Our attorneys handle car accident claims across Houston and Harris County, including DWI crash cases where over-service by a bar or restaurant may be part of the picture. If you have questions about your situation, a free case review is a good place to start. No commitment, no pressure.
This article provides general information about Texas law, not legal advice for your specific situation. Every case is different. If you've been injured in Houston or anywhere in Texas, talk with a licensed attorney about the facts of yours. Free case review here, or call (713) 842-9442.

### Common questions
In Raoger v. Myers, the Texas Supreme Court ruled that a post-crash blood alcohol content reading alone is not sufficient direct evidence that someone was obviously intoxicated at the time a bar served them. Plaintiffs must now support their claim with contemporaneous observation evidence, such as eyewitness accounts, surveillance video, or drink receipts from the bar itself.
Yes. The Raoger ruling did not eliminate dram shop claims under Texas Alcoholic Beverage Code § 2.02 — it raised the evidentiary bar. You still have a viable claim if you can show the bar served someone who was obviously intoxicated at the time of service and that intoxication directly caused your injuries. The key is gathering direct, observable evidence quickly.
Courts are now looking for evidence of what bar staff could have observed at the moment of service — things like server or bartender testimony, surveillance footage showing the customer's condition, receipts or drink logs documenting heavy service over a short period, and accounts from other patrons who witnessed the driver's behavior before they left. A high BAC number after the crash must be supported by this kind of direct observation evidence.
Under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003, the statute of limitations for personal injury claims is generally two years from the date of injury, and this applies to both the claim against the drunk driver and the dram shop claim against the alcohol provider. However, the most critical evidence — surveillance footage, server recollections, and bar records — can disappear within days, so contacting an attorney quickly matters far more than the two-year deadline suggests.

## Your Pre-Existing Condition Doesn't Kill Your Claim. Texas Law Says So
Source: https://nalawtx.com/blog/texas-eggshell-plaintiff-rule-pre-existing-conditions

Insurance adjusters use your prior back problems, old injuries, and degenerative conditions against you. The Texas eggshell plaintiff rule is the legal doctrine that stops them. Most injured Houstonians have never heard of it.
By Vu Nguyen, Founder & Managing Partner · Updated September 28, 2026
A pre-existing condition does not eliminate your right to recover damages in Texas. Under the eggshell plaintiff rule, an at-fault party must take you as they find you, meaning they are fully responsible for how their negligence worsened your condition, even if you were already vulnerable before the crash.
- The eggshell plaintiff rule means defendants are responsible for the full harm caused to you, not to a hypothetical healthy person.
- You can recover for aggravation of a pre-existing condition — the difference between your health before and after the crash.
- Having a pre-existing condition is not negligence on your part and does not reduce your recovery under Texas comparative fault rules.
- Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003 gives you generally two years from the accident date to file a lawsuit.
You had a bad back before the crash. Maybe you'd been treated for degenerative disc disease, a herniated disc from years ago, or an old football injury from high school. Then someone rear-ended you on the I-45 Gulf Freeway, and now your back is significantly worse. You can barely get out of bed, you've missed work, and the pain is affecting every part of your life.
The insurance adjuster calls. They've already pulled your medical records. And they tell you something that sounds very official and very final: "Your injuries are pre-existing. We're not responsible for a condition you already had."
Here's what they're not telling you: that's not how Texas law works.
Texas recognizes a legal doctrine called the eggshell plaintiff rule. It's one of the most important protections available to injured Texans, and one of the most frequently ignored. Understanding it could be the difference between a fair recovery and walking away with nothing.

### What the Eggshell Plaintiff Rule Actually Says
The rule gets its name from a simple idea: imagine a person whose skull is as fragile as an eggshell. If someone negligently hits that person and they suffer a catastrophic brain injury, one a healthy person wouldn't have suffered from the same impact, is the at-fault party off the hook because of the victim's fragility?
Texas law says no. Emphatically.
Under the eggshell plaintiff rule, a negligent defendant must take their victim as they find them. If you were already vulnerable, because of a prior injury, a degenerative condition, diabetes, osteoporosis, or anything else, the at-fault party is still responsible for the full harm their negligence caused to you specifically, not to some hypothetical healthy person.
The at-fault driver doesn't get a discount because you weren't in perfect health before they hit you.
Texas courts have applied this principle consistently. The logic is straightforward: a wrongdoer who causes harm doesn't get to escape liability just because the person they harmed happened to be more susceptible to injury. You didn't choose to have a vulnerable spine. The other driver chose to drive negligently.

### Why Adjusters Use Pre-Existing Conditions as a Weapon
Insurance adjusters are trained to reduce payouts. That's not cynicism. It's their job. One of the most effective tools they have is your prior medical history, and they will use it against you from the very first phone call.
Here's what that looks like in practice. You're treated at Memorial Hermann or Houston Methodist after the crash. The adjuster requests your complete medical records going back years. They find a note from your primary care doctor three years ago mentioning lower back stiffness, or a 2022 MRI showing mild degenerative disc disease at L4-L5. Suddenly, your entire injury is "pre-existing."
They may use language like:
- "The imaging shows wear-and-tear that predates the accident."
- "Your treating physician noted chronic back pain in prior records."
- "We can only compensate you for injuries directly caused by the accident, not conditions you already had."
All of those statements contain a kernel of truth wrapped around a fundamental lie. Yes, your prior condition exists. No, that doesn't mean the crash didn't significantly worsen it. The worsening is exactly what you're entitled to recover for.
This is deliberate. An unrepresented claimant who doesn't know about the eggshell plaintiff doctrine is far more likely to accept a lowball settlement or give up entirely.

### The Distinction That Actually Matters: Aggravation
Texas law draws a clear line between two things that adjusters constantly blur together:
Your pre-existing condition. what you had before the crash. The defendant is not responsible for that.
The aggravation of your pre-existing condition. how the crash made it worse. The defendant is fully responsible for that.
This is the legal concept of aggravation of a pre-existing injury, and it works alongside the eggshell plaintiff rule. Say you had mild degenerative disc disease that was managed with occasional ibuprofen. After a rear-end collision on Westheimer, you now need surgery, epidural steroid injections, and months of physical therapy. The defendant caused that change. You're entitled to recover for the difference between where you were before and where you are now.
Your medical records before the crash are your baseline. Everything worse than that baseline, after the crash, is the defendant's responsibility.
The challenge, and this is where having experienced legal help matters, is proving that difference clearly. That means getting your pre-accident medical records, getting proper post-accident treatment and documentation, and often working with medical experts who can explain to a jury or an adjuster exactly what changed and why.

### Common Pre-Existing Conditions That Come Up in Houston Injury Cases
Degenerative disc disease is the most common, but it's far from the only condition adjusters try to weaponize. These are the ones that appear most often in Houston car accident claims:
Degenerative disc disease (DDD). Extremely common in adults over 40. The disc material between vertebrae naturally loses water content and elasticity with age. A crash can accelerate that degeneration dramatically, turn a manageable condition into a debilitating one, or cause a previously stable disc to herniate.
Prior soft tissue injuries. An old whiplash injury from a previous crash, a rotator cuff tear from years ago, or a strained neck from a workplace accident. If the new crash aggravates any of those, you have a claim for the aggravation.
Arthritis. Osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis both create joints that are more susceptible to trauma. A crash that would cause minimal joint damage in a young, healthy person can be catastrophic for someone with pre-existing arthritis.
Prior surgeries. If you've had a previous spinal fusion, knee replacement, or other surgery, the affected area may be more fragile and more vulnerable to re-injury in a crash. That vulnerability is yours. The re-injury is the defendant's responsibility.
Neurological conditions. Pre-existing nerve damage, neuropathy, or prior concussions can make a traumatic brain injury more severe. The eggshell plaintiff rule applies here too.

### How Texas Courts Handle the Eggshell Plaintiff Rule at Trial
If your case goes to trial at Harris County District Court, or any Texas court, the jury will receive instructions about how to handle pre-existing conditions. Under Texas law, the jury is told to consider what damages the plaintiff suffered as a result of the defendant's negligence, taking the plaintiff as they found them.
Texas Pattern Jury Charge 81.3, which courts use to instruct juries on personal injury damages, asks jurors to award compensation for the injuries the plaintiff actually sustained, not the injuries an average person would have sustained. That's the eggshell plaintiff rule in action inside the courtroom.
What this means practically: a defendant who rear-ends someone on Highway 59 and causes a herniated disc cannot tell the jury "but this person already had a weak spine." The jury awards damages for what actually happened to this actual person.
Texas also follows modified comparative fault. Your recovery is reduced by your share of blame for the accident itself. But having a pre-existing condition isn't "blame." Your prior health status is not negligence on your part. The two are separate questions.

### What the Insurance Company Will Try to Do Next
Once adjusters realize you know about the eggshell plaintiff rule, their tactics shift. Instead of flatly denying your claim, they typically move to one of two positions:
Disputing causation. They'll argue the crash wasn't severe enough to have caused your worsening symptoms. Expect them to point to property damage photos, repair estimates, and recorded speed data if available. This is why crash documentation, police reports, and consistent medical treatment starting immediately after the accident all matter.
Apportionment disputes. They'll try to assign a percentage of your current condition to "natural progression" of your pre-existing condition rather than to the crash. This requires medical evidence on your side, specifically a treating physician or expert who can speak to the timeline and explain that the significant worsening followed the crash, not the natural disease progression.
Both of these arguments can be countered with the right medical documentation and legal strategy. But they're much harder to counter if you waited months to get treated, didn't document the accident scene, or gave a recorded statement to the adjuster before speaking with an attorney.

### Steps That Protect Your Claim When You Have a Pre-Existing Condition
If you were injured in a Houston crash and you have prior medical history that's relevant, these steps matter more than they do for someone with a completely clean medical record.
Get treated immediately. Same day or the next day. If you've been seen at a facility like CHI St. Luke's or Memorial Hermann, your treatment records establish a clear post-accident baseline. Gaps in treatment are used against you.
Tell your doctors the full story. Don't minimize symptoms, and don't omit your prior history either. Doctors who know your baseline before the crash can document exactly what changed afterward. Honest, complete medical records are your strongest evidence.
Preserve your pre-accident records. If you have prior imaging, treatment notes, or surgical records related to the affected body part, gather them. Your attorney needs to understand your baseline to effectively argue aggravation.
Don't give a recorded statement. The adjuster's recorded statement call is not a formality. It's a data-gathering exercise designed to produce quotes they can use to minimize your claim. Politely decline until you've spoken with an attorney.
Talk to an attorney before accepting any settlement. Once you sign a release, it's over. You can't go back for more money if your condition worsens or you discover additional injuries. An attorney familiar with Texas car accident claims can tell you whether a settlement offer actually accounts for your aggravated condition, or whether it's a lowball number that ignores the eggshell plaintiff doctrine entirely.

### The Statute of Limitations Still Applies
One thing the eggshell plaintiff rule does not change: the deadline to file suit in Texas. Under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003, you generally have two years from the date of the accident to file a personal injury lawsuit. That deadline applies whether you have a pre-existing condition or not.
Two years sounds like a long time. It isn't, especially when you're dealing with ongoing medical treatment, insurance negotiations, and the ordinary demands of life after an injury. Cases involving pre-existing conditions often require additional medical expert work, which takes time to arrange. Starting that process early matters.
If you're not sure where your deadline falls, the safest move is to have a free case review sooner rather than later.

### You Were Hurt Before. That Doesn't Mean You Don't Deserve to Be Made Whole Now.
Nobody lives in perfect health. Most adults over 40 have something in their medical history, a prior injury, a degenerative condition, an old surgery. That history is part of life, not a legal bar to recovery after someone else's negligence hurts you further.
Texas law recognizes this. The eggshell plaintiff rule exists precisely because the alternative, a legal system where you can only sue if you were perfectly healthy before the crash, would be profoundly unjust. The at-fault driver doesn't get to choose their victims. They take them as they find them.
If an adjuster has told you that your pre-existing condition makes your case worth nothing, you've been misled. That's not an accident or a mistake on their part. It's a tactic. And it works, but only on people who don't know the law.
Now you do.

### Watch: How Pre-Existing Conditions Affect Your Injury Settlement

### Common questions
Yes. Under the Texas eggshell plaintiff rule, an at-fault driver is responsible for the harm their negligence caused you specifically, even if you had a prior back condition. You are entitled to recover for the aggravation — the worsening of your condition caused by the crash — not for the pre-existing condition itself.
Aggravation refers to how a crash made an existing condition significantly worse. Texas law separates your pre-existing condition, which the defendant is not responsible for, from the worsening caused by the accident, which the defendant is fully responsible for. Your medical records before the crash establish your baseline, and everything worse than that baseline after the crash is the defendant's responsibility.
The eggshell plaintiff rule is a legal doctrine requiring a negligent defendant to take their victim as they find them. If you were more vulnerable to injury because of a prior condition, the at-fault party still owes you full compensation for the harm their negligence caused. Texas courts apply this principle consistently, and juries are instructed on it through Texas Pattern Jury Charge 81.3.
The deadline is the same regardless of your prior medical history. Under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003, you generally have two years from the date of the accident to file a personal injury lawsuit. Cases involving pre-existing conditions often require additional medical expert work, so starting the process early is important.

## Texas Insurance Bad Faith: When Your Own Insurer Breaks the Law
Source: https://nalawtx.com/blog/texas-insurance-bad-faith-what-houston-claimants-can-recover

Texas gives injured claimants two separate legal pathways to hold insurers accountable when they lowball, delay, or deny valid claims. Here's what those pathways look like, and what you can recover beyond your underlying claim.
By Vu Nguyen, Founder & Managing Partner · Updated October 5, 2026
Texas law requires insurers to handle your claim honestly and on time. When they lowball, delay, or deny a valid claim without reasonable basis, you can sue them separately from your underlying injury claim. A successful bad faith case can recover actual damages, attorney's fees, penalty interest, and in serious cases, additional damages multiplied up to three times your actual losses.
- Your insurer must acknowledge your claim within 15 days under Texas Insurance Code § 542.055.
- A bad faith claim has a two-year deadline that runs from the insurer's wrongful act, not your injury date.
- Winning a bad faith case can include 18% per-year penalty interest and attorney's fees paid by the insurer.
- The Stowers doctrine can hold a liability insurer responsible for a judgment exceeding policy limits if they refused a reasonable settlement.
You paid your premiums for years. You followed the rules. Then you got hurt. maybe on I-610 during rush hour, maybe in a parking lot off Westheimer. and filed a claim with the insurance company you trusted to protect you.
And then the insurer started playing games.
Maybe the adjuster went silent for weeks. Maybe they offered you a fraction of what your medical bills alone cost. Maybe they denied your claim with a vague letter and no real explanation. You're sitting there hurt, confused, and wondering if any of this is even legal.
Here's the short answer: it might not be. Texas law puts real obligations on insurance companies. When they ignore those obligations, you can sue them for it, separately from your underlying injury claim. That's called a bad faith insurance claim, and Texas gives you more than one way to pursue it.

### What "Insurance Bad Faith" Actually Means
Every insurance policy is a contract. Built into that contract, under Texas common law, is an implied duty of good faith and fair dealing. The idea is that your insurer can't treat you as an adversary when you file a claim. They agreed to cover you. Now they have to actually do it, fairly.
Bad faith, in plain terms, is when an insurer knows (or should know) that a claim is valid, and either denies it or delays paying it without any reasonable basis for doing so.
That's the common-law standard. Texas courts have recognized it since the 1987 case Arnold v. National County Mutual Fire Insurance Co. It requires proving that the insurer had no reasonable basis for its conduct and that they knew it (or should have).
That standard can be hard to meet. So Texas also created a statutory path that's easier to use.

### The Statutory Route: Texas Insurance Code Chapter 541 and the DTPA
Texas Insurance Code Chapter 541 lists specific acts that count as unfair or deceptive insurance practices. You don't have to prove the insurer acted with malicious intent. You just have to show they committed one of the prohibited acts and that it caused you harm.
The Texas Deceptive Trade Practices Act (commonly called the DTPA) also applies to insurance companies in many situations. The DTPA, found at Texas Business & Commerce Code § 17.41 et seq., lets consumers sue businesses that use false, misleading, or deceptive practices. Insurance companies are businesses. Policyholders are consumers. The DTPA gives you another legal tool when your insurer lies to you or misrepresents your coverage.
Both Chapter 541 and the DTPA can allow recovery of attorney's fees and, in cases of knowing violations, additional damages on top of your actual losses.

### Specific Acts That Trigger a Bad Faith Claim in Texas
Texas Insurance Code § 541.060 lays out a list of prohibited practices by insurers. These aren't abstract legal concepts. They describe things that actually happen to real policyholders in Harris County and across Texas every week.
Some of the most common violations:
- Misrepresenting the policy. Telling you that something isn't covered when it actually is, or describing your coverage inaccurately to get you to accept less.
- Failing to acknowledge your claim promptly. Under Texas Insurance Code § 542.055, your insurer must acknowledge receipt of your claim within 15 days. Many don't.
- Not accepting or rejecting your claim within a reasonable time. Texas law requires insurers to accept or deny a claim within 15 business days after receiving all items, statements, and forms they asked for, sometimes up to 45 days if they request an extension. Letting your claim sit in limbo indefinitely isn't allowed.
- Failing to conduct a reasonable investigation. If the insurer decides your claim before they've actually looked at the facts, that's a problem.
- Offering an unreasonably low settlement. Known in the industry as "lowballing." If the insurer knew your claim was worth significantly more and offered a fraction of it anyway, that can constitute bad faith.
- Refusing to pay a claim without explaining why. You're entitled to a written explanation that references the specific policy provision they're relying on.
Texas law doesn't just say insurers should treat you fairly. It spells out exactly what "fair" looks like, and gives you a legal remedy when they fall short.

### First-Party vs. Third-Party Bad Faith
This distinction matters a lot. It's worth understanding before you decide what to do.

#### First-party bad faith
This is a dispute between you and your own insurer. The clearest example: you have uninsured motorist (UM) coverage, you get hit by an uninsured driver on the Gulf Freeway, and your own insurance company refuses to pay out what your policy promises. That's first-party bad faith. Your insurer owes you a direct duty of good faith because you're their policyholder.

#### Third-party bad faith
This comes up when someone else's insurer mistreats you. Say the driver who hit you at Westheimer and Gessner had liability coverage, and their insurer is dragging its feet, misrepresenting the policy, or offering you $800 for a claim that clearly involves serious injuries. Texas recognizes some third-party bad faith claims, though they're more complex because you don't have a direct contract with that insurer.
Your ability to sue a third-party insurer for bad faith is more limited in Texas, but it's not zero. If the at-fault driver assigns their rights to you as part of a settlement, or if you can show the insurer committed an unfair act under Chapter 541, you may still have a path forward.
The strongest bad faith claims in Texas are almost always first-party, against your own insurer.

### What You Can Recover in a Texas Bad Faith Case
This is where bad faith law gets meaningful for injured Texans. A successful bad faith claim can get you more than just what you were owed under the policy in the first place.

#### Actual damages
This covers the harm the bad faith conduct itself caused you, not just the underlying claim amount. If you racked up credit card debt because the insurer delayed your claim for six months and you couldn't pay your medical bills, that interest and those costs may be recoverable. If you had to pay out of pocket for treatment you couldn't postpone, that matters too.

#### Attorney's fees
Under both Chapter 541 and the Texas Prompt Payment of Claims Act ( Texas Insurance Code § 542.051 et seq. ), you may be able to recover your attorney's fees from the insurer if you prevail. That's significant. It means the insurer potentially pays the cost of your fight against them.

#### Penalty interest
The Texas Prompt Payment of Claims Act adds an 18% per-year interest penalty on claims that weren't paid on time. This accrues on top of the claim amount. When an insurer delays payment for months, that penalty adds up fast. It's meant to deter exactly the kind of delay tactics that adjusters routinely use.

#### Additional damages for knowing violations
Under Texas Insurance Code § 541.152, if the insurer's violation was committed knowingly, a court can award up to three times the amount of actual damages. This is what's sometimes called "treble damages." It's not automatic. You have to prove the insurer knew what it was doing was wrong. But it's available in serious cases.
Under the DTPA, a similar multiplier applies for knowing or intentional violations.

### Common Insurer Tactics That May Cross the Line
Not every frustrating insurance experience rises to the level of bad faith. Insurers can investigate claims, request documentation, and even deny claims, as long as they have a reasonable basis for doing so. The question is always whether there was any legitimate reason for what they did.
That said, some patterns show up repeatedly in bad faith cases handled out of Harris County district courts:
- Blanket denials with no investigation. The insurer sends a denial letter within days of a claim, before they've even looked at police reports, medical records, or any evidence.
- Using your recorded statement against you. The adjuster calls you early, gets you to describe your injuries in vague terms before you understand the full extent of them, then points to your own words as a reason to deny or limit your claim. (If you haven't yet, read our post on what to know before giving an insurer a recorded statement.)
- Disputing causation with no medical basis. The insurer hires a "paper doctor" who reviews records without ever examining you and concludes your injuries aren't related to the accident. This happens in whiplash cases, brain injury cases, and soft-tissue claims constantly.
- Delaying to pressure a settlement. Some adjusters are trained to let time pass, to let your bills pile up and your stress build, so you'll accept a low offer just to put it behind you.
- Misrepresenting policy limits. Telling you the at-fault driver only had $30,000 in coverage when they actually had $100,000, hoping you'll settle before you find out.
If the insurer's explanation for denying your claim doesn't make sense, if it seems designed to avoid paying rather than to honestly evaluate your situation, that's worth a second look by an attorney.

### Deadlines You Need to Know
Bad faith claims in Texas have their own limitations period. Under Texas Insurance Code § 541.162, you have two years from the date the cause of action accrues to file a bad faith claim. That generally means two years from when the insurer committed the act, not necessarily two years from when your underlying injury claim was resolved.
This matters. If your insurer denied your claim in January, you can't wait three years to challenge it as bad faith and assume you're still within the window. The clock runs from the denial or the bad act itself.
Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003 generally governs two-year statutes of limitations in personal injury cases, and the two-year window on bad faith claims tracks similarly. But the starting point can differ depending on the specific conduct.
If you're already past one year from a denial or a lowball offer, talk to an attorney soon. Don't wait to find out you're time-barred.

### What to Do If You Think Your Insurer Is Acting in Bad Faith
Start documenting everything now. The strength of a bad faith claim rests heavily on the paper trail: what the insurer said, when they said it, and how they handled your claim over time.
Keep records of:
- Every phone call, including date, time, name of the person you spoke with, and what they said
- Every letter, email, and text from the insurer
- Every document request they made and when you provided it
- Every deadline they missed under the Texas Prompt Payment Act
- Any written denial, including the stated reason
Request everything in writing. If an adjuster tells you something over the phone that surprises you, follow it up with an email: "Just confirming what you told me today, that my claim is denied because of X." That creates a record.
Then talk to an attorney. A bad faith claim isn't something you want to handle on your own. The insurer has lawyers whose entire job is handling these disputes. You should too.
Our team at Nguyen & Associates handles insurance disputes and personal injury claims across Houston and Harris County. We can review what happened with your claim and tell you whether what you're describing sounds like bad faith under Texas law.

### One More Thing: The Stowers Doctrine
If you're the injured party dealing with someone else's insurer, there's another legal concept worth knowing: the Stowers doctrine. Named after a 1929 Texas Supreme Court case, it holds that if a liability insurer fails to settle a claim within policy limits when a reasonable insurer would have done so, the insurer can be held responsible for a judgment that exceeds those limits.
This matters in cases where the at-fault driver's insurer refuses a reasonable settlement offer within their client's policy limits, the case goes to trial, and the jury awards more than the policy covers. The insurer, not just the at-fault driver, may be on the hook for the excess. It's a powerful doctrine that gives liability insurers a real reason to settle reasonable claims rather than gamble with their policyholders' personal assets.
The Stowers doctrine is a third-party bad faith remedy recognized under Texas common law. It gives you real negotiating power when the at-fault driver's insurer is being unreasonable.

### The Bottom Line
Insurance companies in Texas aren't free to do whatever they want with your claim. They have legal obligations: hard deadlines, specific duties, and requirements to deal with you honestly. When they don't, Texas law gives you real remedies. Penalty interest, attorney's fees, and in serious cases, additional damages multiplied on top of what you were already owed.
If an adjuster has been giving you the runaround, delaying your claim, offering you a fraction of what you're owed, or denying you without explanation, you may be dealing with more than just a difficult negotiation. You may be dealing with a legal violation.
A free case review costs you nothing and tells you where you stand.

Bad faith is when an insurer knows or should know a claim is valid but denies or delays it without any reasonable basis. Texas Insurance Code Chapter 541 also lists specific prohibited acts, such as misrepresenting your policy, failing to investigate properly, or offering an unreasonably low settlement. You do not have to prove malicious intent to bring a statutory claim.
Under Texas Insurance Code § 541.162, you generally have two years from the date the insurer committed the bad act to file a bad faith claim. That clock typically starts from the denial or the specific wrongful conduct, not necessarily when your underlying injury case ends. If you are approaching one year from a denial, speak with an attorney soon.

## The 2025 Texas Supreme Court Ruling That Shifted the Ground Under Workplace Injury Lawsuits
Source: https://nalawtx.com/blog/texas-nonsubscriber-employer-lawsuit-2025-the-ruling-that

If your employer opted out of workers' comp and you got hurt on the job, a landmark April 2025 ruling means the company can now point fingers at other parties and potentially reduce what it owes you. Here's exactly what changed and what it means for your case.
By Vu Nguyen, Founder & Managing Partner · Updated October 26, 2026
A April 25, 2025 Texas Supreme Court ruling in In re East Texas Medical Center Athens lets nonsubscriber employers — those that opted out of workers' comp — point to third parties like contractors or equipment makers to reduce their share of fault. Your employer still cannot blame you or a coworker, but it now has a new tool to lower what it owes you.
- Nonsubscribing employers can now designate 'responsible third parties' under Chapter 33 to shift some fault away from themselves.
- Your employer still cannot use your own negligence or a coworker's negligence as a defense under Texas Labor Code § 406.033.
- If your employer points to a third party, your attorney may be able to pursue that party too, potentially increasing total recovery.
- Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003 gives you two years from your injury date to file — that deadline did not change.
Texas is the only state in the country that lets employers skip workers' compensation insurance entirely. Employers that do this are called nonsubscribers. When you work for one and get injured on the job, you can't file a workers' comp claim. But you can sue the employer directly in civil court. Historically, that lawsuit came with a major advantage for injured workers: the employer couldn't use your own negligence against you the same way it could in an ordinary injury case.
On April 25, 2025, the Texas Supreme Court issued its opinion in In re East Texas Medical Center Athens (No. 23-1039). The ruling changed one critical piece of how those nonsubscriber lawsuits work, and not in workers' favor. If you've been hurt on the job in Texas and your employer opted out of workers' comp, you need to understand what this decision means before you talk to an adjuster, sign anything, or assume your case looks the same as it would have a year ago.

### First: What Is a Nonsubscriber Employer?
Under Texas law, private employers can choose not to carry workers' compensation insurance. There's no penalty for opting out. It's completely legal. Roughly one-third of Texas employers are nonsubscribers, and that number is especially high in industries like construction, retail, and food service.
When an employer subscribes to workers' comp, an injured employee gets a no-fault benefit system: medical bills and some lost wages, in exchange for giving up the right to sue the employer. When an employer doesn't subscribe, the injured worker keeps the right to sue. That lawsuit is governed by Texas Labor Code § 406.033, which strips the nonsubscribing employer of several defenses it would normally have, including the ability to blame the employee's own negligence or the negligence of a coworker.
That's been the core of what makes nonsubscriber lawsuits powerful for injured workers. Your employer can't say "it was your own fault" and use that to gut your case. Or at least, that was the rule before April 2025.

### What the East Texas Medical Center Athens Ruling Actually Decided
The Texas Supreme Court's decision in In re East Texas Medical Center Athens addressed whether a nonsubscribing employer can designate a responsible third party under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code Chapter 33.
Here's what that means in plain English. Chapter 33 is Texas's proportionate liability law. It governs how fault gets divided up when more than one party contributed to an injury. Under Chapter 33, a defendant can point to someone else (a "responsible third party") and ask the jury to assign some of the fault to that person or company instead. That third party doesn't even have to be in the courtroom. If the jury assigns them 40% of the fault, the defendant's liability can shrink by that same 40%.
Before this ruling, nonsubscribers had a problem using Chapter 33. The Labor Code already stripped them of certain defenses, and courts were divided on whether designating a responsible third party was just another back-door way to sneak in those forbidden defenses. The Texas Supreme Court resolved that split, ruling that yes, nonsubscribing employers can designate responsible third parties under Chapter 33.
The practical effect: an employer that would have been on the hook for 100% of your damages can now tell the jury that a contractor, an equipment manufacturer, or another company shares the blame, and walk away paying less.

### What the Employer Can. and Still Cannot. Do
It's worth being precise here, because this ruling is being misread in both directions.
What changed: Nonsubscribing employers can now designate responsible third parties under Chapter 33 and argue to the jury that someone else (a subcontractor, an equipment maker, a staffing agency, a premises owner) bears part of the fault. If the jury agrees, your employer's share of liability goes down.
What did not change: The Labor Code's core protections still stand. A nonsubscribing employer still cannot use your own negligence as a defense. It cannot blame a coworker's negligence to escape liability. Those defenses, removed by Texas Labor Code § 406.033, remain off the table.
So the employer can't say "you were being careless." But it can now say "that third-party equipment rental company was also responsible." The distinction matters, and it's one a defense lawyer will exploit if they can.

### Why This Matters for Workers in Harris County and Beyond
Think about how construction sites in Houston actually work. On a typical job site in Harris County, say a commercial build in the Energy Corridor or a residential project near Katy, you might have a general contractor, multiple subcontractors, a staffing agency providing labor, and equipment owned by a rental company. Your direct employer might be a subcontractor with relatively thin assets.
Before this ruling, if that employer was a nonsubscriber and you got hurt because of dangerous site conditions they controlled, they couldn't point at the general contractor or the equipment company to dilute their fault. Now they can try.
For workers, that creates two new problems. First, your employer now has a litigation tool to reduce what it owes you, even if it was clearly responsible. Second, you and your attorney need to think more broadly from the start, identifying every potentially responsible party early, because the employer is now motivated to point at all of them.
This also changes settlement dynamics. Before the ruling, a nonsubscriber facing a clear liability case had fewer places to hide. Now defense counsel has a new argument to bring to mediation. That doesn't mean your case is weaker on the merits. It means the defense playbook got longer.

### The Silver Lining: Multiple Defendants Can Mean More Recovery
Here's the flip side that's easy to miss in the initial reaction to this ruling. If your employer designates a third party as responsible and the evidence actually supports it, that third party is now a viable defendant in your case too.
Say your employer points at an equipment manufacturer whose machine malfunctioned and caused your injury. Your attorney can now pursue both the employer and the manufacturer. If the jury assigns 60% fault to the employer and 40% to the manufacturer, you may be able to collect from both.
The key is acting fast. Under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code Chapter 33, a responsible third party designation triggers deadlines for the plaintiff to add them as a defendant. Miss that window and you might be limited in what you can recover from them. This is another reason why getting an attorney involved quickly after a workplace injury is so important, not just for preserving evidence, but for protecting your legal options as the litigation strategy develops.
The ruling cuts both ways. Your employer can use it to reduce its share of fault. You can use it to bring more defendants into the case and potentially increase the total pool of recovery.

### How Employers Will Use This. and How to Prepare for It
Defense attorneys for nonsubscribing employers started working this ruling into their strategy almost immediately after the April 2025 decision. Here's what that looks like in practice.
Early investigation into third parties. Employers and their insurers will start investigating potential third-party targets from day one: equipment manufacturers, property owners, general contractors, staffing agencies. They're looking for anyone they can plausibly point to.
Aggressive third-party designations. Expect defense lawyers to designate responsible third parties broadly, sometimes as a tactical move to create confusion at trial even when the third party's fault is marginal. The goal is to get the jury thinking about shared responsibility.
Pressure in settlement talks. A third-party designation gives the employer's insurer a talking point to justify a lower offer. They'll argue their client's proportionate share is reduced, so the settlement number should be too.
The counter to all of this is preparation. Document the scene of your accident before anything is cleaned up or repaired. Identify and preserve evidence related to any equipment, machinery, or conditions that contributed to your injury. Get witness information. And talk to a personal injury attorney who handles workplace injury cases before the employer's legal team has had weeks to build their narrative.

### The Statute of Limitations Still Applies. Don't Delay
Nothing about this ruling changed the deadline to file your lawsuit. Under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003, you generally have two years from the date of your injury to file a personal injury claim in Texas. That clock starts the day you're hurt, not the day you understand what happened, not the day you finish treatment.
Two years sounds like a lot. It goes fast. Medical treatment takes time. Evidence disappears. Witnesses move or forget details. And now, with third-party designation strategy in play from the earliest days of a case, you have less runway to wait before engaging an attorney.
If you were injured on a job site anywhere in the greater Houston area (Harris County, Fort Bend County, Montgomery County, Galveston County) and your employer opted out of workers' comp, the clock is running.

### Questions to Ask When You Talk to an Attorney
If you consult with a lawyer about a nonsubscriber workplace injury claim, here's what's worth discussing specifically in light of this ruling:
- Has the employer already designated any responsible third parties? If litigation has started or a claim has been filed, find out immediately.
- What third parties might legitimately share responsibility? A good attorney will investigate this independently, not just react to who the employer nominates.
- What's the deadline to add those third parties as defendants? Chapter 33 has procedural requirements, and missing them has consequences.
- How does this affect the valuation of my case? The answer depends on the facts, the identity of the third parties, and their assets or insurance coverage.
You can start that conversation with our team at no cost. Free case review here. we handle nonsubscriber workplace injury cases and we've been tracking this ruling since it came down.

### The Bigger Picture: Texas Still Protects Injured Workers, But You Have to Fight for It
Texas has always been an unusual state when it comes to workplace injury law. Opting out of workers' comp is legal here. The Legislature made a deliberate choice when it wrote those nonsubscriber protections into the Labor Code: if an employer was going to skip the no-fault system, it had to give up some defenses in exchange.
The East Texas Medical Center Athens decision doesn't eliminate those protections. Your employer still can't blame you. A coworker's negligence still can't be used against you. Those rights are intact.
What changed is that employers now have a new tool to distribute fault, and well-resourced employers with experienced defense counsel will use it. That's not a reason to give up on your claim. It's a reason to take it seriously from the start, move quickly, and work with an attorney who understands how things actually work after this ruling.
Texas workers deserve to know their rights. This ruling complicates the picture. It doesn't erase it.
This article provides general information about Texas law, not legal advice for your specific situation. Every case is different. If you've been injured in Houston or anywhere in Texas, talk with a licensed attorney about the facts of yours. Free case review here, or call (713) 842-9442.

### Common questions
On April 25, 2025, the Texas Supreme Court ruled that nonsubscribing employers — those that opted out of workers' compensation — can designate responsible third parties under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code Chapter 33. This allows them to ask a jury to assign some fault to outside parties like contractors or equipment makers. If the jury agrees, the employer's share of what it owes you can shrink by that percentage.

Those core protections were not changed by the 2025 ruling. What changed is that your employer can now point to unrelated third parties, such as an equipment manufacturer or a subcontractor, to reduce its share of fault.
The ruling gives defense attorneys a new argument to bring to mediation: that their client's proportionate share of fault is reduced because a third party also bears responsibility. This can be used to justify a lower settlement offer. However, the same third-party designation can open the door for your attorney to pursue additional defendants, potentially increasing the total pool of money available to you.
