## Texas Personal Injury Deadlines: The Clock Is Already Running
Source: https://nalawtx.com/blog/texas-personal-injury-deadlines-the-clock-is-already-running

Texas law gives most injury victims two years to file a lawsuit — but that window can shrink fast, and missing it usually ends your case forever. Here's what every Texan needs to know about these deadlines before it's too late.
By Vu Nguyen, Founder & Managing Partner · Updated May 13, 2026
Texas law gives most injury victims two years from the date of injury to file a lawsuit under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003. If a government entity is involved, you may need to give written notice within six months or even 90 days. Missing the deadline almost always ends your case permanently, no matter how strong your evidence is.
- Most Texas personal injury claims must be filed within two years of the injury date.
- Claims against government entities require formal written notice within six months — sometimes just 90 days.
- Negotiating with an insurer does NOT pause the two-year statute of limitations.
- For injured minors, the clock is generally paused until their 18th birthday, but evidence can still disappear.
You were hurt. Maybe it happened last week on I-45 near the South Loop. Maybe it was six months ago at a job site in Harris County. You've been focused on getting better, dealing with doctors, missing work, trying to hold things together. A lawsuit felt like a distant problem.
Here's the hard truth: while you were healing, a legal clock was ticking. In Texas, that clock has a hard stop. Once time runs out, it doesn't matter how serious your injuries are, how clearly the other party was at fault, or how strong your evidence is. The courthouse door closes.
This post explains the Texas statute of limitations for personal injury — what the deadline is, when it starts, and the situations where it runs differently than you'd expect.

### The Basic Rule: Two Years
For most personal injury cases in Texas, the deadline to file a lawsuit is two years from the date of the injury. This comes from Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003.
That two-year rule covers the most common injury claims: car accidents, truck accidents, slip-and-fall injuries, dog bites, and motorcycle crashes.
Two years sounds like plenty of time. It rarely is. Building a strong injury case takes months — tracking down witnesses, gathering medical records, retaining accident reconstruction experts, negotiating with insurance carriers. Attorneys who handle these cases routinely see people come in at month 22 or 23 with evidence that's stale and witnesses who've disappeared.
The two-year deadline isn't a goal line to sprint toward. It's the wall you never want to hit. The earlier you start, the stronger your position.

### When Does the Clock Actually Start?
Usually, the clock starts the day the injury happens. You were rear-ended on the Katy Freeway on March 1 — your two-year window opens March 1 and closes March 1, two years later.
But "when the clock starts" gets complicated in several common situations.

#### The Discovery Rule
Some injuries aren't obvious right away. A toxic exposure at work might not show up as a diagnosable condition for months or years. A defective medical device might cause harm that's misdiagnosed for a long time before the real cause is identified.
In those situations, Texas courts apply what's called the discovery rule. The clock doesn't start until you knew — or reasonably should have known — that you were injured and that someone else caused it. This is a narrow exception, and courts scrutinize it closely. It doesn't apply just because you didn't feel pain immediately after an accident.

#### Wrongful Death Cases
When an injury is fatal, the family's wrongful death claim runs on its own timeline. Under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003(b), the two-year clock for a wrongful death lawsuit starts on the date of death — not necessarily the date of the accident. If your family member was injured on January 1 and died from those injuries on February 15, the two-year clock for the wrongful death claim starts February 15.
The estate can also bring a survival claim — the claim the deceased person could have brought themselves. That clock runs from the date of injury.

#### When the Victim Is a Minor
If the injured person is under 18, the two-year statute of limitations is tolled — paused — until their 18th birthday. A child injured at age 10 generally has until age 20 to file. Texas law protects minors from losing their rights simply because their parents didn't act in time.
That said, evidence doesn't wait. Surveillance footage gets deleted. Witnesses move. Memories fade. Waiting until a child turns 18 to investigate is rarely a good strategy, even if the law permits it.

### Shorter Deadlines: When Two Years Is Too Long to Wait
The two-year rule is the default — but several categories of cases have shorter deadlines that catch people off guard.

#### Claims Against Government Entities
This one surprises a lot of people. If your injury involved a government entity — the City of Houston, Harris County, TxDOT, Houston Metro, a public school district — you face a dramatically shorter timeline.
Under the Texas Tort Claims Act, you typically must give the government entity formal written notice within six months of the incident before you can file suit. Some municipalities have local ordinances requiring notice even sooner — within 90 days. Miss that notice window and your claim can be dead before the two-year mark ever arrives.
Government entity claims come up more often than people expect. A pothole on a Houston city street that causes a crash. A defective traffic signal maintained by TxDOT on a stretch of US-59. A slip on a wet floor in a Harris County courthouse. If a government body had a role in your injury, check that shorter deadline immediately.

#### Injuries Involving Commercial Trucks
The two-year deadline applies to 18-wheeler and commercial truck accident claims just as it does to car accidents. But there's a practical problem: trucking companies and their insurers begin preserving — and sometimes disposing of — records almost immediately after a crash. Electronic logging device data, dashcam footage, and driver qualification files can be lost or overwritten within weeks if no legal hold is in place.
The legal deadline is two years. The practical deadline for preserving usable evidence is much shorter. An attorney can send a spoliation letter demanding document preservation within days of an accident — that option disappears if you wait a year and a half.

### Longer Deadlines: When the Clock Runs More Than Two Years
A few situations extend the standard window.

#### Legal Disability
Texas law tolls the statute of limitations if the injured person is under a "legal disability" at the time of the injury — which includes being a minor (discussed above) or being of unsound mind. The clock pauses while the disability continues and begins running again once it ends.

#### Defendant Absence from Texas
If the person who hurt you leaves Texas after the accident and before a lawsuit can be served, time spent outside the state may not count against the two-year window. This is a narrow, fact-specific exception — don't rely on it as a planning tool.

#### Fraud or Concealment
If the person or company responsible for your injury actively concealed their role — destroyed evidence, misrepresented facts — a court may toll the limitations period during the concealment. This requires proof and isn't guaranteed.

### What Happens If You Miss the Deadline
The other side files a motion to dismiss. The court grants it. Your case is over.
It doesn't matter that you have medical bills, lost wages, and documented pain. It doesn't matter that the other driver was texting on I-610. Once the statute of limitations expires, the defendant has an absolute defense. Courts virtually never make exceptions for people who simply didn't know about the deadline or ran out of time.
There are extremely rare situations — fraud, active concealment, legal disability — where a court might consider equitable tolling. But "I didn't know the deadline existed" is not one of them.
The statute of limitations isn't a technicality. It's the law. Missing it ends your case — period.

### Common Misconceptions That Get People in Trouble

#### "The insurance company is handling it — I don't need to worry about a lawsuit deadline."
This is one of the most dangerous assumptions injury victims make. An insurance claim and a lawsuit are two completely separate things. Negotiating with an adjuster does not pause the statute of limitations. Insurance companies know this. Some adjusters deliberately string out negotiations past the two-year mark, then deny the claim, knowing you've lost the ability to sue.
If you're still negotiating with an insurer and the two-year mark is approaching, you may need to file suit to protect your rights — even if you still hope to settle without going to trial.

#### "I signed a release, so the clock doesn't matter anymore."
If you've already signed a release of claims, the issue isn't the statute of limitations — it's whether that release is binding. Releases signed under pressure, without full understanding of your injuries, or before you knew the full extent of your damages deserve a close legal look. An attorney at our firm can review what you signed and explain your options.

#### "My injuries didn't seem bad at first, so I waited."
Soft-tissue injuries, traumatic brain injuries, and internal injuries sometimes don't fully manifest for days or weeks after an accident. The two-year clock doesn't care about your symptom timeline — it starts on the date of the accident. Don't wait to see how bad things get before you start the process.

### A Realistic Texas Timeline for a Personal Injury Claim
Here's roughly how the months break down after a serious injury in Texas:
- Months 1–3: Medical treatment, diagnosis, missing work. This is when most people are in survival mode, not thinking about lawsuits.
- Months 3–6: Ideally when you consult an attorney, gather evidence, and send insurance carriers written notice of your claim.
- Months 6–12: Medical records accumulate. Treatment continues. Your attorney begins building the case file — police reports, witness statements, expert opinions.
- Months 12–18: Demand package sent to insurance carrier. Negotiations begin.
- Months 18–22: If negotiations stall, your attorney files suit to protect the deadline. Discovery begins.
- Month 24: The hard stop. No lawsuit filed by this date means no lawsuit, ever.
That timeline leaves almost no margin for delay at the start. If you consult an attorney in month 18, you're working backward from a wall that's already visible.

### When to Call an Attorney — Honest Answer
If your injuries are minor and you've fully recovered, you may be able to handle an insurance claim on your own. But if any of the following are true, talk to an attorney as soon as possible:
- Your injuries required emergency treatment, surgery, or ongoing care
- You've missed work or expect to miss work in the future
- A government vehicle or government-maintained road was involved
- A commercial truck was involved
- The insurance company is offering a fast settlement
- You're not sure who was at fault — or multiple parties may share responsibility
- The injury was fatal
The consultation is free. Our practice areas cover car accidents, truck accidents, workplace injuries, slip-and-fall cases, and more — all on a contingency fee basis, meaning you owe nothing unless your case resolves in your favor.

### The Short Version
Texas personal injury law gives most people two years to file a lawsuit. That clock starts the day you're hurt. Government claims require written notice within six months — sometimes less. Missing the deadline ends your claim, no exceptions. The earlier you get an attorney involved, the more options you have.
If you were recently hurt — in Houston, Harris County, or anywhere in Texas — find out where you stand before you lose the option. Call us and get a straight answer about your specific situation and your actual deadline.

## What Every Houston Driver Must Know About Uninsured and Underinsured Motorist Coverage in Texas
Source: https://nalawtx.com/blog/texas-uninsured-motorist-coverage-what-houston-drivers-need

Roughly 1 in 7 Texas drivers carries no insurance at all. This post explains what UM/UIM coverage is, why so many Houston drivers accidentally waived it, and what your options are when an uninsured driver hits you.
By Vu Nguyen, Founder & Managing Partner · Updated May 18, 2026
Uninsured/underinsured motorist (UM/UIM) coverage pays your medical bills, lost wages, and other damages when the at-fault driver has no insurance or too little to cover your losses. Texas law requires insurers to offer it, but you must accept it in writing — many Houston drivers unknowingly signed it away. Check your declarations page now to see if you have it.
- Roughly 1 in 7 Texas drivers carries no insurance, making UM/UIM coverage especially important in Houston.
- You must sign a written rejection to waive UM/UIM — many drivers do this accidentally during signup.
- UM/UIM can cover medical bills, lost wages, pain and suffering, and future medical costs — not just ER visits.
- Texas's two-year filing deadline under § 16.003 applies to UM/UIM claims; missing it ends your recovery.
Picture this: you're stopped at the light at I-10 and Bunker Hill when a driver rear-ends you at highway speed and takes off. Or they stop, hand you an insurance card, and you find out three days later the policy lapsed six months ago. Your car is totaled. Your neck hurts. And the person who did this to you has nothing.
This isn't a hypothetical. It plays out in Harris County courts and hospital emergency rooms constantly. Texas has one of the highest uninsured driver rates in the country. Roughly 14% of drivers on the road have no coverage at all. In a metro area as large as Houston, that means hundreds of thousands of uninsured vehicles sharing the freeways with you every single day.
The insurance product designed to protect you in exactly this situation is called uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage, UM/UIM for short. Most drivers have no idea how it works, and many have quietly signed it away without realizing it. Here's what you need to know.

### What Is UM/UIM Coverage, Exactly?
Texas requires every driver to carry a minimum amount of liability insurance. Currently that's $30,000 per person for bodily injury under Texas Transportation Code requirements. That's the other driver's policy. It pays you when the other driver is at fault.
But what happens when the at-fault driver has no policy at all? Or their policy limit is $30,000 and your hospital bill from Memorial Hermann is $85,000? That's where UM/UIM coverage steps in.
Uninsured motorist (UM) coverage pays your medical bills, lost wages, and other damages when the at-fault driver has zero insurance, including hit-and-run crashes where the driver flees and can't be identified.
Underinsured motorist (UIM) coverage kicks in when the at-fault driver has insurance, but their policy limit is too low to cover your actual losses. If they carry $30,000 in liability and your damages are $120,000, UIM coverage can bridge that gap.
Both coverages come from your own insurance company. You're essentially buying a backstop policy that protects you from other people's bad decisions.

### Texas Law Requires Your Insurer to Offer It. Not to Give It to You
Here's where a lot of Houston drivers get blindsided. Under Texas Insurance Code § 1952.101, every auto insurer must offer UM/UIM coverage to every Texas policyholder. But the law doesn't require you to accept it.
To decline UM/UIM coverage, you have to sign a written rejection. That rejection form is often buried in a stack of paperwork when you're signing up for a new policy. Sometimes it's online, where it's one checkbox among dozens. Many drivers check the box without understanding they're giving up meaningful protection.
If you've never specifically thought about UM/UIM coverage, there's a real chance you declined it without knowing. Pull up your declarations page right now and look. If you don't see "UM" or "UIM" listed, you probably don't have it.
Insurers aren't required to explain what you're waiving. They're required to offer it and get your signature. That's it. The result: countless Houston drivers are out there every day believing they're covered, and they're not.

### Why This Matters More in Houston Than Almost Anywhere Else
Houston already carries the highest full-coverage auto insurance rates of any major Texas city. That makes cost pressure real. People look for ways to trim premiums, and UM/UIM is an easy target because the benefit isn't obvious until you actually need it.
At the same time, Houston's road conditions make that coverage more valuable here than most places. The city logged 301 traffic fatalities in 2024, the highest annual total on record. The corridors along US-59, I-45 South toward Galveston, and the I-610 loop see some of the state's highest crash densities. Hit-and-run crashes are a particular problem too: Harris County routinely ranks among Texas counties with the most hit-and-run incidents reported to TxDOT.
When a driver who hits you on the Southwest Freeway has no insurance and no assets, your UM coverage may be the only real source of recovery available to you. Without it, you're left pursuing a civil judgment against someone who likely has nothing collectible. That process costs time and money and often yields nothing.

### What UM/UIM Coverage Actually Pays For
People often assume UM/UIM is just for medical bills. It's more than that. Depending on your policy, UM/UIM coverage can compensate you for:
- Medical expenses. emergency room visits, surgery, physical therapy, follow-up care
- Lost wages. income you couldn't earn while recovering
- Pain and suffering. compensation for the physical and emotional toll of the injury
- Future medical costs. if your injuries require ongoing treatment
- Property damage. some policies include uninsured motorist property damage (UMPD) as a separate coverage
The coverage limits you carry determine the ceiling. If you bought a policy with $30,000 in UM coverage and your losses are $90,000, you're still exposed for the difference. This is why attorneys generally recommend purchasing UM/UIM limits that match or exceed your liability limits.

### Hit-and-Run Crashes: A Special Situation
Hit-and-run accidents are one of the most frustrating situations an injury victim faces. The driver who hurt you is gone. There may be no witnesses. Police may not find them.
Your UM coverage is specifically designed for this scenario. Under Texas law, a hit-and-run driver qualifies as an "uninsured motorist," meaning your own UM policy can respond even when you never identify who hit you.
There is one important catch. Most Texas UM policies require that the hit-and-run vehicle made physical contact with your vehicle. If someone cut you off and ran you into a barrier without touching your car, some insurers will dispute the claim. This is a known area of policy interpretation, and it's worth understanding before you need it.
If you were hit and the driver fled, call 911 immediately and get a police report, even if the damage looks minor. That report is often essential for a UM claim. Without it, your insurer has grounds to push back.
Witnesses matter too. If anyone saw the crash, get their name and phone number before they leave the scene. Dashcam footage, nearby surveillance cameras, and traffic cameras along Houston's managed lanes can all support your version of events.

### How UM/UIM Claims Actually Work. And Why They're Not Simple
Filing a UM/UIM claim means filing against your own insurer. That might sound straightforward. It often isn't.
Your insurance company has a financial interest in paying you as little as possible on a UM/UIM claim, just like any other insurer would. They may dispute the severity of your injuries, question whether the accident caused them, or argue that your medical treatment was excessive. They have adjusters and attorneys working these files. People whose job is claim management, not your recovery.
Texas does impose some protections. Under Texas Insurance Code § 542, insurers must acknowledge your claim promptly, investigate it in good faith, and pay valid claims within specific timeframes. Violations can result in penalty interest and attorney's fees under what's commonly called the Texas Prompt Payment of Claims Act. But those protections only help if you know to invoke them.
A few things UM/UIM claimants routinely underestimate:
- The recorded statement request. Your insurer may call shortly after the crash and ask for a recorded statement. You're generally not required to give one immediately, and what you say can be used to limit your claim. Talk to an attorney first if your injuries are serious.
- The early settlement offer. Some insurers move fast with a low offer before you know the full extent of your injuries. Accepting it typically closes your claim permanently.
- The two-year deadline. Under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003, personal injury claims in Texas generally must be filed within two years of the date of the accident. Miss that window and your claim is gone, including your UM/UIM claim.

### What to Do Right After an Accident With an Uninsured Driver
The steps you take in the first 48 hours shape everything that comes after. Here's what matters most:
- Call 911. Get a police report. This is non-negotiable if you think the other driver may be uninsured or if they flee the scene.
- See a doctor, that day or the next. Even if you feel okay, get evaluated. Soft tissue injuries from crashes often don't peak for 24-72 hours. A gap in medical treatment gives insurers ammunition to deny your claim.
- Document everything. Photos of the scene, your vehicle, your injuries. Screenshot the other driver's insurance card before they drive away. Note the plate number.
- Notify your own insurance company. You're required to report the accident under your policy terms. Do it, but stick to basic facts. You don't need to characterize fault or your injuries in detail at this stage.
- Don't sign anything from an adjuster until you understand what you're agreeing to.
If your injuries are significant, anything beyond minor soreness, talk with a Houston car accident attorney before giving a recorded statement to your own insurer. This isn't paranoia. It's practical. Once you've signed a release or given a statement that minimizes your injuries, it's very difficult to undo.

### Stacking: Can You Use Multiple UM/UIM Policies?
Texas allows something called "stacking" in limited circumstances, combining the UM/UIM limits from multiple policies to cover your losses. For example, if you have two vehicles on separate policies, you may be able to stack those coverages if one policy doesn't prohibit it.
This is genuinely complicated. Some policies have anti-stacking provisions. How stacking interacts with subrogation rights (the insurer's right to recover what it paid you from a third party) adds another layer. If you're in a situation where your losses may exceed your single-policy UM limit, an attorney can help you figure out whether stacking is available and what it would mean for your claim.

### Should You Buy More UM/UIM Coverage?
If you don't currently have UM/UIM on your policy, the honest answer is: you should seriously consider adding it. The premium difference is usually modest, often a few dollars a month, relative to the protection it provides.
At minimum, match your UM/UIM limits to your liability limits. If you carry $100,000 per person in liability, carry at least $100,000 in UM/UIM. Texas allows you to purchase UM/UIM limits up to the amount of your liability coverage.
Given what Houston roads look like, the uninsured driver rate, the crash volume, the hit-and-run problem, UM/UIM coverage is one of the few insurance products that actually earns its cost on a regular basis. Talk to your insurance agent about your current limits and get the specifics in writing.
This article provides general information about Texas law, not legal advice for your specific situation. Every case is different. If you've been injured in Houston or anywhere in Texas, talk with a licensed attorney about the facts of yours. Free case review here, or call (713) 842-9442.

### Watch: Uninsured Driver Hit You? What to Do Next

### Common questions
If you have UM coverage on your own policy, you can file a claim with your own insurer to cover medical bills, lost wages, and other damages. Without UM coverage, your main option is pursuing a civil judgment against the at-fault driver, which costs time and money and often yields nothing if that person has no assets.
Yes. Under Texas law, a hit-and-run driver qualifies as an 'uninsured motorist,' so your UM policy can respond even if you never identify who hit you. However, most Texas UM policies require that the hit-and-run vehicle made physical contact with your car. Getting a police report immediately after the crash is essential, as insurers can push back without one.
Your own insurer has a financial interest in paying as little as possible, so disputes over injury severity or medical treatment are common. Texas Insurance Code § 542 requires insurers to investigate in good faith and pay valid claims within specific timeframes, with penalty interest and attorney's fees possible for violations. ## Texas Wrongful Death Claims: Who Can Sue, What You Can Recover, and the Deadline You Cannot Miss
Source: https://nalawtx.com/blog/texas-wrongful-death-claims-who-can-sue-and-when

If someone you love was killed by another person's negligence, Texas law gives your family the right to seek compensation. But that right has strict limits on who can file and how long you have to act.
By Vu Nguyen, Founder & Managing Partner · Updated November 21, 2026
In Texas, the surviving spouse, children, and parents of someone killed by another's negligence can file a wrongful death claim under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 71.002. You have two years from the date of death to file under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003. Missing that deadline almost always means losing your right to sue.
- Only a surviving spouse, children, or parents have legal standing to file a Texas wrongful death claim.
- The two-year filing deadline is strict — courts routinely dismiss cases filed even one day late.
- If a government entity is involved, you may need to file a formal notice within six months.
- Texas's modified comparative fault rule reduces your recovery if your loved one was partly at fault.
Losing a family member to a preventable accident is devastating. Then come the bills, the calls from insurance adjusters, the funeral arrangements. Somewhere in the middle of all that grief, you start wondering whether your family has any legal recourse.
Texas wrongful death law exists for exactly this situation. It holds the people responsible for your loved one's death financially accountable. But it only works if you file the right claim, with the right people, before the clock runs out. This post walks you through how that works in plain language.

### What Is a Wrongful Death Claim in Texas?
A wrongful death claim is a civil lawsuit, separate from any criminal case, that your family files against whoever caused your loved one's death. You're not seeking to send anyone to prison. You're seeking compensation for what your family lost.
Texas created this legal right in the Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 71.002. The law says that when a person dies because of another party's "wrongful act, neglect, carelessness, unskillfulness, or default," surviving family members can sue.
That covers a wide range of situations: an 18-wheeler driver who ran a red light on I-10, a drunk driver who crossed the centerline on Highway 290, a negligent doctor, a dangerous property owner, a defective product manufacturer. The common thread is that someone else's failure, not an unavoidable accident, took your family member's life.
A wrongful death claim is not about revenge. It's about making sure your family doesn't bear the financial consequences of someone else's negligence alone.

### Who Has the Right to File Under Texas Law?
Texas law is specific about who can bring a wrongful death claim. Not every family member qualifies. Under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 71.004, only three categories of people have standing to sue:
- Surviving spouse. legally married at the time of death
- Children. biological or legally adopted; adult children qualify, not just minors
- Parents. biological or adoptive parents of the deceased
Siblings, grandparents, aunts, uncles, and other relatives do not have standing to file a wrongful death claim in Texas, no matter how close the relationship was. This surprises a lot of families.
The eligible family members can file together in one lawsuit, or they can file separately. If none of them files within three months of the death, the estate's executor or administrator can file on the family's behalf. But the surviving family members can block that by objecting.

#### What about unmarried partners?
Common-law marriage is recognized in Texas. If you and your partner lived together, agreed to be married, and held yourselves out publicly as a married couple, you may qualify as a surviving spouse even without a formal ceremony. This is fact-specific and worth discussing with an attorney quickly. The clock is already running.

#### What if the deceased was a child?
Parents can file a wrongful death claim when a child is killed. Texas law also allows a separate survival action (discussed below) that can be filed on behalf of the child's estate for pain and suffering the child experienced before death.

### The 2-Year Deadline. and Why It's Absolute
Texas gives families two years from the date of death to file a wrongful death lawsuit. This is the statute of limitations under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003.
Miss that deadline and you almost certainly lose your right to sue. It doesn't matter how strong your case is or how sympathetic your circumstances are. Courts routinely dismiss cases filed even one day late.
Two years sounds like a long time. It isn't. Here's why families run out of time:
- Grief makes it hard to think about legal action in the first weeks and months
- Investigations, especially in commercial truck crashes, take time to complete
- Families sometimes wait to see if the insurance company will "do the right thing" voluntarily (they rarely do)
- Finding the right attorney and building a case takes time
Starting early also matters for evidence. Truck companies are required to preserve driver logs, GPS data, and dash cam footage, but only if they receive a legal hold notice promptly. Waiting months can mean critical evidence is overwritten or destroyed.
The two-year clock starts on the date of death, not the date of the accident if they're different. An attorney can help you identify the exact date that governs your case.

#### Are there exceptions to the 2-year rule?
A few narrow situations can pause or extend the clock. If a government entity (like TxDOT or the City of Houston) is involved, you actually face a shorter deadline: a formal notice of claim must typically be filed within six months. If the defendant fraudulently concealed their role in the death, the clock may be extended. For minor beneficiaries, tolling rules may apply.
These exceptions are narrow and fact-specific. Don't assume they apply to your situation without talking to an attorney.

### What Damages Can Your Family Recover?
Texas wrongful death law lets surviving family members seek compensation for what they personally lost because of the death. These are called beneficiary damages. They're different from the deceased person's own losses, which fall under a separate survival action.

#### Beneficiary damages in a Texas wrongful death claim
- Loss of financial support. the income, benefits, and financial contributions your family member would have provided over their lifetime
- Loss of companionship and society. the love, comfort, companionship, and guidance the deceased provided; available to both spouses and children
- Loss of parental care and guidance. for children who lost a parent, the nurturing, advice, and emotional support they will no longer receive
- Mental anguish. the grief, sorrow, and mental suffering caused by the loss
- Loss of household services. the practical value of work the deceased performed around the home
- Medical expenses. costs incurred for care of the deceased between the accident and the death
- Funeral and burial expenses
Loss of companionship is one of the most significant, and most misunderstood, categories. It's not just about missing someone emotionally. Texas law recognizes that a spouse, a parent, a child provides real, tangible value to the people who loved them. That value can be presented to a jury.

#### The survival action. a separate but related claim
Under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 71.021, the deceased person's estate can also bring what's called a survival action. This claim captures what the deceased person experienced and lost before death: the pain and suffering they went through, any lost wages between the accident and their death, and property damage.
A survival action is filed by the estate's legal representative, not directly by the family members. In many cases, a wrongful death claim and a survival action are filed together. An attorney can help your family understand how both apply to your situation.

### How Fault Works in Texas. and Why It Matters
Texas uses a system called modified comparative fault. If your loved one was partially at fault for the accident that killed them, the damages your family can recover are reduced by that percentage of fault.
If a jury finds the deceased was 20% at fault, the family's total recovery is reduced by 20%. There's a hard cutoff: if the deceased is found more than 50% responsible, the family recovers nothing.
This is exactly why insurance companies spend so much time after a fatal crash trying to build a narrative that blames the victim. They're not doing it out of curiosity. They're doing it to reduce or eliminate what they have to pay.
An attorney's job, in part, is to gather the evidence that tells the accurate version of what happened: crash reconstruction reports, witness statements, black box data from commercial trucks, surveillance footage. Along I-45, US-59, and the Beltway, where a disproportionate number of Houston's fatal crashes occur, that evidence often exists and it can be obtained if you act quickly.

### When the Defendant Is a Company
Many Texas wrongful death cases don't just involve an individual driver. They involve corporations: trucking companies, employers, property owners, product manufacturers. This matters for several reasons.
Companies have professional claims teams and insurance carriers whose job is to limit payouts from day one. They will have investigators at the scene before most families even know what happened. They will pull electronic logging device data and internal records, and in some cases they will work to keep that data from ever reaching you.
Cases involving commercial 18-wheelers are a good example. Under federal regulations, trucking companies must maintain driver qualification files, hours-of-service logs, vehicle inspection records, and more. All of it is potentially relevant to a wrongful death claim. Getting a legal hold notice to the company immediately, before routine data purges happen, is critical.
Texas has seen several high-profile wrongful death suits involving commercial fleets in recent years. Families who waited to act faced real obstacles. Families who moved quickly had the evidence they needed.

### What Happens If There's Also a Criminal Case?
Sometimes the person who caused the death is criminally charged: DWI manslaughter, criminally negligent homicide, vehicular manslaughter. A civil wrongful death claim is completely separate from that criminal case.
You don't need a criminal conviction to win a civil wrongful death case. The standard of proof is different. In a criminal case, the prosecution must prove guilt "beyond a reasonable doubt." In a civil case, the standard is "preponderance of the evidence," basically, more likely than not.
A criminal acquittal does not bar your family from pursuing civil claims. The two tracks run independently. Talk to a civil attorney regardless of what is happening on the criminal side.

### Practical Steps for Families Right Now
If you've recently lost a family member and believe someone else's negligence was involved, here's what matters most in the near term.
Preserve everything you have. Photographs from the scene, the official accident report from HPD or the county sheriff's department, any communications from insurance adjusters, medical records, and anything the deceased shared about the incident before they died.
Do not give recorded statements to insurance adjusters. Adjusters for the at-fault party are not on your side. Anything you say can be used to assign blame to your loved one and reduce what you can recover. You are not required to give them a statement.
Talk to a Texas wrongful death lawyer before you sign anything. Releases, settlement offers, and authorization forms from insurance companies can permanently affect your family's rights. Once you sign, it's very difficult to undo.
Don't wait to see if the insurance company will offer something fair. They may make an early offer. Early offers are almost always low, sometimes dramatically so. They know your family is grieving and may not know the full value of what you've lost. An attorney can evaluate whether any offer is reasonable.
Our attorneys handle commercial truck accident and car accident wrongful death cases across Harris County, Fort Bend County, Montgomery County, and the surrounding Houston area. If you have questions about whether your family has a claim, a free case review costs you nothing and tells you where you stand.
This article provides general information about Texas law, not legal advice for your specific situation. Every case is different. If you've been injured in Houston or anywhere in Texas, talk with a licensed attorney about the facts of yours. Free case review here, or call (713) 842-9442.

### Common questions
Under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 71.004, only the surviving spouse, biological or adopted children, and biological or adoptive parents can file a wrongful death claim. Siblings, grandparents, and other relatives do not have standing, no matter how close the relationship was. If none of the eligible family members files within three months of the death, the estate's executor or administrator may file on the family's behalf.
Texas law gives you two years from the date of death to file a wrongful death lawsuit under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003. Missing this deadline almost certainly means losing your right to sue, regardless of how strong your case is. If a government entity like TxDOT is involved, the deadline can be even shorter, requiring a formal notice of claim typically within six months.
Your family may seek compensation for loss of financial support, loss of companionship and society, loss of parental care and guidance, mental anguish, loss of household services, medical expenses incurred before death, and funeral and burial expenses. These are damages for what your family personally lost. A separate survival action under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 71.021 can also recover for the deceased person's own pain, suffering, and lost wages before death.
No. A civil wrongful death claim is completely separate from any criminal case. You do not need a criminal conviction to win a civil case because the standard of proof is lower — 'preponderance of the evidence' rather than 'beyond a reasonable doubt.' A criminal acquittal does not prevent your family from pursuing a civil wrongful death claim.

## Texas's 51% Fault Rule: How It Can Reduce — or Eliminate — Your Recovery
Source: https://nalawtx.com/blog/texass-51-fault-rule-how-it-can-reduce-or-eliminate-your

Texas law lets injured people share some of the blame and still recover. But once you cross the 51% line, you walk away with nothing. Here's how the rule actually works — and why insurance adjusters love it.
By Vu Nguyen, Founder & Managing Partner · Updated May 13, 2026
Picture this: you're stopped at the light where I-10 meets Blalock Road. Someone blows the red and T-bones your driver's door. Clear-cut case, right? Then the other driver's insurance company calls and says you were "partially responsible" because your brake light was out. Suddenly a case that felt simple has a number attached to it — your percentage of fault.
That number matters enormously under Texas law. It can cut your recovery by a third, by half, or — past a certain threshold — down to zero. This is the Texas comparative fault rule, and understanding it is one of the most practical things you can do after any accident.

### The Basic Idea: You Can Be Partly at Fault and Still Recover
Texas uses a system called modified comparative fault. The rule lives in the Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 33.001. In plain terms: if you were hurt partly because of your own actions, your compensation gets reduced by your share of the blame — but only as long as that share stays below 51%.
So if a jury decides your damages are $100,000 and you were 20% at fault, you collect $80,000. Simple subtraction. Your fault percentage comes right off the top.
But if that same jury finds you were 51% or more responsible? Under Texas law, you recover nothing. Zero. The 51% threshold is a hard cutoff — not a sliding scale that keeps going.
The 51% rule is a cliff, not a slope. At 50% fault, you still recover half your damages. At 51%, you get nothing.

### How Fault Percentages Get Decided
In a trial, the jury gets a special verdict form — called a charge — asking them to assign percentages to every party involved. Those percentages must add up to 100%. The jury weighs the evidence: police reports, witness statements, dashcam footage, accident reconstruction testimony, and medical records, along with how each person's actions contributed to the crash.
Most cases never reach a jury. They settle. But the same math happens in the background during every settlement negotiation. Both sides know what a jury might decide, and they haggle from there.
That's why the insurance adjuster's first move after a Houston accident is often to dig for anything that makes you look partly responsible. A text on your phone two minutes before impact. A medication listed in your medical records. A lane change that happened seconds before the other car hit you. Any of those details can move your fault percentage up — and your payout down.

### A Real-World Example of the Math
Say you're driving on the Katy Freeway during rush hour. A driver merges without looking and clips your front bumper. Your car spins and hits the barrier. You end up with a broken arm, three months of physical therapy, and $15,000 in medical bills — plus eight weeks out of work.
Your total damages — medical costs, lost income, pain and suffering — come to $90,000.
Now the other driver's insurer argues you were following too closely, and a jury assigns you 30% of the fault.
- Total damages: $90,000
- Your fault: 30%
- Reduction: $27,000
- What you actually recover: $63,000
Still meaningful money. But if that same jury bumped your fault to 51%, you'd collect nothing on a $90,000 injury.

### Why Insurance Adjusters Push This Rule Hard
Insurance companies have one financial goal: pay out as little as possible on every claim. The Texas comparative fault rule is one of their sharpest tools for doing that.
When an adjuster calls you — often within hours of your accident — they're not checking on your well-being. They're building a file. Every word you say gets recorded and reviewed for anything that suggests you share responsibility.
"I didn't see them coming." That could suggest you weren't paying attention. "I was running a little late." That hints you might have been speeding. "I probably should have slowed down sooner." That one speaks for itself.
You aren't required to give a recorded statement to the other driver's insurance company. That's worth knowing before you pick up that call. If you've already given one, an attorney can sometimes work to limit how it's used — but the earlier you get advice, the more options you have.
Anything you say to an insurance adjuster can and will be used to raise your fault percentage. That's not paranoia — it's how the system works.

### Multiple Defendants: How Fault Gets Split Three Ways (or More)
Sometimes more than two parties contributed to a crash. A truck blows a stop sign, you swerve to avoid it, and a third car rear-ends you in the chaos. Now there are three parties — potentially all carrying some fault.
Under Texas's modified comparative fault framework, fault can be distributed across every responsible party. If the truck driver is 60% at fault, the third driver is 25%, and you're assigned 15%, you'd recover 85% of your total damages (100% minus your 15% share).
Texas also follows a rule called proportionate responsibility — meaning each defendant generally pays only their own share. So if the truck driver is judgment-proof (no money, no insurance), collecting your 60% from them may be difficult even if it's legally owed. An attorney can help you think through that situation, including whether other coverage might apply.

### What Counts as "Fault" Under Texas Law
Fault isn't just about who caused the initial collision. Texas courts look at whether each person acted as a reasonably careful person would have in the same situation — what lawyers call the negligence standard.
Common factors weighed against injured plaintiffs in Houston-area cases:
- Speeding, even slightly over the limit
- Failing to wear a seatbelt (though Texas limits how this affects damages)
- Distracted driving — phone use, adjusting the radio, eating
- Following too closely on congested Houston freeways like the 610 Loop or Highway 290
- Jaywalking or crossing mid-block as a pedestrian
- Failing to signal a lane change
- Pre-existing conditions that made your injuries worse (this affects the damages analysis more than fault, but it shows up)
Some of these feel minor. But minor can mean 10% or 15% added to your fault percentage — and that's real money off your recovery.

### How to Protect Your Fault Percentage After an Accident
You can't undo what happened on the road. But what you do in the hours and days after an accident shapes how fault gets assigned — and how much of your damages you keep.

#### Get the police report and read it carefully
Houston Police Department and Harris County Sheriff's Office crash reports aren't legally binding on a jury, but they carry weight. If the officer noted contributing factors — following distance, cell phone use, speed — those details will show up in your fault analysis. If anything in the report is wrong, you have a window to request a supplement or correction. Don't let errors sit.

#### Document the scene yourself
Photos and video from your phone create a record the other side can't easily dispute. Capture skid marks, road conditions, traffic signals, weather, and the position of both vehicles before anything moves. If there are witnesses, get their names and phone numbers on the spot.

#### See a doctor that day
Delayed medical care creates two problems. First, it may worsen your injuries. Second, a gap between the accident and your first doctor visit gives the defense an argument that you weren't really hurt — or that something else caused your injuries. Memorial Hermann, UTHealth, and the Harris Health system all have trauma centers that can document acute injuries right away.

#### Watch what you say — everywhere
This includes social media. A post saying you "feel fine" or showing you at a family event two weeks after an accident can become evidence used to challenge the severity of your injuries. It sounds extreme, but it happens in Harris County courtrooms regularly.

#### Talk to an attorney before you take a settlement offer
Once you accept a settlement and sign a release, you typically can't go back. If the offer is based on an inflated fault percentage — one the insurer built by cherry-picking your statements — you may be leaving significant money behind. A car accident attorney can evaluate the fault analysis and push back if it's off.

### The 51% Cutoff in Practice: Who Decides?
In a lawsuit, the jury decides. But in a settlement — which is how most Texas injury cases resolve — fault percentages are negotiated. The insurer puts a number on the table. Your attorney counters with evidence. Both sides go back and forth until they agree or the case goes to trial.
The practical implication: a fault percentage isn't handed down from on high. It's argued. Evidence, documentation, and how your story is told all affect where that number lands. That's not a legal abstraction — it's the difference between a fair recovery and walking away empty-handed.
If you're handling a claim on your own, the adjuster knows this law better than you do and negotiates dozens of claims every week. That's a real information gap. It doesn't mean you need an attorney for every fender-bender — but for anything involving real injury or a disputed fault split, having someone who knows how this math works can change the outcome significantly.

### A Few Things This Rule Does Not Apply To
Texas's comparative fault framework covers most civil injury claims — car accidents, slip-and-fall cases, premises liability. But a few situations work differently:
Workers' compensation claims in Texas follow a separate system entirely. Your fault as an employee generally doesn't bar or reduce your workers' comp benefits.
Product liability cases can involve comparative fault, but the analysis gets more complex when a defective product contributed to the injury alongside someone's negligence.
Wrongful death claims in Texas follow the same proportionate responsibility rules — but the people bringing the claim are the deceased's family members, not the person who was hurt, so the fault analysis focuses on the decedent's conduct.
If your situation is more complicated than a standard two-car crash, an attorney can walk through which rules apply to your specific facts. Our FAQ page covers some common scenarios, or you can request a free case review directly.

### The Short Version
Texas gives you a fair shot at recovery even if you weren't perfect. You can be 50% at fault and still collect half your damages. But that 51% threshold is real and unforgiving — cross it, and Texas law says you collect nothing.
Insurance companies know this rule cold. They use it to push fault percentages up and payouts down. Your job — starting at the scene — is to protect the factual record so that nobody assigns you more blame than you actually deserve.
If you've been hurt in a crash in Houston, Harris County, or anywhere else in Texas and you're hearing that you were "partly at fault," that claim deserves a hard look before you accept it.

## Texas's New 2026 Autonomous Vehicle Law: What Happens When a Driverless Car Injures You in Houston?
Source: https://nalawtx.com/blog/texass-new-2026-av-law-driverless-car-accident-liability

A new Texas law took effect May 28, 2026, putting the TxDMV in charge of authorizing driverless vehicles statewide and reshaping who you can hold responsible when one of those vehicles causes a crash.
By Vu Nguyen, Founder & Managing Partner · Updated November 21, 2026
A new Texas law effective May 28, 2026, puts the TxDMV in charge of authorizing driverless vehicles and makes the company operating the autonomous vehicle legally responsible in the role a driver would otherwise occupy. Depending on what caused the crash, the AV operator, vehicle manufacturer, or software developer may all be liable. Acting quickly to preserve vehicle data is critical.
- The 2026 Texas law makes the TxDMV-authorized AV operator legally responsible in place of a human driver.
- Autonomous vehicles record massive amounts of data — a litigation hold letter must be sent fast, sometimes within days.
- Multiple parties — operator, manufacturer, software developer — can be liable depending on what caused the crash.
- Texas's personal injury statute of limitations is generally two years under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003.
Imagine you're stopped at the light on Westheimer at Beltway 8. A delivery van with no driver behind the wheel rolls through the intersection and T-bones your car. You're hurt. The van belongs to a tech company. There's no human driver to point to. Who do you call? Who pays your medical bills?
That scenario is no longer hypothetical in Houston. Texas leads the nation in commercial autonomous vehicle miles traveled, and driverless vehicles are already running on Houston-area roads: freight corridors along I-10, package deliveries in the Heights, passenger shuttles near the Texas Medical Center. With the new 2026 AV law now in effect, the rules around liability for these crashes just changed. Here's what you need to know if you're the one who got hurt.

### What the 2026 Texas AV Law Actually Does
Before May 28, 2026, Texas had a patchwork approach to autonomous vehicles. The Texas Transportation Code permitted AVs on public roads under certain conditions, but no single agency had clear authority to authorize or regulate commercial driverless operations statewide.
The 2026 law changes that. It gives the Texas Department of Motor Vehicles (TxDMV) explicit authority to issue operating authorizations for fully autonomous vehicles. Companies that want to run driverless vehicles commercially in Texas now have to apply, demonstrate safety compliance, and maintain authorization from TxDMV. Lose that authorization and they can't legally operate.
That regulatory structure matters for injury victims. When a company holds a state authorization to run a driverless vehicle on public roads, it has accepted a formal set of responsibilities. That authorization paper trail becomes important evidence in any crash investigation.

### Who Is Legally Responsible When an AV Hits You?
This is the question most injured people ask first. It's also the most complicated one, because there's rarely a single clean answer.
In a traditional car accident, you identify the negligent driver. With an autonomous vehicle, the "driver" is software, and behind that software is a web of potential defendants. Texas courts and injury attorneys are already working through these questions. Several parties can be on the hook depending on what caused the crash.

#### The AV company (the "operator")
Under Texas law, the entity that deploys the AV (the company that holds the TxDMV authorization) is treated as the operator. Texas Transportation Code provisions address this directly: when no human is in the driver's seat, the company operating the automated driving system steps into the legal role that a driver would otherwise occupy. That means the company can be liable for crashes caused by the system's failures the same way a negligent driver would be liable for theirs.
This is a significant shift from older vehicle accident law. The company can't simply point to the software and walk away.

#### The vehicle manufacturer
If the crash happened because of a defect in the vehicle itself. faulty sensors, brake failure, a hardware problem. the manufacturer may face a product liability claim. Product liability in Texas doesn't require proving the manufacturer was careless. You have to show the product was defective and that the defect caused your injury. Under Texas law, that can include design defects, manufacturing defects, or failure to warn.

#### The software developer
AV technology sometimes involves separate companies: one that makes the vehicle, another that writes the autonomous driving software. If the crash traces back to a software decision (the system misread a stop sign, failed to detect a pedestrian, or made a faulty lane-change calculation), the software developer could be a separate defendant.

#### A human driver in the mix
Many crashes don't involve a fully autonomous vehicle operating alone. Semi-autonomous systems, where a human is still required to monitor and take over, create a murkier situation. If the human driver failed to intervene when the system gave a warning, that driver's negligence re-enters the picture. Texas uses modified comparative fault : your recovery is reduced by your share of the blame, and you're barred from recovering anything if you're more than 50% at fault. In crashes involving partial automation, sorting out who was responsible for what, and when, requires detailed data analysis.
When an AV is involved, there are more potential defendants. More defendants means more insurance policies, more corporate lawyers, and more complexity. The flip side: more avenues to pursue full compensation for your injuries.

### The Data Black Box: Your Best Evidence
Autonomous vehicles generate an enormous amount of data. Every second the system is running, it's recording: sensor readings, speed, steering inputs, system alerts, camera footage, the state of every software module. That data is the equivalent of a dashcam, an event data recorder, and an expert witness rolled into one, captured automatically on every trip.
That data is also in the possession of the company that hurt you. They have lawyers. They know what the data shows.
One of the most critical steps after an AV crash is sending what's called a litigation hold letter. It's a formal legal demand that the company preserve all data related to the incident. Without it, companies can argue that data was deleted through routine processes. With it, destroying evidence after notice exposes them to serious legal consequences.
This isn't something to try to do yourself. An attorney needs to send that letter fast, sometimes within days of the crash, before data retention cycles wipe the records.

### Houston Is Ground Zero for This New Reality
Texas isn't just experimenting with autonomous vehicles. It's one of the leading commercial AV markets in the country. Houston's flat terrain, mild winters, and dense freight corridors along I-45, I-10, and US-290 make it attractive for AV operators. Autonomous long-haul trucks running between Houston and Dallas have been in commercial operation for years. Driverless delivery vehicles have been spotted in Midtown, Montrose, and near Hobby Airport.
Harris County roads are also some of the most dangerous in the state. When you combine high AV activity with heavy traffic and aggressive driving conditions, crashes involving autonomous systems are going to happen. In Houston, they already have.
The Harris County District Clerk's office and the Southern District of Texas federal court in Houston will likely see the first wave of significant AV injury litigation in this state. The legal frameworks are still forming. That cuts both ways: the law is unsettled, which creates uncertainty, but it also means there are no unfavorable precedents locked in yet for injured plaintiffs.

### What to Do Right After an AV Crash
The steps after an autonomous vehicle crash are similar to any serious accident, with a few additions specific to AV cases.
Call 911 and get medical attention. Your health comes first. If you're injured, go by ambulance to Ben Taub, Memorial Hermann, or the nearest trauma center. Don't refuse treatment at the scene because you feel okay. AV crash investigations are complex, and your documented medical records are the foundation of any future claim.
Document everything at the scene. Photograph the vehicle. Get photos of its markings, company name, any visible sensor hardware (cameras, LIDAR units on the roof or bumpers), and license plates. If there's an operator or safety monitor nearby, get their name and employer. Note the exact location, time, and direction the vehicle was traveling.
Get the police report. Officers responding to the crash in Houston will file a report with HPD or the Harris County Sheriff's Office. That report should identify the vehicle as autonomous and note the operating company. If the officer doesn't flag it as an AV, that's something your attorney can address later.
Don't talk to the company's representatives. AV companies often deploy incident response teams quickly after crashes. They may approach you at the scene or call within hours. They are not there to help you. Refer them to your attorney.
Contact an attorney fast. The data preservation issue alone makes speed critical. Beyond that, Texas's statute of limitations for personal injury claims is generally two years from the date of injury under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003. Two years sounds like a long time until you're dealing with an injury, medical treatment, and a large corporation's legal team all at once.
The two-year clock is real. But the data preservation window is even shorter. If an AV hit you, days matter. Not just months.

### What the Insurance Picture Looks Like
Under the 2026 Texas AV law, companies seeking TxDMV authorization must demonstrate financial responsibility, meaning they need to carry insurance or meet self-insurance requirements. The specific minimums are set through the authorization process, and commercial AV operators are typically required to carry substantially higher limits than a standard personal auto policy.
That sounds like good news, and it is, in theory. In practice, large corporations with large policies also have large legal departments whose job is to minimize what gets paid out. Expect the same insurance tactics you'd see in any serious crash: early contact, requests for recorded statements, lowball initial offers, and delays. The scale is just bigger.
One important difference from a standard car crash: there's no individual driver whose personal auto insurance is the primary policy. The corporate insurer steps in directly. Negotiations happen at a corporate level from day one, which is another reason having an attorney early changes the dynamic significantly. You can read more about how car accident claims work and what to expect from the insurance process.

### What About Semi-Autonomous Vehicles?
Not every AV crash involves a fully driverless vehicle. Many vehicles on Houston roads right now have partial automation: Tesla's Autopilot, GM's Super Cruise, Ford's BlueCruise, and similar systems. These systems assist the driver but still require human supervision. They are not covered the same way under the 2026 law, which focuses on vehicles operating without any human driver required.
If a semi-autonomous system was engaged when a crash happened, the liability analysis gets more layered. The human driver behind the wheel still has legal responsibilities. But if the system behaved in a way that contributed to the crash (sudden unexpected braking, phantom steering correction, failure to detect a vehicle in the lane), the manufacturer's product liability exposure comes into play alongside the driver's negligence.
These cases require pulling the vehicle's onboard data, often through a subpoena or formal discovery process, to establish what the system was doing at the moment of impact. That doesn't happen automatically. It requires legal action to compel.

### The Bigger Picture: Texas Is Making the Rules in Real Time
Texas made a deliberate choice to be a permissive state for autonomous vehicles. The 2026 law is part of a longer pattern: Texas was one of the first states to allow AV testing without a human safety driver, and state leadership has consistently signaled that it wants AV companies operating here.
That's not inherently bad. The technology has real safety potential, and much of the innovation in this space is happening because Texas gave it room to develop. But permissive regulation also means the full consequences of accidents involving these systems are still being sorted out in courts and legislatures.
For injured people, the honest answer is: AV accident cases are harder than standard car accident cases. There are more defendants, more data, more lawyers on the other side, and less settled precedent to guide expectations. That doesn't mean they're unwinnable. It means they require attorneys who understand both personal injury law and the specific technical and regulatory layers these cases involve.
If you've been hurt by an autonomous or semi-autonomous vehicle anywhere in the Houston area, whether on Loop 610, in the Energy Corridor, in Katy, or on the Ship Channel freight corridors, the same fundamental principle applies as in any injury case: the company whose vehicle hurt you should be accountable for the harm they caused. The 2026 law creates a clearer framework for establishing that accountability. Use it.

### Common questions
Under the 2026 Texas AV law, the company that holds the TxDMV authorization to operate the driverless vehicle steps into the legal role a driver would normally occupy. Depending on what caused the crash, the vehicle manufacturer or software developer may also be liable. There is rarely one single defendant in these cases.
Autonomous vehicles continuously record sensor readings, speed, steering inputs, system alerts, and camera footage. That data is held by the company whose vehicle hurt you, so an attorney needs to send a litigation hold letter quickly — sometimes within days — before routine data deletion cycles wipe the records.

Semi-autonomous systems like Tesla Autopilot still require human supervision, so the human driver retains legal responsibilities. However, if the system's behavior contributed to the crash, the manufacturer's product liability exposure may still apply alongside the driver's negligence.
Texas's statute of limitations for personal injury claims is generally two years from the date of injury under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003. However, the window to preserve critical vehicle data is far shorter, making it important to contact an attorney as quickly as possible after the crash.

## The First 48 Hours After a Texas Car Wreck — What You Do Now Matters Later
Source: https://nalawtx.com/blog/the-first-48-hours-after-a-texas-car-wreck-what-you-do-now

The steps you take in the two days after a crash can protect your health, preserve your legal rights, and keep the insurance company from using your own words against you. Here's a clear, honest rundown of what to do — and what to avoid.
By Vu Nguyen, Founder & Managing Partner · Updated May 12, 2026
The steps you take in the first 48 hours after a Texas car wreck can protect your health and preserve your legal rights. Document the scene thoroughly, get medical attention even if you feel fine, and be careful what you say to insurance adjusters before you fully understand your situation.
- Get a police report at the scene — it's an official record that's hard to dispute later.
- See a doctor the same day, even if you feel okay; some injuries take 24–72 hours to appear.
- You are not required to give a recorded statement to the other driver's insurance company.
- Texas law gives most crash victims two years to file a lawsuit under Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003.
You just got hit. Your hands are shaking. The airbags may have gone off. Strangers are slowing down to look. Your first instinct is probably to figure out if everyone's okay — and then, a few minutes later, to panic about what happens next.
That moment of confusion is exactly when mistakes get made. Not because you're careless — because nobody tells you what's actually important until it's too late. This post walks you through it, step by step, from the scene of the crash through the next 48 hours.

### Right at the Scene: Don't Skip These Steps
The scene clears fast. Police write their report, tow trucks arrive, everyone goes home. Once that happens, a lot of the best evidence is gone. So while you're still there, do these things.
Call 911. Even if the other driver says "let's just exchange info and skip the cops." Even if the damage looks minor. A police report is an official record of what happened, who was there, and what was observed. It's much harder to dispute later. In Harris County, Houston Police Department or the Harris County Sheriff's Office will respond depending on where the crash happened — make sure an officer actually files a report before you leave.
Don't move your car unless you have to. If your vehicle is blocking traffic or creating a safety hazard, move it to the shoulder. Otherwise, leave it where it is. The position of the cars tells a story about how the crash happened. Once you move them, that story changes.
Take photos — a lot of them. Every vehicle, every angle. Skid marks. Debris on the road. Traffic signals. Street signs. The intersection itself. Your injuries, even if they look minor right now. Your phone's camera is good enough. Shoot more than you think you need.
Get the other driver's information. Name, phone number, license plate, driver's license number, insurance company, and policy number. If there are passengers in their car, get their names too. If there are witnesses — people who saw it happen from the sidewalk or another vehicle — ask for their contact information before they walk away.
Watch what you say. Don't apologize. Don't speculate about fault. Don't say "I didn't see you" or "I was going too fast." These statements can be used against you later, even when you're not actually at fault. You can be polite without narrating what happened.

### Get Medical Attention — Even If You Feel Fine
This is the step most people skip, and it's often the most damaging mistake they make.
Adrenaline is a powerful thing. In the minutes and hours after a crash, your body is flooded with it. You may feel okay — maybe even fine — and then wake up the next morning barely able to turn your neck. Whiplash, soft-tissue injuries, and even some traumatic brain injuries don't show up immediately. Symptoms can take 24 to 72 hours to fully emerge.
A gap in medical care — even a few days — gives the insurance company a reason to argue your injuries weren't caused by the crash. Don't give them that opening.
If you have any pain, dizziness, headache, or stiffness after the wreck, go to the emergency room or an urgent care clinic the same day. In Houston, Ben Taub General Hospital and Memorial Hermann operate major trauma centers. If it's not an emergency, at minimum call your doctor and get an appointment within 24 hours.
At the appointment, be specific. Tell the doctor exactly where it hurts, when it started, and that it happened in a car accident. This creates a documented medical record linking your injuries to the crash. That documentation matters — both for your health and for any claim you file.

### The Insurance Company Will Call. Here's What to Know Before They Do.
Within hours of a crash — sometimes the same afternoon — you may get a call from an insurance adjuster. It might be your own insurance company. It might be the other driver's. Either way, the call has a purpose: gather information that helps the insurance company manage what they pay out.
Adjusters are trained at this. They're not villains, but they're not on your side either. A few things to keep in mind:
You are not required to give a recorded statement to the other driver's insurance company. They will often ask, and they may imply it's required or that they can't process your claim without it. That's not accurate under Texas law. You can decline politely.
With your own insurance company, the situation is more nuanced. Your policy likely has a cooperation clause that requires you to participate in their investigation. Even so, you have the right to be represented before you give any recorded statement. If you've hired an attorney, the attorney handles that communication for you.
Don't accept a quick settlement offer. Early offers — especially ones that arrive before you've finished treating — often don't account for ongoing medical costs, lost wages, or long-term impact. Once you sign a release, that's typically final. You can't go back for more if your injuries turn out to be worse than they looked.
If you're unsure how to handle the insurance call, our FAQ page covers common questions about adjusters and recorded statements in plain English.

### Gather and Preserve Your Evidence
The 48 hours after a crash are a window. Evidence fades, memories blur, witnesses become harder to find. Use the time you have.
Get a copy of the police report. In Houston, you can request HPD crash reports through the Texas Department of Transportation's TxDOT crash records portal or directly through HPD. The report number should be on the card the officer hands you at the scene. Review it carefully — errors happen, and they can affect how fault is assigned.
Write down what happened while it's fresh. Not for anyone else — just for yourself. Date and time, direction you were traveling, weather conditions, what you saw before impact, what the other driver said at the scene. Details you take for granted right now are hard to reconstruct six months later.
Save everything related to the crash. Medical bills, prescription receipts, estimates for vehicle repair, any correspondence from insurance companies. If you miss work because of your injuries, keep a record of the days and the wages lost. Create a folder — digital or physical — and put everything in it.
Don't post about the crash on social media. Photos, status updates, even a vague "had a rough week" — insurance companies and opposing attorneys do look at social media. Anything you post can potentially be used to contradict your account of the crash or your injuries.

### Understand Texas Law on Fault and Deadlines
Texas uses a system called modified comparative fault — basically, if you're partly to blame for a crash, Texas law reduces what you can recover by your percentage of fault. If you're found to be 51% or more at fault, you can't recover anything at all. This is spelled out in the Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 33.001.
Why does this matter in the first 48 hours? Because fault is built from evidence, and evidence disappears fast. The more you document now — photos, witness contacts, your own written account — the more accurately fault can be assessed later.
The other deadline you need to know: Texas gives most car accident victims two years from the date of the crash to file a personal injury lawsuit. This deadline comes from Texas Civil Practice & Remedies Code § 16.003. Two years sounds like a long time. It's not — building a case takes months, and waiting too long limits your options.
Two years feels distant when you're focused on healing. But attorneys need time to investigate, gather records, and negotiate. Starting the conversation early costs you nothing.

### When Should You Call an Attorney?
Not every crash requires an attorney. A minor fender-bender with no injuries, clear fault, and a straightforward insurance process might resolve fine on its own.
But in these situations, you should seriously consider talking to one:
- You or anyone in your car was injured — even if it seems minor right now
- The other driver was uninsured or underinsured
- Fault is disputed — the other driver is blaming you, or the story is complicated
- A commercial vehicle (18-wheeler, delivery truck, rideshare) was involved
- The insurance company has already made a settlement offer
- You're being asked for a recorded statement
A consultation costs you nothing. Most car accident attorneys in Texas, including our firm, work on contingency — meaning you pay nothing unless your case resolves in your favor. So there's no financial risk in at least having the conversation.
The call you make in the first 48 hours is not a commitment. It's information. And information right now, before you've signed anything or said the wrong thing to an adjuster, is worth a lot.

### A Practical Hour-by-Hour Summary
If you're overwhelmed and just want a quick reference:
At the scene: Call 911. Stay calm. Document everything with your phone. Get the other driver's information and any witness contacts. Don't apologize or speculate about fault.
Within hours: Seek medical attention — ER, urgent care, or your doctor — even if you feel okay. Notify your own insurance company that a crash occurred (but don't give a recorded statement yet). Write down everything you remember about how the crash happened.
Within 24 hours: Request a copy of the police report. Start saving all documents related to the crash. If the other driver's insurance company calls, you can acknowledge the call and tell them you'll be in touch — you don't have to answer questions on the spot.
Within 48 hours: Follow up with your doctor if your symptoms have changed or worsened. Consider a free consultation with an injury attorney, especially if you were injured or fault is in dispute. Avoid posting about the crash online.

Call 911 and make sure an officer files a report before you leave the scene. Take photos of every vehicle, skid marks, debris, and your injuries. Collect the other driver's insurance and license information, and get contact details from any witnesses.
